11/A11  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 25 concepts)
  Q Why can giving a user more control over movement in a virtual world reduce their risk of cybersickness?  [11/S1/F1, 8/S2/F0; control over motion, presence, cybersickness, virtual world]
    A Control over motion in a virtual world directly affects presence, the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated. Greater presence in virtual reality generally reduces cybersickness, while more control means greater presence and less control means lower presence. Therefore, giving users more movement control can lower cybersickness through increased presence.
  Q Why is changing the field of view of a virtual reality headset a trade-off between immersion and cybersickness?  [11/S2/F0, 11/S2/F1, 11/S2/F2, 11/S2/F3; field of view, virtual reality headset, immersion, cybersickness, head movement, field of vision]
    A A field of view is the extent to which the display captures the user's field of vision, and a larger field of view generally results in greater immersion. Reducing the field of view can be an effective way to alleviate symptoms of cybersickness. However, an excessively narrow field of view can decrease immersion and increase head movement to look for things in the environment, which may exacerbate or increase cybersickness.
  Q Why can longer exposure to turbulent visual motion induce cybersickness while brief exposure alone may not?  [11/S0/F2, 11/S0/F3, 11/S0/F6; visual motion, vection, self-motion, peripheral stimulus, turbulent visual motion, cybersickness]
    A Visual motion is one of the primary causes of cybersickness, and higher visual motion can increase the risk, while the way the content moves also affects severity. Vection, the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli and is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus. Brief exposure to turbulent visual motion alone is not enough to induce cybersickness, but longer exposure to turbulent visual motion can induce cybersickness.
  Q Why can physiological or biometric signals complement questionnaire-based reports when measuring cybersickness?  [11/S4/F4, 11/S5/F0, 11/S6/F5; questionnaire-based input, physiological and biometric information, cybersickness]
    A Questionnaire-based input uses self-report ratings and is a subjective category of input for measuring cybersickness. Physiological or biometric inputs are objective, and they can detect cybersickness because questionnaires can be subjective, prone to inaccuracies, and may not always be reliable. Using them together can combine user-reported discomfort with objective signals.

  Q Why might a developer of a machine-learning cybersickness evaluator need to weigh prediction accuracy against understandability when comparing transparent, interpretable, and black-box models?  [12/S0/F1, 12/S0/F4, 12/S0/F7, 11/S7/F3; transparent model, interpretable model, black-box model, prediction accuracy, machine learning, cybersickness]
    A Transparent models provide clear insight into the decision-making process, and interpretable models are similar, offering more flexibility in customization and more precise details about the relationship between input and output. Black-box models cannot easily be understood or explained because they take an input and produce an output without revealing how or why that output is generated. Black-box models generally provide higher prediction accuracy than transparent and interpretable models, but they require large amounts of data and processing power.
  Q How does prediction differ from detection in cybersickness evaluation, and why can prediction still support mitigation even though most evaluation work focuses on detection?  [12/S1/F0, 12/S1/F1, 12/S2/F0; detection, prediction, cybersickness evaluation technique, mitigation measures, cybersickness mitigation, cybersickness]
    A Detection uses input generated after the experience to determine whether cybersickness has occurred, whereas prediction occurs before the experience to determine whether it will occur. Most cybersickness evaluation focuses on detection, but prediction is important because it can enable mitigation measures before cybersickness occurs. Because complete prevention is generally not possible, mitigation uses measures to reduce or eliminate cybersickness or at least lessen its impact.
  Q Why can a field-of-view adjustment reduce cybersickness while also creating a cost for user experience?  [12/S2/F1, 12/S3/F1, 12/S3/F2, 12/S3/F4; field of view, field of view adjustment, peripheral optical flow, presence, user experience, cybersickness]
    A Field of view is the amount of virtual environment visible at any moment, and adjusting it can mitigate cybersickness because restricting the field of view reduces peripheral optical flow. However, this restriction can reduce presence or sense of presence and impair performance in visual tasks. Since mitigation strategies often affect presence, and presence affects user experience, field-of-view adjustment can improve comfort while degrading user experience.
  Q How do hybrid cybersickness-evaluation models try to balance the higher accuracy of black-box models with the transparency of transparent or interpretable models?  [12/S0/F7, 12/S0/F8, 12/S0/F10; hybrid model, transparent model, interpretable model, black-box model, prediction accuracy, machine learning, cybersickness]
    A Black-box models generally provide higher prediction accuracy than transparent and interpretable models, but they require large amounts of data and processing power. Hybrid models are combinations of different machine learning models designed to provide high accuracy and transparency in their decision-making process. They can combine the strengths of transparent and black-box models by providing good predictive accuracy and some interpretability, which is useful in application domains where both high accuracy and transparency are essential.

13/A4  quiz  13/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 18 concepts)

    - Head-mounted displays

  Q What capability of tracked handheld controllers helps avoid the break-in presence that can occur with non-tracked handheld controllers?  [13/S4/F4, 13/S4/F5]
    - They require the user to keep hands in front of an IR camera
    - They provide only discrete button and trigger input
    * Six-degree-of-freedom tracking of their movement in 3D space
    - They are worn on the fingers instead of held in the hand
    because: Non-tracked handheld controllers are not tracked in 3D space, so virtual hands may not move with the user. Tracked handheld controllers have 6DoF tracking, so their movement can be reflected in the virtual world.
  Q Why may tracked handheld controllers not let users fully touch and feel passive virtual objects?  [13/S4/F6]

    because: Because the hands are occupied with the controller, users cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction.
  Q What problem is specifically tied to recognizing many gestures with hand-worn input devices?  [13/S4/F11]

    - The user’s hands must remain visible to a wide-angle camera
    because: When many gestures are possible, hand-worn devices may require frequent recalibration or force users to remember many gestures, which can be difficult for some users.
  Q What enables bare-hand input to leave the user’s hands completely free?  [13/S4/F12]
    - A tracked controller reports six degrees of freedom
    - A data glove processes continuous bend-sensor data
    - An HMD uses head yaw, roll, and pitch to infer hand gestures
    * Computer vision detects the hand gestures and converts them into commands
    because: In bare-hand input, the system tracks the user’s bare hand with computer vision and translates detected gestures into virtual-environment commands, so no wearable or controller is needed.

13/A5  put_in_order  13/S4  "Order the signal steps of a Leap Motion hand-tracking sensor"  (1 facts, 8 concepts)
  Order the signal steps of a Leap Motion hand-tracking sensor: IR LEDs emit infrared light > Infrared light reflects from the user's hands > Cameras pick up the reflected light > Software converts the signals into gestures  [13/S4/F13]

    - It prevents users from using hand-based input

13/A9  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (16 facts, 53 concepts)
  Q Why does a complete view of a virtual reality system include the surrounding physical environment in addition to the user and the virtual reality hardware?  [13/S0/F0, 13/S2/F0, 13/S2/F1, 13/S2/F2, 13/S2/F4; complete view, organism, virtual reality hardware, surrounding physical environment, user motion, robotic arm]
    A The complete view of a VR system consists of the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world. The environment is included because the user may respond to real-world stimuli and is not completely detached, so it can affect the user's behavior. The user's physical movement can change the environment, and VR hardware can also change it, for example by moving objects with a robotic arm.
  Q How does the tracking data flow help a virtual reality system satisfy the requirement that a user's actions partially determine what happens in the environment?  [13/S1/F0, 13/S1/F1, 4/S1/F0; virtual reality system, tracking data flow, stimulation data flow, sensor, user motion, head tracking, button press, controller movement, eye movement, body part movement]
    A A virtual reality system is defined by an artificial environment in which the user's actions partially determine what happens. The tracking data flow uses sensors to track user motion, so the hardware can adjust the stimulation data flow carrying stimuli to the user. Head tracking is commonly used and is the most important tracked motion, while tracking may also include button presses, controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.
  Q Why can a tracked handheld controller reduce break-in presence while still limiting the user's tangible interaction with passive virtual objects?  [13/S4/F4, 13/S4/F5, 13/S4/F6, 8/S2/F0; presence, non-tracked handheld controller, three-dimensional space, break-in presence, tracked handheld controller, six degrees of freedom tracking, tangible interaction, passive virtual object, force feedback controller]
    A Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated. A non-tracked handheld controller is not tracked in three-dimensional space, so the user's untracked hand movements may not produce a corresponding change in the virtual hands, causing break-in presence and affecting presence. A tracked handheld controller has six degrees of freedom tracking, so break-in presence is avoided, but the user's hands are occupied with the controller and cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction, although force feedback controllers may sometimes resolve the issue.
  Q What makes bare-hand input more natural than controller-based hand input, and what practical problems can a Leap Motion device introduce?  [13/S4/F12, 13/S4/F13, 13/S4/F14, 13/S4/F15; bare-hand input, computer vision, gesture, Leap Motion device, infrared, hand-tracking sensor, light-emitting diode, wide-angle camera, head-mounted display, low-cost head-mounted display, fatigue, line-of-sight issue]
    A Bare-hand input is the most natural hand input because computer vision tracks the user's bare hand, detects gestures, and leaves the hands free without any worn device. The Leap Motion device is an infrared hand-tracking sensor with light-emitting diodes and wide-angle cameras, and it can be attached to a head-mounted display to support low-cost head-mounted displays. However, it can cause fatigue if the hands are held in front of its sensor, requires the hand to be in the line of sight of its camera, and may have inconsistent gesture recognition across users.

    * Treadmills
    - Motion platforms
    because: Treadmills provide the sense of walking or running while staying in one place by providing different inputs to the feet or legs.

14/A6  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 44 concepts)
  Q Why is graphics processing unit support generally preferable in a virtual reality system even though modern central processing units are quite powerful?  [14/S1/F3, 14/S1/F6; graphics processing unit, central processing unit, virtual reality system, rendering, parallel processing]
    A A graphics processing unit is used to speed up rendering because it has inherent parallel processing abilities and the rendering process has inherent parallelism, making it useful for complex graphics and scenes in realistic virtual reality experiences. Modern central processing units are powerful but have many other tasks, so a CPU-only virtual reality processing system with minimal GPU support can have performance issues, and GPU support is preferable.
  Q How do the two broad full-body tracking approaches differ in the data they rely on, and why can full-body tracking strengthen the user's sense of being present in a social virtual environment?  [14/S0/F2, 14/S0/F3, 14/S0/F4, 14/S0/F5; full-body tracking, motion capture suit, camera-based tracking, self-embodiment, social presence, inertial measurement unit, fiducial marker]
    A Full-body tracking can add to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence because its output can show the user a fuller representation of themselves. One broad approach uses a motion capture suit, where sensors such as inertial measurement units capture and transmit raw movement data that are combined into full-body movement. The other broad approach uses multiple surrounding cameras that observe fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from their motion.
  Q How does a cave system apply the general virtual reality system idea that user movement is tracked and visual output is returned to the user?  [14/S2/F9, 14/S2/F12, 13/S0/F1; virtual reality system, tracking, world-fixed display, cave]
    A In a virtual reality system, data flow from the organism to the hardware is labeled tracking, and data flow from the hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation. A cave is a world-fixed display because it renders graphics onto a fixed surface or screen that does not move with the user's head, while the user can move within a physical space. A cave typically has three to six large surrounding screens and requires elaborate tracking of user movement, while it is usually driven by powerful graphics engines.
  Q How do the three head-mounted display categories differ in their typical use for virtual reality, augmented reality, and augmented virtuality?  [14/S2/F7, 14/S2/F8, 1/S2/F1; head-mounted display, non-see-through head-mounted display, optical see-through head-mounted display, video see-through head-mounted display, virtual reality, augmented reality, augmented virtuality]
    A Head-mounted displays can be categorized as non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through. Non-see-through head-mounted displays are typically used in virtual reality, optical see-through head-mounted displays are typically used in augmented reality, and video see-through head-mounted displays are typically used in augmented virtuality. Augmented reality is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content, while augmented virtuality is the case in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

15/A7  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 29 concepts)
  Q Why is field of view both a design advantage of AR headsets over AR smart glasses and a display factor that was linked to cybersickness in VR?  [15/S1/F0, 15/S2/F0, 11/S2/F0; augmented reality headset, augmented reality smart glasses, field of view, virtual reality]
    A AR headsets are larger and more immersive, present more content in the form of real-world content and augmented digital content, and provide a wider field of view. AR smart glasses are lighter, less immersive, less powerful, and usually have a smaller field of view, making them more comfortable to wear for extended periods. Field of view was described as a content-related factor affecting susceptibility to cybersickness in VR, so the size of the displayed view matters for both immersion and comfort.
  Q How does the need to present a real-world view shape the component differences between an AR headset such as the Microsoft HoloLens and a VR headset?  [15/S1/F1, 15/S1/F4, 15/S1/F5, 5/S0/F1; augmented reality, augmented reality headset, virtual reality headset, camera, depth sensor, Microsoft HoloLens, hologram]
    A An AR system is expected to combine the real world with virtual content, interact in real time, and register in 3D, so an AR headset may include cameras and depth sensors to obtain a real-world view. A VR headset does not need to provide a real-world view, so it may omit some advanced AR features and typically has fewer components than an AR headset. For example, the Microsoft HoloLens integrates high-definition holograms with the real-world view obtained through its special glasses.
  Q Why can spatial augmented reality support simultaneous multi-user interaction more directly than AR headsets, smart glasses, and handheld AR devices?  [15/S3/F0, 15/S3/F1, 15/S3/F2; spatial augmented reality, augmented reality headset, smart glasses, handheld device, interaction]
    A Spatial augmented reality systems overlay digital content directly on physical objects in the real world rather than on the user's own view. Their display element is not tied to or held by a single user, which can make the interface more natural and intuitive. This shared augmented physical content allows multiple users to interact simultaneously, unlike headsets, glasses, or handheld devices where each user interacts only with content on that user's own device.
  Q Why are AR contact lenses considered a future wearable display that can be placed directly on the eye without being visible to outsiders, and what unresolved user-effect issue remains with them?  [15/S4/F3, 15/S4/F4, 15/S4/F8; augmented reality contact lens, wearable technology, field of vision]
    A AR contact lenses are very small, can be placed directly on the eye like a regular contact lens, and are not visible to outsiders, making them an emerging future wearable display technology. They superimpose digital images or information directly onto the wearer's field of vision. Their effect on the user is not well known or researched, and seeing a lot of changing information directly in front of the eyes may affect normal behavior or cause some sort of sickness.

16/A3  quiz  16/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q What are the four broad steps of the tracking process?  [16/S3/F1]
    - Calibration, registration, integration, and pose correction
    * Calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction
    - Calibration, localization, integration, and drift correction
    - Calibration, registration, interpolation, and drift correction
    because: The tracking process broadly consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
  Q In tracking, what does calibration primarily do?  [16/S3/F2]
    * Transforms imperfect sensor output toward the real value, reducing sensor error
    - Compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation
    - Estimates the sensor's initial position and orientation, setting the start point
    - Aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors at discrete time points
    because: Calibration is the step that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error.
  Q In tracking, what is the purpose of registration?  [16/S3/F3]
    - Compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation
    * Determines the sensor's initial position and orientation before movement is tracked
    - Transforms imperfect sensor output toward the real value, reducing sensor error
    - Aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors at discrete time points
    because: Registration estimates or determines the initial position and orientation of the sensor, so that the starting point is known before movement can be tracked.
  Q In tracking, what does integration do?  [16/S3/F4]
    - Transforms imperfect sensor output toward the real value, reducing sensor error
    * Aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or data sources at discrete time points
    - Compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation
    - Determines the sensor's initial position and orientation before movement is tracked
    because: Integration aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment.
  Q In tracking, what does drift correction do?  [16/S3/F5]
    - Transforms imperfect sensor output toward the real value, reducing sensor error
    - Determines the sensor's initial position and orientation before movement is tracked
    * Compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation, reducing estimation error
    - Aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or data sources at discrete time points
    because: Drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, the user's sense organs, body parts, or objects in the environment, reducing estimation error.

  Order the steps of the tracking process: Transform imperfect sensor output > Estimate sensor position and orientation > Combine measurements from multiple sensors > Compensate position and orientation drift  [16/S3/F1, 16/S3/F2, 16/S3/F3, 16/S3/F4, 16/S3/F5]

16/A6  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 47 concepts)
  Q How do pose estimation and environment tracking together support the registration of digital content in augmented reality?  [1/S2/F1, 9/S3/F5, 16/S0/F3, 16/S1/F8, 16/S1/F7; augmented reality, pose, anchor, environment tracking, digital content, physical object, three-dimensional space, field of view, real-world view, virtual reality]
    A Augmented reality is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content. To register virtual content in augmented reality, the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, because without proper pose estimation three-dimensional registration is difficult or impossible. In augmented reality, tracking also requires moving real-world objects in the field of view, and a moved physical object must be tracked in the real-world view so that digital content can be appropriately registered. Environment tracking is more important in augmented reality for this purpose, although it is also important in virtual reality.
  Q How does the position of a sensor determine the two broad ways to obtain tracking input, and why does that affect where outside-in tracking can work?  [16/S2/F1, 16/S2/F2, 16/S2/F4, 16/S2/F5; tracking, tracker position, outside-in tracking, inside-out tracking, external sensor, sensor range, head-mounted display, pose, motion]
    A Tracking is categorized based on the position of the tracker or sensor into outside-in and inside-out tracking. In outside-in tracking, the experience device does not contain the sensors; external sensors such as cameras or markers provide data to identify and track motion, pose, and orientation. Outside-in tracking works only within the sensor range where those external sensors are placed. Inside-out tracking locates cameras or other sensors within the experience device, such as a head-mounted display, so no external devices are needed and there is no such placement restriction.
  Q What different errors are reduced by calibration and drift correction in the tracking process?  [16/S3/F1, 16/S3/F2, 16/S3/F5; tracking, tracking process, calibration, drift correction, sensor error, estimation error, position, orientation]
    A The tracking process broadly consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. Calibration transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error. Drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation, reducing estimation error.
  Q How does sense-organ tracking support a display attached to a user's sense organ, and when might eye tracking be added to head tracking in virtual reality?  [16/S1/F1, 16/S1/F2, 16/S1/F3; sense-organ tracking, sense organ, display, body-controlled degree of freedom, virtual world, user experience, head tracking, eye tracking, rendering, display technology, eye movement]
    A Sense organs such as eyes and ears have body-controlled degrees of freedom, and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience. In virtual reality, sense-organ tracking mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears. Eye tracking may be required if rendering and display technology require compensating for eye movement, and eye tracking may be part of head tracking.

17/A0  quiz  17/S0  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q Which three sensors are mainly contained in an inertial measurement unit?  [17/S0/F0]
    - An accelerometer, a microphone, and a magnetometer
    - A gyroscope, a camera, and a projector
    * A gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer
    - A gyroscope, an actuator, and a compass
    because: An inertial measurement unit is a composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer.
  Q In an inertial measurement unit, what does a gyroscope capture?  [17/S0/F1]
    - Magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes
    * Angular velocity
    - Linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes
    - The initial orientation of the headset
    because: In an inertial measurement unit, a gyroscope captures angular velocity, while an accelerometer captures linear acceleration and a magnetometer captures magnetic field strength.
  Q Which sensor readings does inertial measurement unit sensor tracking rely mainly on?  [17/S0/F2]
    - Magnetometer readings of magnetic field strength
    - Registration readings of initial orientation
    * Gyroscope readings of angular velocity
    - Accelerometer readings of linear acceleration
    because: IMU sensor tracking relies mainly on gyroscope readings of angular velocity; the accelerometer and magnetometer do not directly contribute to the tracking estimation.

17/A1  quiz  17/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q How is gyroscope measurement error defined when calibrating an IMU?  [17/S1/F0]
    - As the actual angular velocity minus the measured angular velocity, omega_a - omega_g.
    - As the squared difference between the measured and actual angular velocities.
    - As the calibrated angular velocity minus the measured angular velocity, omega_cal - omega_g.
    * As the measured angular velocity minus the actual angular velocity, omega_g - omega_a.
    because: The measured angular velocity may differ from the actual angular velocity, and the measurement error is defined as omega_g minus omega_a.
  Q What is the goal of calibrating IMU sensor readings?  [17/S1/F1]
    * To bring the measured angular velocity and the actual angular velocity as close together as possible.
    - To replace the gyroscope with an accelerometer or magnetometer.
    - To reduce cybersickness by occluding the visual periphery.
    - To make the expensive benchmark sensor exact and ideal.
    because: Calibration aims to reduce the measurement error, making the measured and actual angular velocities as close as possible.
  Q What two types of sensors provide the paired samples used for calibration?  [17/S1/F3]
    - A head-mounted display and a computer used for rendering.
    - A magnetometer and a camera used for drift correction.
    * A cheap, inaccurate IMU sensor and an expensive, highly accurate benchmark sensor.
    - A gyroscope and an accelerometer inside the same IMU.
    because: The calibration uses many paired samples from an inexpensive IMU sensor for measured values and a highly accurate benchmark sensor for actual values.
  Q What quantity does the simple calibration method minimize when finding C1 and C2?  [17/S1/F4]
    * The sum of squared differences between C1 + C2 omega_g and the actual angular velocities omega_a.
    - The sum of squared differences between the fitted constants C1 and C2 and the ideal constants a = 0 and b = 1.
    - The sum of squared differences between C1 + C2 omega_a and the measured angular velocities omega_g.
    - The sum of squared differences between the measured angular velocities omega_g and the actual angular velocities omega_a.
    because: The method uses linear least squares regression to minimize squared errors between the expression C1 + C2 omega_g and the actual values omega_a.
  Q After C1 and C2 are determined, how is a cheap gyroscope reading used?  [17/S1/F5]
    - It is mapped in the opposite direction, omega_g = C1 + C2 omega_a.
    * It is transformed into a calibrated value, omega_cal = C1 + C2 omega_g.
    - It is replaced by the actual benchmark value, omega_a, at every sampling instant.
    - It is added to the initial orientation theta_0 to compute the current orientation.
    because: Calibration mathematically maps the inexpensive measured angular velocity to a calibrated angular velocity that approximates the actual value.

17/A2  put_in_order  17/S1  "Order the steps of IMU sensor calibration"  (3 facts, 8 concepts)
  Order the steps of IMU sensor calibration: Collect paired samples from cheap and benchmark sensors > Minimize squared differences to find calibration constants > Map measured angular velocity to a calibrated value  [17/S1/F3, 17/S1/F4, 17/S1/F5]

17/A3  quiz  17/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q In XR sensor tracking, what is the main role of registration?  [17/S2/F0]
    - Reduces measurement error by matching a cheap gyroscope to a benchmark sensor
    - Blends gyroscope and camera orientations to reduce drift over time
    - Computes the current orientation by adding calibrated gyro samples to the initial orientation
    * Sets the initial orientation and alignment of the real and virtual worlds
    because: Registration is the step that finds the initial pose or initial orientation and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds.
  Q Under the simplified registration assumption, what determines the initial headset orientation?  [17/S2/F1]
    - The direction from the headset to a nearby fiducial marker
    - The direction of the magnetic field sensed by a magnetometer
    - The direction indicated by the first calibrated angular velocity sample
    * The direction the headset is facing when tracking is turned on
    because: The simplified understanding takes the direction the headset is facing when tracking starts as the initial orientation, with the initial alignment set to forward.
  Q What is true about using fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags during registration?  [17/S2/F2]
    * They can simplify registration, but it can also be done without them using computer vision
    - They provide calibrated angular velocity samples for integration
    - They correct drift by blending two sensor orientations
    - They are required whenever a tracking system is turned on
    because: Registration can be aided by fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags, but it can also be performed without them using computer vision techniques, and is simpler when such aids are present.
  Q How does integration obtain the current sensor orientation at a discrete time step?  [17/S2/F3]
    - It replaces the initial orientation with the latest calibrated angular velocity sample
    - It blends the gyro-derived orientation with the camera-derived orientation at each step
    * It adds the accumulated calibrated angular-velocity changes to the initial orientation
    - It multiplies the initial orientation by the elapsed sampling interval
    because: Integration computes the current orientation by adding to the initial orientation the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples multiplied by the sampling interval.
  Q In orientation integration, what does one calibrated angular velocity sample represent?  [17/S2/F4]
    - The absolute orientation of the headset at that instant
    - The linear acceleration of the headset along one axis
    - The measurement error between a cheap and a benchmark gyroscope
    * A change in orientation equal to the sample multiplied by the sampling interval
    because: A calibrated angular velocity sample from the gyroscope indicates a change in orientation equal to that sample multiplied by the sampling interval.

17/A4  quiz  17/S3  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q What is generally needed for drift correction that blends sensor values?  [17/S3/F0]
    * At least two sensors whose values are blended
    - A single high-accuracy sensor working alone
    - A fiducial marker and an initial pose
    - A benchmark sensor and a calibration model
    because: Drift correction usually uses extra sensors and generally requires at least two sensors whose values are blended to estimate and correct drift.
  Q Besides a gyroscope, which sensors are mentioned as usable for drift correction?  [17/S3/F1]
    - Benchmark sensors, raw movement data, and markers
    * Cameras, accelerometers, and magnetometers
    - Displays, energy sources, and tracking devices
    - Yaw, roll, and pitch
    because: A gyroscope may be used together with other sensors such as cameras, and in an IMU accelerometer and magnetometer readings can be used in addition to gyroscope values.
  Q In the classic drift-correction expression, what is the role of the gain parameter alpha?  [17/S3/F2]
    * It is a normalized gain used to blend the gyroscope and camera orientations.
    - It is a sampling interval used to integrate angular velocity samples over time.
    - It is a measurement error value obtained from comparing two angular velocity sensors.
    - It is an initial orientation value established when the tracking system is turned on.
    because: alpha is the gain parameter in the weighted combination of the gyroscope orientation and the camera orientation.

[17/S0/F0, 17/S3/F1]

17/A7  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 33 concepts)
  Q How do the four tracking stages build on one another to produce a usable orientation estimate in an XR system?  [16/S3/F1, 17/S1/F5, 17/S2/F0, 17/S2/F3, 17/S3/F0; tracking, calibration, registration, integration, drift correction, calibrated value, initial orientation, current sensor orientation, calibrated angular velocity sample, sampling interval, drift]
    A The tracking process is described as four stages: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. Calibration transforms a measured sensor reading into a calibrated value, and registration supplies the initial orientation. Integration computes the current sensor orientation by adding calibrated angular velocity samples multiplied by the sampling interval to that initial orientation. Drift correction then uses values from at least two sensors to estimate and correct drift.
  Q Why is the gyroscope the main sensor used for orientation tracking in an inertial measurement unit, while the accelerometer and magnetometer serve a different role?  [17/S0/F0, 17/S0/F1, 17/S0/F2; inertial measurement unit, gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer, angular velocity, tracking, drift error]
    A An inertial measurement unit mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer. The gyroscope captures angular velocity, and IMU tracking relies mainly on those angular velocity readings. The accelerometer and magnetometer do not directly contribute to tracking estimation, but they can be used to detect drift errors and take corrective measures.
  Q How do paired samples from a cheap inertial measurement unit and a benchmark sensor allow calibration to reduce measurement error?  [17/S1/F0, 17/S1/F1, 17/S1/F3, 17/S1/F4, 17/S1/F5; calibration, measured angular velocity, actual angular velocity, measurement error, paired samples, inertial measurement unit, benchmark sensor, linear least squares regression, calibrated value]
    A Calibration aims to make the measured angular velocity and the actual angular velocity as close as possible, which reduces the measurement error. It uses many paired samples from a cheap IMU sensor that produces the measured values and a highly accurate benchmark sensor that produces the actual values. It finds constants by linear least squares regression that minimize the sum of squared differences between C1 + C2 omega_g and omega_a, then maps omega_g to the calibrated value omega_cal.
  Q How does a classic drift-correction method combine a gyroscope-based orientation with a camera-based orientation, and what does the gain parameter do?  [17/S3/F0, 17/S3/F1, 17/S3/F2; drift correction, sensor, gyroscope, camera, orientation, drift-corrected orientation, gain parameter, drift]
    A Drift correction generally requires at least two sensors, and it can use a gyroscope together with a camera. In the classic approach, the drift-corrected orientation is theta_dk = alpha theta_gk + (1 - alpha) theta_ck, where theta_gk is the orientation obtained by integrating gyroscope values and theta_ck is the orientation obtained with a camera at the same time instant. The gain parameter alpha is a normalized value between 0 and 1 used in that combination.

    - When precise indoor positioning is required
    because: GPS is useful outdoors but generally has low accuracy, especially indoors, and allows only positional tracking; it is typically used when an approximation is good enough or as part of a hybrid tracking system.
  Q How can RTK improve a basic GPS sensor?  [18/S8/F7]
    - By removing the need for a GPS sensor
    - By switching to inertial tracking only
    * By using GPS signal carrier waves to improve detection accuracy
    - By measuring absolute orientation
    because: RTK can be used with a basic GPS sensor to improve detection accuracy by using GPS signal carrier waves for measurement.

18/A12  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (18 facts, 53 concepts)
  Q How are electromagnetic tracking and acoustic tracking similar in their sensor placement, and what practical difference matters when obstacles may be present?  [18/S2/F0, 18/S2/F2, 18/S2/F3, 18/S2/F4; electromagnetic tracker, acoustic tracking, transmitter, receiver, line of sight, head-mounted display]
    A Both use a stationary transmitter in the environment and a receiver that moves with the head-mounted display. In electromagnetic tracking, position is obtained from the magnetic field direction and the system does not require line of sight. Acoustic or ultrasonic tracking uses ultrasonic signals and requires an unobstructed line of sight between transmitter and receiver.
  Q How can a hybrid tracking system improve on the limitation of an inertial tracker found in many head-mounted displays?  [18/S8/F0, 18/S8/F1, 18/S9/F6, 18/S9/F7; inertial tracker, head-mounted display, hybrid tracker, single-technology-based tracking]
    A Inertial trackers measure changes in orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration rather than absolute values. They are typically MEMS-based and can be part of a head-mounted display. A hybrid tracker combines two or more basic tracking systems, and hybrid trackers typically perform better than single-technology-based tracking.
  Q Why can fiducial tracking and natural feature tracking both be part of visible light tracking, yet one requires added landmarks while the other depends on existing scene features?  [18/S4/F0, 18/S4/F1, 18/S4/F2, 18/S5/F0, 18/S5/F1, 18/S5/F2, 18/S5/F3; visible light tracking, optical camera, fiducial tracking, natural feature tracking, fiducial, feature, feature descriptor, camera pose]
    A Visible light tracking uses optical cameras, which are common in consumer and wearable devices, and it includes fiducial and natural feature tracking. Fiducial tracking adds artificial landmarks, called fiducials, to aid registration and tracking. Natural feature tracking uses features already present in the environment, such as points, corners, or line intersections, and uses feature descriptors to match them and estimate camera pose.
  Q How does 3D structure tracking support the idea of augmented reality as a state that augments the real environment?  [1/S2/F1, 18/S7/F0, 18/S7/F2; augmented reality, three-dimensional structure tracking, three-dimensional model, real-world view, Kinect Fusion, structured light depth sensor]
    A Augmented reality is the intermediate state where the real environment is augmented with virtual content. 3D structure tracking obtains 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view. Kinect Fusion uses structured light depth sensor data to create such models and also tracks the pose of the Kinect.

    - A selected virtual location reached without physical movement

    * Moving oneself in the virtual world while the real-world physical motion is not matched
    - Translating movement within a safe region to movement elsewhere in the virtual world
    - Pointing to a desired virtual location and being sent there without physical movement

    * So that cyber sickness can be addressed
    - So that the visual renderer can always use the correct head viewpoint

19/A8  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (21 facts, 69 concepts)
  Q How does virtual reality software turn the bidirectional data flow between a user and hardware into a controlled virtual reality experience?  [19/S0/F0, 19/S1/F0, 19/S1/F1, 19/S1/F2; virtual reality software, data flow, input device, output device, human sense organs, virtual reality experience]
    A In a virtual reality system, data flows bidirectionally between the hardware, the physical world, and the user, with tracking and stimulation occurring between the user and the hardware. The user operates input devices to generate data for the system, and the system sends processed data back to output devices that generate stimuli affecting the user's sense organs. Proper interaction and perceptual design and modeling, plus software, ensure the data flow drives the hardware so the stimuli suitably stimulate the human sense organs and create a virtual reality experience.
  Q How does the virtual world generator coordinate a virtual reality system's inputs, internal world, and multiple sensory outputs?  [19/S3/F0, 19/S3/F1, 19/S3/F2, 19/S3/F3; virtual world generator, black box, head tracker, input event, queue, renderer, visual renderer, aural renderer, haptic renderer, synchronization, input-output match]
    A The virtual world generator is an abstraction of the whole virtual reality software, treated as a black box. It receives low-level input from devices such as a head tracker, keyboard, mouse, and game controller, and queues simultaneous input events. It maintains an internal reality, converts incoming input into renderer output, and keeps output synchronized with input to maintain an input-output match. It can drive visual, aural, and haptic renderers for different displays.
  Q How do matched motion and user locomotion differ in virtual reality, and why can teleportation be a useful locomotion choice?  [19/S4/F0, 19/S4/F1, 19/S4/F5, 19/S4/F6, 19/S4/F8, 19/S4/F9, 11/S1/F3; matched motion, matched zone, user locomotion, teleportation, cybersickness, locomotion operation]
    A Matched motion maintains correspondence between a user's real-world motions and the virtual world, with a matched zone where real and virtual worlds align and physical movement is restricted. User locomotion moves the user through the virtual world while the user's real motion is not matched, often to move outside the matched zone. Some locomotion operations that avoid physical movement may lead to cybersickness, but teleportation sends the user to a selected virtual location without physical movement and, as an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement. Software should support different locomotion operations so cybersickness can be addressed.
  Q Why might a virtual reality developer use a headset software development kit together with a game engine as middleware, and what limitation does a non-virtual-reality game engine have?  [19/S2/F2, 19/S2/F3, 19/S2/F4, 19/S2/F5, 19/S2/F6, 19/S2/F7; virtual reality software, software development kit, platform, device driver, head tracking, display output, game engine, middleware, virtual reality engine, high-level description, low-level detail]
    A Virtual reality software should help a developer create a virtual environment, render the stereoscopic output view, and incorporate interaction, ideally from high-level descriptions that determine low-level details automatically. A platform-dependent software development kit can handle lowest-level operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output, while a game engine can act as middleware to avoid substantial initial effort. In practice the developer may still implement functionality from scratch, and if the game engine is not specifically a virtual reality engine it can be cumbersome for ideas outside standard video games and reduce flexibility.

    - It depends on the GPU to synchronize sound with three-dimensional motion
    because: An audio engine can perform its calculations on a CPU or a dedicated ASIC and does not require a GPU, while GPUs are generally associated with graphics or rendering.

20/A9  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (19 facts, 64 concepts)
  Q Why can building a virtual world generator from a basic software development kit give a developer more control over performance than using a ready-made generator, while also creating a larger implementation burden?  [20/S2/F1, 20/S2/F2, 20/S2/F3, 20/S2/F4, 20/S2/F6, 20/S2/F7; virtual world generator, software development kit, physics, performance, collision detection, collision response, audio support, lighting model]
    A A ready-made virtual world generator or engine comes with physics and collision support and its own algorithm implementations, which reduces effort but restricts the developer. A basic SDK typically provides drivers, tracking-data access, and calls to graphical rendering libraries, but it does not typically cover every aspect of locomotion, matched motion, physics, or collaborative virtual reality. Therefore the developer must build physics-related support such as avatar movement, collision detection and response, lighting models, and audio support from scratch, can choose and implement physics algorithms according to performance, but must understand and implement the overall system, which is a difficult burden.
  Q In a networked collaborative virtual reality experience, why must the virtual reality system still manage virtual collisions even when users are in separate real-world matched zones, and what should collision support include?  [20/S0/F5, 20/S1/F1, 20/S1/F2; networked collaborative virtual reality experience, matched zone, shared virtual world, virtual reality system, collision, physical collision, collision support, collision detection, collision response, body]
    A Each user has a distinct matched zone, and unwanted physical collision must be avoided when users are close, while users spread around the globe have no possibility of physical collision. Within the shared virtual world, however, user interactions, including collisions, must be managed by the virtual reality system whether users are close or spread around the world. Collision support should therefore include collision detection, which determines whether bodies intersect, and collision response, which determines how they should behave after a collision occurs.
  Q Why are a game engine's rendering engine and audio engine associated with different kinds of hardware even though they can be components of the same engine?  [20/S3/F2, 20/S4/F0, 20/S4/F2, 20/S4/F3, 20/S4/F5, 20/S4/F6; game engine, rendering engine, audio engine, three-dimensional graphics, rendering method, application programming interface, graphics processing unit, central processing unit, application-specific integrated circuit]
    A A game engine can be thought of schematically as comprising components such as a rendering engine and an audio engine. The rendering engine helps generate animated three-dimensional graphics by methods such as rasterization or ray tracing and is typically built on rendering APIs that provide software abstractions of a graphics processing unit, which is the hardware used for speeding up rendering. The audio engine uses algorithms for loading, modifying, and generating sound, and it can perform its calculations on a central processing unit or on a dedicated application-specific integrated circuit, so it does not require a graphics processing unit.
  Q How does native deployment of a virtual reality application depend on a platform-specific software development kit, and how does web deployment change the deployment options available to a developer?  [20/S5/F0, 20/S5/F1, 20/S5/F2, 20/S6/F0; deployment, native application deployment, web application deployment, software development kit, platform, operating system, hardware, web deployment tool]
    A Native application deployment requires SDKs tailored to the platform and hardware, and a platform typically means the operating system plus the hardware. An SDK is a collection of software development tools in one installable package specific to a hardware and operating-system combination, providing fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual reality experiences. Web application deployment allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device and can use web deployment tools such as cloud hosting and rendering tools, libraries for development support, complete development and deployment tools, generic development editors, or SDK support.

21/A5  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 48 concepts)
  Q Why can a tracking-focused low-level AR library by itself produce only a rudimentary AR system, and what role can a scene graph library take in a combined AR framework?  [21/S1/F4, 21/S1/F5, 21/S1/F9; low-level library and framework, AR Toolkit, scene graph, tracking, rendering, interaction]
    A Low-level AR toolkits such as ARToolKit primarily provide tracking and only low-level primitive OpenGL rendering, with no built-in interaction or complex realistic graphics, so a complete realistic application requires writing interaction from scratch. A scene graph library can take care of low-level object rendering, allowing the developer to focus on interaction while ARToolKit remains responsible for tracking.
  Q How does the skill-based hierarchy of AR software tools order categories from the most to the least programming skill, and why can rapid prototyping tools be useful before major development?  [21/S0/F1, 21/S0/F2, 21/S2/F1; skill-based hierarchy, low-level software library or framework, rapid prototyping tool, plugin, standalone augmented reality authoring tool, programming skill, programming ability, design prototyping skill, prototype]
    A The hierarchy places low-level software libraries or frameworks first, then rapid prototyping tools, plugins for existing developer tools, and standalone AR authoring tools, according to decreasing programming skill. Low-level tools require strong programming or coding ability and understanding of library functions, while rapid prototyping tools need some programming or design prototyping skill, plugins require skill with the original developer tool, and standalone authoring tools assume no programming ability. Rapid prototyping tools are useful because they let an AR idea be visualized with simple means and shown to users or clients, so an unsuitable idea does not require further coding.
  Q How do tracking and three-dimensional registration work together in a marker-based AR example where a phone detects a marker and a 3D cow appears, and how can ARToolKit and Open Scene Graph be assigned to those tasks?  [3/S2/F2, 21/S1/F13, 21/S1/F14; marker, augmented reality, tracking, three-dimensional registration, AR Toolkit, Open Scene Graph, three-dimensional object]
    A In marker-based AR, a marker placed in the real environment triggers the augmented experience when a device detects it, so digital content appears at the marker's position. In the marker-cow example, tracking recognizes the marker and its position, while three-dimensional registration creates and renders the cow at that position. Combining ARToolKit with Open Scene Graph can assign tracking and three-dimensional registration to ARToolKit and the creation of the rendered AR scene with the cow to Open Scene Graph.
  Q How can AR software tools be categorized by platform and tracking technology, and what do DroidAR and Vuforia show about mobile AR tracking choices?  [21/S0/F0, 21/S1/F17, 21/S1/F18; augmented reality software tool, application platform, mobile augmented reality application, tracking technology, computer vision-based tracking, computer vision, sensor, global positioning system, DroidAR, Vuforia, ARToolKit for mobile, Open Scene Graph, iPhone operating system, Android]
    A AR software tools can be categorized by target application platform, such as desktop or mobile AR applications, or by tracking technology, such as computer-vision-based tracking or other sensors like GPS. Mobile-specific AR frameworks include ARToolKit for mobile, DroidAR, and Vuforia. DroidAR uses sensors for tracking support, while Vuforia uses computer vision for tracking support. ARToolKit for mobile is a mobile version of ARToolKit available for the iPhone operating system and Android and integrated with Open Scene Graph.

22/A5  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 42 concepts)
  Q When a developer adds an augmented reality plugin to an existing interactive three-dimensional graphics authoring tool, what makes the approach quick, and what aspects of the final augmented reality system can still be constrained by the host tool?  [22/S1/F0, 22/S1/F1, 22/S1/F5; plugin, content authoring tool, tracking, augmented reality visualization, three-dimensional registration, user interface, interaction design, software configuration, hardware configuration, proprietary player software]
    A A plugin is added to an existing content authoring tool and adds AR-specific functions such as tracking, visualization, and three-dimensional registration, while the host tool handles content authoring. It is quick when the developer already knows the host authoring tool because they only need to understand the plugin. However, user interface and interaction design, software and hardware configuration, and in most cases dependence of the content on proprietary player software are constrained by the underlying authoring tool.
  Q Why might a developer choose low-level software development tools instead of a higher-level augmented reality tool or plugin, and what does that choice demand of the developer?  [22/S1/F6, 21/S1/F0; low-level software development tool, software library, low-level library, low-level framework, higher-level tool, plugin, third-party tool, programming skill, tracking, augmented reality application]
    A Low-level software development tools such as software libraries can resolve limitations of higher-level tools or plugins by letting the developer build the system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool. They demand the highest programming skill because low-level libraries and frameworks provide access to the core tracking and display functionality used to build an augmented reality application.
  Q How does Wikitude's client-server structure shape the role of the mobile device in augmented reality prototyping, and how does available content affect its usefulness?  [22/S0/F3, 22/S0/F4, 22/S0/F5; Wikitude, browser application, mobile device, client, rendering device, backend server, user interface element, mobile prototyping tool, prototyping]
    A Wikitude is a free augmented reality browser application that runs on mobile devices and can be used as a mobile prototyping tool. It treats the mobile device primarily as a client or rendering device, connecting to backend servers for content and user interface elements, with computation possibly taking place on the backend server. It makes prototyping easier or faster when developers have their own content; without content, developers depend on default content, which may reduce flexibility but is still usable.
  Q How do standalone augmented reality authoring tools differ from plugins in what they provide to a developer, and what user skills are enough to begin using many of them?  [22/S2/F0, 22/S2/F1, 22/S2/F2, 22/S2/F3; standalone authoring tool, plugin, content authoring tool, content authoring, augmented reality, scene construction, animation, interactive behavior, graphical user interface, personal computer]
    A Standalone authoring tools allow users to create augmented reality experiences without programming experience and are complete packages that include content authoring and augmented reality support, unlike plugins, which require a basic content authoring tool on which augmented reality support is provided. They typically support scene construction, animation, and adding interactive behavior. Most provide drag-and-drop graphical user interfaces, so users with basic personal computer skills and non-programmers can learn and use them.

23/A7  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q Why are extended reality systems treated as interactive systems, and what does that classification imply about the user they should serve?  [23/S0/F0, 23/S1/F0, 23/S1/F1; extended reality system, interactive system, interaction, lay person]
    A Extended reality systems belong to the broad class of interactive systems, in which interaction takes place between the system and the user. Because the user in such systems is a lay person who is not necessarily a technology expert and wants to use the system rather than understand how it works, the design implication is that the system should serve the user's use of it rather than expose technical internals.
  Q How do disappearing technology and presence point to the same design goal?  [23/S0/F1, 23/S0/F2, 23/S0/F3, 8/S2/F0; disappearing technology, presence]
    A Weiser's claim that the most profound technologies disappear means that a very advanced technology should ideally not be visible to the user, and the user should feel like dealing with any other item rather than a specialized technological item. Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated. The disappearing-technology ideal and presence refer to the same thing: the technological aspect surrounding the user should disappear from the user's perception, and the goal is to build systems that do not make it apparent that the user is using a specialized technological product.
  Q What can happen when an interactive system intended for lay users gives an error message containing terms such as event log, safe mode, or a hexadecimal status code?  [23/S1/F2, 23/S1/F3, 23/S1/F4; error message, lay person, event log, safe mode, hexadecimal status code, interactive system]
    A Technical terms in an error message, such as event log and safe mode, are not expected to be understood or acted upon by a lay end user, and a hexadecimal status code is generally incomprehensible to a layperson. A jargon-based error message can make the user anxious, leave the user not knowing what is wrong or how to get out of it, and may lead the user to refrain from using the system further and lose motivation. Designers of such interactive systems should not force users to learn the underlying technology or understand the relevant technical terms.
  Q Why do human factors considerations in system design lead to a user-centric approach, and what design decisions does that approach shape?  [23/S2/F0, 23/S2/F1, 23/S4/F0; human factors, system design, user-centric approach, user characteristic, interface element, layout, system state, interaction, goal state, interface]
    A Human factors in system design requires designers to know users' characteristics and design the system accordingly, because users who perform the same broad task can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills and therefore require different interfaces. The user-centric approach starts by understanding user characteristics and what users need and expect, and then designs the system based on that. It shapes interface elements, layouts that organize interface elements, ways for users to perceive system state from their own point of view, and interactions that take users to desired system states or goal states.

24/A7  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 32 concepts)
  Q Why is the novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization useful at the start of interactive-system design when empirical field studies are not always practical?  [24/S0/F0, 24/S0/F1, 24/S0/F3; field study, novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization, novice user, intermittent user, expert user, interactive-system design]
    A Empirical or field studies are typically needed to understand users and their behavior, but they are time-consuming, laborious, and require elaborate setup and planning, so designers can rely on the categorization instead of always starting with field studies. The categorization separates first-time, occasional, and regularly using long-term users, and because users in different classes are likely to behave differently, it provides a starting point for understanding users and making design decisions.
  Q Why might a word processing application provide both a menu option and a hotkey combination for the same task, such as saving a file?  [24/S0/F1, 24/S0/F3, 24/S0/F4, 24/S0/F5; word processing application, menu option, hotkey combination, task, file, novice user, intermittent user, expert user]
    A A word processing application can provide multiple options, such as a hotkey combination and a menu option, for the same task to cater to different user groups. The novice, intermittent, and expert classes consist of first-time, occasional, and regularly using long-term users, and users in different classes are likely to behave differently. The menu option takes longer but is suitable for novice first-time users because remembering hotkey combinations is generally difficult for them, while the hotkey combination may be better for intermittent users and is always preferable for expert users.
  Q How does user-centered design build on the user-centric approach when developing software for virtual reality or augmented reality systems?  [24/S1/F1, 24/S3/F0, 24/S3/F2, 23/S2/F0; user-centered design, user-centric approach, design lifecycle, development lifecycle, usability, virtual reality, augmented reality, software, user characteristic]
    A The user-centric approach starts by understanding user characteristics, what users need and expect, and then designing the system based on that. User-centered design results from applying this approach and involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle, with the objective of increasing usability. An application software developer building virtual reality or augmented reality software therefore incorporates user characteristics by following a development or design lifecycle that accounts for users' characteristics, needs, and expectations, so the system is easier to use and better matches their needs and expectations.
  Q Why should an extended reality system use user-centered design for both interaction design and perceptual design?  [24/S4/F1, 24/S4/F5, 24/S4/F6; extended reality system, human factors, interaction design, user input modeling, perceptual design, output modeling, user-centered design, input, output, input data, output stimulus, perception]
    A Extended reality systems are highly interactive, and human factors are important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output. Interaction design and modeling of user input should follow user-centered design so the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily. Perceptual design and modeling of output also requires user-centered design because output stimuli must match the user's perception so the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

25/A8  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 28 concepts)
  Q How do interaction design and perceptual design work together to support presence through an illusion of reality?  [25/S0/F0, 25/S0/F1; interaction design, perceptual design, presence, illusion of reality, perceptual stimuli]
    A Interaction design deals with input and the ease of interacting, while perceptual design deals with output and the perceptual stimuli generated by the system. In an XR system, these designs are used to create the best possible illusion of reality rather than actual reality. That illusion of reality is intended to enhance presence, the sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.
  Q What kinds of virtual-world output questions can perceptual psychology help an interactive system designer answer?  [25/S2/F0, 25/S2/F2; perceptual psychology, interactive system, virtual world, video resolution, pixel, frames per second, virtual sound]
    A Perceptual psychology is the science of how the brain converts sensory stimulation into perceived phenomena. It helps answer questions such as how much video resolution is needed to avoid seeing pixels in a virtual world or virtual object, how many frames per second are enough to perceive motion as continuous, and where virtual sound appears to come from.
  Q How can generally inconsistent sensory signals in virtual reality lead to either adaptation or cybersickness?  [2/S1/F0, 25/S1/F1, 25/S1/F3, 25/S1/F4, 25/S1/F5; virtual reality, sensory signal, adaptation, non-adaptation, cybersickness]
    A In virtual reality, the user receives input only from the virtual world, and artificial stimulation affects biological mechanisms that evolved for the real world. The virtual system generally provides sensory signals that are inconsistent with real-life experience. If the body adapts, the user may become unaware of flaws and believe the virtual system is the real world; if it does not adapt, fatigue, headaches, or cybersickness such as dizziness or nausea may result.

26/A6  quiz  26/S5  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q Why can an immersive virtual reality system create a sensory mismatch?  [26/S5/F1]
    - Because the cerebral cortex instantly learns new familiar interpretations
    * Because the brain cannot quickly retune its long-term learned sensory processing to new inputs
    - Because immersive virtual reality replaces hierarchical neural processing with a simpler signal path
    - Because real-time sensory input alone is enough to override long-term memory
    because: An immersive VR system can interfere with the brain's long-term learned sensory processing. The brain cannot be retuned to process the new inputs in a short span of time.
  Q What can a sensory mismatch in virtual reality cause for a user whose brain does not adapt to it?  [26/S5/F2]
    * Cybersickness, including fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea
    - A permanent retuning of the brain's sensory processing
    - Uniform acceptance of the artificial experience by all users
    - Conscious awareness that the experience is more natural than expected
    because: A sensory mismatch may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness. Symptoms include fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.
  Q In vection, which combination of signals creates the sensory conflict?  [26/S5/F4]
    - Visual input reports stillness while proprioception reports acceleration
    - Auditory input reports acceleration while visual input reports stillness
    * Visual input reports movement or acceleration while proprioception reports no motion
    - Proprioception reports movement while visual input reports no motion
    because: Vection is the illusion of self-motion in which a person physically stationary receives visual input reporting movement or acceleration. The balance sense or proprioception reports no motion, creating a sensory conflict.
  Q How can a sensory mismatch compromise presence in a virtual reality experience?  [26/S5/F3]
    - By letting the brain retune quickly and accept the experience as natural
    * By making the user consciously aware of the conflict and understand the experience is artificial
    - By strengthening the user's familiar learned sensory processing
    - By making the user feel the virtual environment is more real than expected
    because: A mismatch between sensory inputs and familiar processing can make the user consciously aware of the conflict. That awareness makes the user immediately understand that the experience is artificial rather than natural or real.
  Q What design implication follows from the need to avoid sensory conflicts in extended reality?  [26/S5/F5]
    * Balance the experiences presented by the various senses so the brain processes them as intended
    - Remove proprioceptive input so no motion can be reported
    - Prioritize visual stimulation alone to reduce the chance of sensory conflict
    - Present deliberately conflicting sensory signals to train rapid adaptation
    because: Extended reality design should carefully balance the experiences presented by the various senses. This can create an immersive experience by fooling the brain into processing information in the intended way.

26/A9  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (11 facts, 41 concepts)
  Q How do a sense organ and the cerebral cortex work together to turn a stimulus into a perception, and why is the final interpretation not determined by sensory input alone?  [26/S0/F0, 26/S2/F1, 26/S3/F0, 26/S3/F2; perceptual process, sense organ, stimulus, neural impulse, hierarchical processing, signal, receptor, cerebral cortex, interpretation of a stimulus, sensory input, long-term memory, perception]
    A A stimulus first stimulates a sense organ, which converts that input into neural impulses, so sensing is the lowest level of the perceptual process. Hierarchical processing then combines receptor signals at successive levels until the cerebral cortex is reached, where the interpretation of the stimulus is produced. This interpretation combines real-time sensory input with long-term memory or experience, so perception is an outcome of more than the raw sensory signal alone.
  Q How does proprioception differ from direct perception through the five senses, and what neural signal supports it?  [26/S4/F0, 26/S4/F1; proprioception, perception, sensory organ, vision, auditory sense, touch, smell, taste, muscular effort, body motion, motor cortex, efference copy, cerebral cortex]
    A Direct perception comes through sensory organs such as vision, auditory sense, touch, smell, and taste, whereas proprioception has no direct sensory organ. It is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them. The motor cortex sends efference copies to other parts of the brain, including the cerebral cortex, to report executed body motion, and this information is processed to support proprioception.
  Q How do presence and cybersickness explain why a VR user who is visually moving while physically stationary can feel sick or aware that the experience is artificial?  [26/S5/F4, 26/S5/F2, 26/S5/F3, 8/S2/F0, 10/S0/F0; presence, cybersickness, virtual reality system, virtual environment, vection, visual input, acceleration, balance sense, proprioception, sensory mismatch]
    A Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated, and cybersickness, also known as visually induced motion sickness, is primarily relevant to virtual reality. Vection is an illusion of self-motion in which visual input reports movement or acceleration while the balance sense or proprioception reports no motion, creating a sensory mismatch. If the user's brain cannot adapt, the mismatch can cause fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea, or it can compromise presence by making the user consciously aware that the experience is artificial.

27/A9  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (17 facts, 43 concepts)
  Q How do light propagation through the lenses of a virtual reality headset and the human eye connect display output to visual perception?  [27/S0/F0, 27/S4/F1, 27/S0/F1; virtual reality headset, display, lens, human eye, light propagation, visual perception, retina, cornea]
    A In a virtual reality headset, light emitted by the displays reaches the retina and is guided by engineered lenses in the headset and natural lenses in the eye. The cornea and lens of the human eye refract light so that images are focused on the retina. Knowledge of how light propagates through lenses and the human eye is therefore important for understanding how virtual reality headsets lead to visual perception.
  Q Why are central vision and peripheral vision different in acuity and color perception?  [27/S4/F4, 27/S6/F1, 27/S6/F3, 27/S4/F7, 27/S4/F6, 27/S6/F4, 27/S6/F5; central vision, peripheral vision, fovea, cone, rod, photopic vision, scotopic vision, color perception, photoreceptor density]
    A The fovea is the small central retina where cones are mainly located and where the concentration of cones is greatest, and central vision requires the eye to be focused and pointed straight at an object to perceive a sharp color image. Photopic cone vision is the mode in which color is perceived, while scotopic rod vision is more related to peripheral vision and does not provide good color. Peripheral vision is supported by the peripheral retina, where photoreceptor density and cone density are lower, and it is better at detecting movement but does not provide effective color perception.
  Q How do the photon, wave, and ray views of light support different parts of building a virtual reality experience?  [27/S1/F0, 27/S1/F1, 27/S1/F2, 27/S1/F3, 27/S0/F2, 27/S0/F3, 27/S0/F4; photon view, wave view, ray view, sensor, receptor, color spectrum, lens, visibility, light propagation, virtual world, rendering, camera, human eye, panoramic video, tracking hardware, tracking software]
    A The photon view of light is helpful for calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor, the wave view helps explain the color spectrum, and the ray view helps explain how lenses work and the concept of visibility. In constructing a virtual world, modeling light propagation is used to determine what should be rendered, while understanding light propagation, lenses, the human eye, and cameras helps choose camera positions and present panoramic video. Understanding how cameras work also helps build tracking hardware and tracking software.

    - The aqueous fluid and the vitreous fluid

    - Its flat focal plane behind the cornea
    - Its variable-power natural lens
    * Its non-planar, spherically curved retina

    - To replace the eye's natural lens

    - So a real image is formed in front of the user's face

    * A real image must be formed on the retina
    - A stereoscopic image must be formed in the air

    - Only the left eye sees the common region

    - It replaces peripheral vision with central vision

    * A three-dimensional view of the objects

    - Spatial resolution, field of view, and intensity resolution

    - The minimum pixel density needed for a display to be called a retina display
    - A frame rate too low to make displayed motion appear smooth
    * A sharp diagonal line appearing jagged when individual display lights are visible.
    because: Aliasing is the perception of a sharp diagonal line as jagged or staircase-shaped when individual display lights are visible.
  Q Why is the usual distant-display retina resolution criterion less suitable for VR headsets?  [28/S3/F5, 28/S3/F6]

    - VR headsets rely on LCD projectors, which produce a screen door effect
    - VR displays need lower pixel density because immersive motion needs higher frame rates
    * A magnifying lens places the display close to the eye, increasing required pixel density.
    because: For displays close to the eye, such as VR headsets, the traditional distant-display retina criterion is not very suitable because a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye, requiring much higher pixel density.

  Q What does motion perception in an immersive VR environment require of temporal resolution?  [28/S3/F8]

    - Frame rates comparable to ordinary television or movie standards
    * Frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards.
    - Only a frame rate high enough to avoid diagonal-line aliasing
    because: Temporal resolution for VR motion perception requires frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards, with higher frame rates preferred.
