28/A6  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 52 concepts)
  Q How does a virtual reality headset use its engineered lens and close screen to make a virtual image that the eye still perceives as a real visual scene?  [28/S0/F6, 28/S0/F7, 28/S0/F8; virtual reality headset, screen, engineered lens, virtual image, real image, retina]
    A A virtual reality headset places a screen very close to the eyes and uses a convex lens to focus the screen's light on the retina. For the best experience, the screen is placed at the focal length of the engineered lens, so the screen appears as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance. Even though the user perceives a virtual image, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina, and perception requires real images on the retina.
  Q Why can two flat two-dimensional images shown to the left and right eyes produce a three-dimensional view in an immersive display?  [28/S1/F2, 28/S1/F3, 28/S1/F4, 28/S1/F5; binocular vision, left eye, right eye, stereoscopy, two-dimensional image, three-dimensional view, stereoscopic vision, depth perception, three-dimensional object, three-dimensional space]
    A In binocular vision, when both eyes focus on infinity, they see the same image over a common region of about 120 degrees, while areas outside that region are seen by only one eye. In stereoscopy, the left eye processes the left two-dimensional image and the right eye processes the right two-dimensional image. When those images are processed simultaneously, the result is a three-dimensional view; this stereoscopic vision, aided by binocular vision, helps perceive three-dimensional objects and enhances depth perception of object relationships in three-dimensional space.
  Q Why is the 326 pixels per linear inch retina display criterion useful for some augmented reality experiences but not for virtual reality headsets or other wearable displays close to the eye?  [28/S3/F4, 28/S3/F5, 28/S3/F6; retina display, pixels per linear inch, retina display criterion, augmented reality, head-mounted display, virtual reality headset, wearable display, magnifying lens, display]
    A A retina display is defined as a display with a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch. Because augmented reality experiences are typically experienced using displays at a distance from the eye, that criterion can be taken into account for distant displays. For augmented reality head-mounted displays, virtual reality headsets, or other wearable displays close to the eye, a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye, so the required pixels per linear inch is probably 7 to 8 times higher than the retina display criterion.
  Q How do supported degrees of freedom in a virtual world connect to the frame-rate requirements for motion perception in an immersive environment?  [28/S2/F0, 28/S2/F2, 28/S2/F3, 28/S3/F1, 28/S3/F8; virtual world, translational movement, rotational movement, six degrees of freedom, yaw, roll, pitch, x axis, y axis, z axis, motion, temporal resolution, frame rate, jitter, immersive environment]
    A In three-dimensional space, an object can have six degrees of freedom: yaw, roll, and pitch rotation, plus movement along the x, y, and z axes. A virtual world may allow translational movement for navigating in three-dimensional space and rotational movement for moving at different angles, and motion is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported. Temporal resolution is the frame rate, and it must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter; for motion perception in an immersive environment, a virtual reality headset requires frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards such as 24 frames per second or 60 frames per second.

    - Shape, color, brightness, motion, and speed

29/A1  quiz  29/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q Why can sound not propagate in a vacuum?  [29/S1/F0]
    - It needs a vacuum to carry pressure variations.
    - It needs a light wave to create pressure variations.
    - It needs a surface point to reflect pressure variations.
    * It needs a medium for pressure variations to propagate.
    because: Sound is vibration in a medium and requires a medium to propagate. A vacuum has no medium, unlike light, which can propagate without one.
  Q What physical variation carries sound through a medium?  [29/S1/F1]
    - Temperature alternates between hot and cold extremes.
    - Sensor signals alternate between input and output states.
    - Light intensity alternates on a surface point.
    * Pressure alternates between compression and rarefaction.
    because: Sound propagation is caused by pressure variations in the medium, ranging from high-pressure compression to low-pressure rarefaction.
  Q What does the frequency of a sound wave describe?  [29/S1/F5]
    * The number of alternations between one maximum and another maximum per second.
    - The maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave.
    - The start position of a cycle of the wave.
    - The pressure variation at the human eardrum as a function of time.
    because: Frequency is the number of alternations between one maximum and another maximum per second, measured in hertz.
  Q What does the amplitude of a sound wave describe?  [29/S1/F7]
    - The number of alternations between one maximum and another maximum per second.
    - The start position of a cycle of the wave.
    * The maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave.
    - The pressure variation at the human eardrum as a function of time.
    because: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave.
  Q What does the phase of a sound wave describe?  [29/S1/F8]
    - The maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave.
    * The start position of a cycle of the wave.
    - The number of alternations between one maximum and another maximum per second.
    - The pressure variation at the human eardrum as a function of time.
    because: Phase is the start position of a cycle of the wave.

    - The eardrum, the ossicles, and the cochlea

    - It boosts the wave's pressure for a range of frequencies

  Q When a sound wave reaches the middle ear, what does the tympanic membrane do?  [29/S2/F3]

    - It attenuates high-frequency sound waves

    * It converts sound energy into neural impulses for the brain

    - It attenuates high-frequency sound waves in the canal
    because: The cochlea is the sense organ for hearing, and it converts sound energy into neural impulses that are transmitted to the brain.

29/A5  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 37 concepts)
  Q Why does adding sound to a visually rich virtual environment matter for the immersive experience and for presence?  [29/S0/F1, 29/S0/F5, 8/S2/F0; visual sense, audio component, immersive experience, presence]
    A The visual sense alone may not give a full picture of the surroundings, so augmenting vision with audio enhances the immersive experience. Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated. Presence requires reinforcing the virtual experience as believable and developing attachment, and the auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence.
  Q How does a sound wave move from the air to a signal the brain can use, and why does the medium matter?  [29/S1/F0, 29/S1/F1, 29/S1/F2, 29/S2/F5; sound, medium, pressure variation, eardrum, cochlea, neural impulse, brain]
    A Sound is a vibration in a medium, so it requires a medium to propagate and cannot occur in a vacuum. Its propagation is caused by pressure variations in the medium, and the pressure variation at the human eardrum is converted into a perceptual auditory experience. The cochlea then converts sound energy into neural impulses that are transmitted to the brain through the neural network.
  Q Why can audio change how users judge properties of a virtual environment, and how does that connect to making the experience believable?  [29/S0/F3, 29/S0/F4; audio component, visual sense, virtual environment, size, volume, material, intensity, distance, virtual experience, believable, emotional connection]
    A Combining sound with vision affects perception of properties of the virtual environment, such as size, volume, material, intensity, and distance, and reinforces what visual sense alone only partly gives. Audio reinforces a virtual experience as believable, meaning closer to reality and everyday experience. Vision coupled with audio also helps create or increase an emotional connection with the virtual environment.
  Q How do frequency and amplitude define whether a sound wave is audible to humans and how its level is expressed?  [29/S1/F4, 29/S1/F5, 29/S1/F6, 29/S1/F7; sound wave, frequency, hertz, human audible frequency range, human ear, amplitude, decibel]
    A A sound wave is primarily characterized by frequency, amplitude, and phase. Frequency, measured in hertz, must fall inside the human audible frequency range from 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz for the human ear to perceive it. Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave, measured in decibel relative to the minimum sound detectable by humans at 1000 hertz.

30/A1  quiz  30/S1  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q How does psychoacoustics differ from psychophysics?  [30/S1/F0, 30/S1/F1]
    - It studies only the physical properties of sound, not perception.
    - It studies the engineering of virtual reality sound hardware.
    - It studies perceptual phenomena produced by any physical stimulus.
    * It studies perceptual phenomena produced specifically by acoustic stimuli or sound.
    because: Psychophysics is the study of perceptual phenomena produced by physical stimuli, while psychoacoustics is the more specific area concerned with acoustic stimuli or sound.
  Q In a power-law model of perception, what does the exponent represent?  [30/S1/F2]
    * The relationship between actual stimulus magnitude and perceived magnitude.
    - The minimum angular variation that can be detected by a human listener.
    - The constant that depends on the units used.
    - The amount of change needed to detect a change in at least half of trials.
    because: In the power-law equation, the exponent is the value that relates the actual magnitude of the stimulus to its perceived magnitude.
  Q In the psychophysical law that captures the just noticeable difference, how does the noticeable change depend on stimulus magnitude?  [30/S1/F4]
    - It is equal to perceived magnitude raised to a constant power.
    - It decreases as the stimulus magnitude increases.
    - It remains a fixed amount for all stimulus magnitudes.
    * It grows in proportion to the stimulus magnitude.
    because: Weber's law expresses the just noticeable difference as delta M / M = C, equivalently delta M = M times C, so the noticeable change grows with stimulus magnitude.
  Q What is the just noticeable difference (JND)?  [30/S1/F3]
    * The stimulus change needed for subjects to perceive a change in at least 50 percent of trials.
    - The amount of change needed for a subject to notice a change in every trial.
    - The minimum frequency difference that can be detected at 10,000 hertz.
    - The minimum angular variation that can be detected by a human listener.
    because: The JND specifies the amount of change in a stimulus required for subjects to perceive it as changed in at least 50 percent of trials.
  Q For a pure tone whose perceived loudness follows a power-law exponent less than 1, what happens when pressure level increases a lot?  [30/S1/F2, 30/S1/F6]
    - Perceived loudness increases more rapidly than the pressure level.
    - Perceived loudness increases by the same factor.
    * Perceived loudness increases only a bit.
    - Perceived loudness stays the same no matter how much pressure rises.
    because: For the perceived loudness of a 3000 Hz pure tone, the power-law exponent is less than 1, so a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder.

    * The location of a sound source from hearing it
    - The arrival-time difference between the two ears
    - The pitch of a sound wave from its frequency

  Q Why is sound localization important in virtual reality?  [30/S3/F1]
    - It lets the user ignore visual position and locate objects using only sound
    - It helps auditory and visual cues disagree in a way that strengthens presence
    - It fixes virtual objects in a global direction independent of the user
    * It helps auditory and visual cues agree about object position and orientation
    because: In VR, sound localization helps the user perceive object orientation and position by matching auditory and visual cues; a mismatch can break presence and cause cybersickness.
  Q What is the minimum audible angle in sound localization?  [30/S3/F2]
    * The smallest angular change a listener can detect
    - The smallest distance change a listener can detect
    - The smallest frequency change a listener can detect
    - The smallest loudness change a listener can detect
    because: The minimum audible angle is the minimum angular variation that can be detected by a human listener, obtained by applying the just noticeable difference concept to sound localization.
  Q Which three parameters represent a sound source location in the spherical coordinate system used for sound localization?  [30/S3/F3]
    - Pitch, loudness, and radius
    * Azimuth, elevation, and radius
    - Azimuth, elevation, and pitch
    - Azimuth, loudness, and radius
    because: The spherical coordinate system uses azimuth for the horizontal-plane angle, elevation for the angle relative to the horizontal plane, and radius for the distance from the listener's head to the source.
  Q How does the minimum audible angle vary?  [30/S3/F4]
    - It depends only on the loudness of the sound
    * It depends on the sound's frequency and the source direction
    - It depends only on the listener's distance to the source
    - It is the same for all frequencies and source directions
    because: The minimum audible angle depends on both the frequency and direction of the sound source; at some combinations it can be as low as 1 degree, while at others localization can be very difficult.

    - They use information from the sound source's distance
    - They use information from a single ear

  Q What does interaural level difference (ILD) refer to?  [30/S4/F1]
    - A difference in sound arrival time at the two ears
    - A difference in perceived pitch between the two ears
    * A difference in sound magnitude received by the two ears
    - A difference in frequency produced by the sound source
    because: ILD is a binaural cue based on the difference in sound magnitude heard by each ear, with the unobstructed ear receiving a stronger sound.
  Q How does interaural time difference (ITD) help a listener locate a sound source?  [30/S4/F3]
    - The sound reaches both ears at exactly the same time
    - The sound is louder at one ear than at the other
    - The sound changes pitch as it moves around the head
    * The sound reaches the two ears at slightly different times
    because: ITD is a binaural cue caused by different sound arrival times at the ears, and that small time difference can be used to locate the source.
  Q Why do XR systems often use an HRTF for an average listener instead of measuring every user's HRTF?  [30/S4/F6, 30/S4/F7]

    - Every listener has the same HRTF, so personal measurement is unnecessary
    * Each person's HRTF is unique and obtaining it for every user is impractical
    - HRTFs can be derived from the user's visual display settings
    because: HRTFs depend on the size and shape of the head, ears, and ear canal, so each person has a unique HRTF, making individual measurement impractical and leading to an average-listener HRTF.
  Q How can a pair of HRTFs be used in an XR audio system?  [30/S4/F8]
    - To produce a single monaural sound for both ears
    - To calculate the minimum audible angle before rendering sound
    * To synthesize binaural sound that creates a localization effect
    - To replace audio localization with visual tracking of the source
    because: A pair of HRTFs for both ears can synthesize binaural sound, and generating sound effects or placing sound receivers according to the HRTF implements a localization effect.

  Q How do psychophysical results apply to auditory perception, and what does Stevens' power law imply about the perceived loudness of a 3000 Hz pure tone?  [30/S1/F0, 30/S1/F1, 30/S1/F5, 30/S1/F2, 30/S1/F6; psychophysics, psychoacoustics, physical stimulus, acoustic stimulus, Stevens' power law, perceived loudness, pure tone, pressure level]
    A Psychophysics studies perceptual phenomena produced by physical stimuli, and its laws also apply to psychoacoustics when physical stimuli are replaced by acoustic stimuli. Psychoacoustics is the more specific area that studies perceptual phenomena produced by acoustic stimuli. For perceived loudness of a 3000 Hz pure tone, Stevens' power law has an exponent of 0.67, so a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder.

    - It fills an entire room with one uniform odor for social experiences.

    - It places electrodes over and under the tongue to simulate taste types.
    * It uses air pumps or micropumps to spray chemical compounds near the nose.
    because: An olfactory display provides odor to the nose, usually by spraying chemical compounds near the nose using air pumps or micropumps.
  Q Why is delivering odor near the user's nose easier than delivering it on a room scale?  [31/S3/F4]
    * Room-scale delivery makes it hard to control intensity, uniformity, and concentration for localization.
    - Room-scale delivery makes it easier to control intensity, uniformity, and concentration for localization.
    - Near-nose delivery makes it harder to create strong cognitive and emotional responses.
    - Room-scale delivery avoids the need to vary odor concentration over a large area.
    because: Room-scale odor delivery is harder because it is difficult to control odor intensity and uniformity and to vary concentration over a large area for localization.
  Q How can a taste interface simulate the main taste types?  [31/S3/F6]
    - By requiring the user to eat food, which is generally convenient in XR.
    - By using air pumps or micropumps to spray chemical compounds near the nose.
    * By placing electrodes over and under the tongue to provide stimulation.
    - By filling a room with one uniform odor for social experiences.
    because: A taste interface can place electrodes over and under the tongue to provide stimulation that simulates the main taste types.

31/A7  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 53 concepts)
  Q How does haptic exploration help a virtual world support the kind of mental-model building that makes an experience feel immersive?  [31/S1/F5, 31/S1/F6, 31/S1/F7; haptic exploration, mental model, immersive experience, virtual reality, haptic perception, geometric mental model, somatosensory signals]
    A Haptic perception is important for creating a mental model of the surrounding world, and mental model creation is an essential part of an immersive experience. Haptic exploration integrates somatosensory signals from in-hand manipulation of an object so that a geometric mental model of shape, size, weight, and hardness is learned. In virtual reality, haptic perception and haptic exploration add an extra dimension by letting users feel the virtual environment through touch, and because real-world immersion also involves haptic exploration, adding it increases the immersive experience.
  Q Why is it not enough to apply a single kind of touch input for all object properties when simulating haptic perception?  [31/S1/F3, 31/S1/F4, 31/S1/F5; haptic exploration, lateral motion, pressure, enclosure, static contact, unsupported holding, contour following, texture perception, hardness perception, global shape perception, temperature perception, weight perception, local shape perception, receptor, spatial information, temporal information, somatosensory signals, geometric mental model]
    A The six types of haptic exploration are lateral motion for texture perception, pressure for hardness perception, enclosure for global shape perception, static contact for temperature perception, unsupported holding for weight perception, and contour following for local shape perception. Each haptic exploration used to perceive different properties involves different kinds of receptors and a combination of spatial and temporal information. The overall goal is to integrate somatosensory signals from in-hand manipulation of an object so that a geometric mental model is learned in terms of shape, size, weight, and hardness.
  Q Why might a tangible user interface be a less challenging path than a fully computer-controlled haptic device when a see-through display is used to combine real and virtual objects?  [31/S2/F3, 31/S2/F4, 31/S2/F5, 31/S2/F6, 31/S2/F7; tangible user interface, virtual avatar, virtual world, haptic device, somatosensory system, touch feedback, see-through display, Microsoft HoloLens, virtual object]
    A A tangible user interface uses a real-world object whose virtual avatar appears in the virtual world, and it can be used in place of a computer-controlled haptic device to provide feedback to the somatosensory system. Using real objects for touch feedback is generally considered less challenging than creating a computer-controlled haptic device, and the basic implementation aligns the real world and the virtual world. A see-through display such as Microsoft HoloLens lets users see and interact with the physical world while wearable device sensors detect the real object and virtual objects are added to the real world.
  Q Why are personal smell interfaces easier to implement than room-scale smell delivery, and what effect can successful smell effects have on an extended reality experience?  [31/S3/F3, 31/S3/F4, 31/S3/F5; smell interface, odor, air pump, micropump, chemical compound, room-scale delivery, odor intensity, uniformity, odor concentration, localization, immersive experience, visually induced motion sickness, extended reality]
    A A smell interface, also called an olfactory display, provides odor stimuli to the nose, usually by using air pumps or micropumps to spray chemical compounds near the nose. Delivering odor near the user's nose for a personal experience is relatively easier than room-scale delivery, because room-scale delivery makes it hard to control odor intensity and uniformity and to vary odor concentration over a large area for localization. When olfactory displays generate odor effects, they can induce strong cognitive and emotional responses that make an immersive experience more attractive and immersive, and pleasant odors can help reduce visually induced motion sickness.

32/A10  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 39 concepts)
  Q Why does building usable XR software as interactive software for laypersons require a highly iterative software development lifecycle, and what role do iterations play?  [32/S0/F0, 32/S0/F2, 32/S2/F2, 32/S2/F3; user-centered design, extended reality software, interactive software, software development lifecycle, iteration, user feedback]
    A User-centered design involves users in the overall design lifecycle to produce usable application software, and the XR application software being developed is interactive software for laypersons. A highly iterative lifecycle is required because users' needs and expectations change the stage sequence and create loops in which a developer can return to a previous stage. Iterations between stages account for user feedback, which means involving users in different ways rather than only through feedback.
  Q Why is the design-prototype-evaluate loop expected to be performed quickly and repeatedly, while loops involving code design, coding, code testing, or empirical study should not be frequent?  [32/S3/F2, 32/S3/F3, 32/S5/F0, 32/S5/F1; design-prototype-evaluate loop, design-prototype-evaluate cycle, code design, coding, implementation, code testing, empirical study, turnaround time, development cost]
    A The design-prototype-evaluate loop refines early designs by prototyping a design, evaluating it to identify problems, and refining it through many iterations until few significantly different problems remain. Its stages must be completed quickly so that many iterations can occur within a reasonable time, because otherwise turnaround time increases significantly. Other loops, such as the loop between code design, coding, and code testing and the loop between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and coding, implementation, and empirical studies, should not be frequent because they significantly affect the project's overall outcome and turnaround time, escalate development cost in manpower, time, and resources, and may lead to project abandonment.
  Q Why is an empirical study needed in interactive system development even when code testing shows that the code executes properly?  [32/S4/F3, 32/S4/F4, 32/S4/F5; code testing, empirical study, executability, usability, usability testing, interactive system development, end user]
    A Code testing tests executability by ensuring that the code is bug-free and executes properly, but it does not establish whether the system is usable from the end user's point of view. The empirical study is a usability-testing stage that uses systematic testing with end users to ensure that the interactive system product conforms to usability. This stage differentiates interactive system development from other software development, in which end users are not involved.
  Q Why must requirement gathering in an interactive-system development lifecycle involve end users as well as the client, and what methods can be used for this stage?  [32/S3/F0, 32/S3/F1, 32/S6/F0; requirement gathering, end user, client, requirement analysis, contextual inquiry, ethnographic study, cultural probe, interactive system development lifecycle]
    A In interactive system development, end users must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards, along with the client, while typical requirement analysis refers to the requirements of the client. Methods for gathering end-user requirements include contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes. Requirement gathering is one stage in which building interactive software differs from building regular software.

33/A7  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 45 concepts)
  Q Why can the Majuli case study be treated as the development of an interactive system, and how does the proposed system satisfy the definition of a virtual reality system?  [33/S0/F0, 33/S0/F1, 4/S1/F0; Majuli case study, extended reality system, interactive system, system development lifecycle, virtual reality system]
    A Extended reality systems are interactive systems, so the same system development lifecycle used for interactive systems can essentially be followed to build them. The Majuli case study focuses on the design, implementation, and evaluation of an extended reality system, specifically a virtual reality system for digital heritage preservation. A virtual reality system is identified by an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment.
  Q How do floods and river erosion make digital heritage preservation necessary for Majuli, and what kinds of heritage need to be preserved?  [33/S1/F3, 33/S1/F4, 33/S1/F10, 33/S2/F2; flood, river erosion, cultural resource, tangible heritage, intangible heritage, ecological heritage, digital heritage preservation]
    A Severe annual floods and erosion endanger Majuli's cultural resources and its material existence, and river erosion consumes the island, reducing its habitable area until formerly habitable areas become sandbars, river banks, underwater areas, or barren areas. Because there is a real possibility that the island may disappear, its tangible heritage, intangible heritage, and ecological heritage must be preserved. Digital heritage preservation uses digital media to preserve heritage and includes archiving, digitizing, and immersive technologies such as virtual reality and augmented reality.
  Q How do the preservation and experience goals of the Majuli VR system connect to the components of digital heritage preservation?  [33/S2/F2, 33/S3/F0, 33/S3/F1, 33/S3/F2; digital heritage preservation, virtual reality system, heritage preservation, multimedia archive, virtual tour, Majuli River Island]
    A Digital heritage preservation involves using digital media to preserve heritage, including archiving, digitizing, and immersive technologies. The preservation goal of the Majuli VR system is to create an archive of heritage information, ideally a multimedia archive comprising images, videos, audio, and text, with images and videos in two-dimensional and 360-degree forms. The experience goal is an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses that archive.
  Q Why can immersive technology help a global audience engage with the heritage that the Majuli VR system aims to preserve?  [33/S2/F6, 33/S2/F7, 33/S3/F0; immersive technology, virtual reality, heritage site, artifact, intangible cultural heritage, heritage preservation]
    A Virtual reality and other immersive technologies permit a global audience to explore heritage sites, artifacts, and intangible cultural heritage remotely from home without visiting the physical site. Their use in heritage preservation is known to play a pivotal role in promoting the preservation of heritage for future generations. The Majuli VR system therefore has two clear-cut goals: to preserve heritage and to let users anywhere on Earth experience that heritage.

35/A1  quiz  35/S1  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 2 concepts)
  Q In a system-centered design approach, what mainly guides what should be built?  [35/S1/F0]
    * What developers can easily build with available tools and what interests them
    - What user context and goals require for the task
    - What client requirements specify for the project
    - What end users need and expect from the system
    because: System-centered design is driven by the developer's skill and interest, what can be easily built on the platform, and what can be created from available tools, rather than by the user's needs and expectations.
  Q A user-centered design approach bases its design primarily on what?  [35/S1/F1]
    - Developers' skills, interests, and programming convenience
    * Users' abilities, context, goals, needs, and expectations
    - Available tools, platform features, and resource limits
    - Client requirements, business goals, and project constraints
    because: User-centered design is a design approach based on the user's abilities, context, goals, needs, and expectations, and is ideally driven from the users' point of view.
  Q What is the main concern in system-centered design, as opposed to user-centered design?  [35/S1/F0]
    - The end user, rather than the client
    * The system, rather than the user
    - The programmer, rather than the designer
    - The user, rather than the system
    because: System-centered design is a design approach in which the main concern is the system rather than the user.

35/A3  quiz  35/S3  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q How are functional requirements characterized in software requirements?  [35/S3/F1, 35/S3/F2]
    * They specify system features that carry out tasks as black-box functions producing output from input.
    - They specify system characteristics related to quality attributes that cannot be expressed as functions.
    - They specify how hardware and software are interfaced with each other.
    - They specify the economic cost of developing and operating the system.
    because: Functional requirements are task features expressed as functions treated as black boxes, while non-functional requirements are quality-related characteristics not expressible as functions.
  Q What type of requirement is a usability requirement?  [35/S3/F3]
    * A non-functional requirement about the user interface design and qualities that make the interface usable.
    - An external system interface requirement between hardware and software.
    - A performance-related requirement about system speed or resource use.
    - A functional requirement about the tasks the system can perform.
    because: Usability requirements are a kind of non-functional requirement concerned with user interface design and usability qualities.
  Q Which category of non-functional requirements includes the user interface where usability issues arise?  [35/S3/F4, 35/S3/F5, 35/S3/F6]
    - Performance-related requirements
    - Lifecycle requirements
    * Interface issues.
    - Economic considerations
    because: Interface issues cover the design or qualities of interfaces that make them usable, and include the user interface where usability issues arise.
  Q Why is usability particularly important for some interactive systems?  [35/S3/F7]
    - They are specified by functional black-box requirements.
    - They have economic operating constraints.
    - They include an external hardware-software interface.
    * They are intended for non-experts or users unaware of how the system works.
    because: Usability matters when interactive systems are intended for non-experts or users who do not know how the system works.

35/A5  quiz  35/S5  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q Why is contextual inquiry important in system development?  [35/S5/F0]
    - It divides end-user requirements into functional and non-functional categories.
    - It provides a standardized ISO definition of a specified context of use.
    * It studies users in their work setting and helps refine the design.
    - It ensures lay users keep control of the system during interaction.
    because: Contextual inquiry studies users, such as managerial staff, in their work setting and reveals their unique behavioral traits, enabling design refinement; without it, designers may treat essential user activities as equally important as unnecessary features.
  Q What must happen to user activities observed in contextual inquiry?  [35/S5/F1]
    - They should be classified only as non-functional requirements.
    - They should be recorded but need not become system features.
    - They should be ranked below optional features.
    * They must be supported as features in the system design.
    because: Observed user activities, such as setting meeting dates and reminders in a managerial staff calendar app, must be supported as features to make the system usable for that user group.

35/A6  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (4 facts, 10 concepts)
  Lifecycle requirement | Performance requirement | *Functional requirement | Operating constraint  (Performance requirements, operating constraints, and lifecycle requirements are categories of non-functional requirements, while a functional requirement is the separate main requirement type.)  [35/S3/F0, 35/S3/F4]
  User context | User abilities | User expectations | *Programmer convenience  (User abilities, user context, and user expectations are factors that user-centered design is based on, whereas programmer convenience is what user-centered design is driven against.)  [35/S1/F1]
  Programmer interest | Available tools | *User expectations | Developer skill  (Developer skill, available tools, and programmer interest are factors that drive system-centered design, while user expectations are the basis for user-centered design rather than system-centered design.)  [35/S1/F0, 35/S1/F1]

35/A7  put_in_order  lecture  "Order the stages of usability requirement handling"  (3 facts, 11 concepts)
  Order the stages of usability requirement handling: End-user usability requirements are identified > Usability requirements are specified > System design, implementation, and deployment plans are created  [35/S0/F0, 35/S0/F1, 35/S2/F4]

35/A8  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 38 concepts)
  Q Why are usability requirements considered a type of non-functional requirement rather than a functional requirement?  [35/S3/F0, 35/S3/F1, 35/S3/F2, 35/S3/F3; requirement, functional requirement, non-functional requirement, quality attribute, usability requirement, user interface]
    A Requirements are divided into functional requirements and non-functional requirements. Functional requirements are system features and abilities, treated as black boxes that produce an output from an input once implemented. Non-functional requirements are system characteristics, typically related to quality attributes of software. Usability requirements are a type of non-functional requirement because they concern the design and qualities of the user interface that make the interface usable.
  Q How does specifying users and their context of use support the gathering of end-user usability requirements?  [35/S4/F0, 35/S4/F1, 35/S4/F2, 35/S4/F3, 35/S4/F6; user group, end-user requirement, usability, context of use, user behavior, contextual inquiry, usability requirement]
    A Users must first be specified or categorized because end-user requirements cannot be gathered without specified users. The ISO definition of usability requires a usable product to have a specified context of use, and knowing user behavior in that work context is essential. Contextual inquiry observes users performing tasks in their natural work setting to gather insight about user behavior and end-user requirements. In usability requirement gathering, those end-user requirements are treated as usability requirements.
  Q Why are decisions about a mobile platform, a programming language, or a relational database management system not treated as end-user usability requirements in the calendar app case?  [35/S0/F0, 35/S2/F1, 35/S2/F2, 35/S2/F3; requirement gathering, end-user requirement, usability requirement, mobile platform, programming language, Java, JavaScript, feasibility stage, relational database management system, my structured query language, code design, interface design, design stage, calendar app]
    A Requirement gathering concerns end-user requirements and is aimed at ensuring usability. In the calendar app, choosing a mobile platform or a programming language such as Java or JavaScript is related to the feasibility stage rather than to end-user usability requirements. Choosing a relational database management system such as MySQL is a code-design decision rather than an interface-design decision or an end-user usability requirement. Some developer questions are therefore part of the design stage rather than being requirements.
  Q How does contextual inquiry connect observed user activities in a work context to features in a system design?  [35/S4/F6, 35/S4/F9, 35/S5/F1; contextual inquiry, user behavior, end-user requirement, task domain, work culture, physical constraint, social constraint, design decision, user activities, feature, system design, calendar app, user group]
    A Contextual inquiry watches users performing tasks in their natural work setting to gather insight about user behavior and end-user requirements. Through observation and interaction, designers learn about the task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints that support design decisions. User activities observed in contextual inquiry must be supported as features in the system design. In the calendar app for managerial staff, observed activities such as setting meeting dates and reminders must be supported to make the app usable for that user group.

    * A usability requirement-gathering method that observes users in their natural work setting.

    - A usability requirement-gathering method that records users and never interacts with them.
    - A usability requirement-gathering method that only asks users what they want.
    because: Contextual inquiry observes targeted or specified users in their natural work setting to understand how they behave and what they do.
  Q In active mode of contextual inquiry, what is true about the observer?  [36/S0/F1]

    * User activities are recorded, later observed, and clarified through interaction with the users.
    because: Passive mode has no observer present; user activities are recorded or videotaped, later observed, and issues are clarified through interaction with the users.
  Q In genuine contextual inquiry, how should the observer treat the users?  [36/S0/F2]

    because: The observer must act as an apprentice or learner and treat users as masters or teachers, learning how they behave rather than advising or teaching them.

36/A3  quiz  36/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 7 concepts)
  Q Which sequence describes the affinity diagram method?  [36/S2/F0]
    - Display ideas, create a group header, sort ideas, generate ideas, and draw the finished diagram
    - Plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect on the contextual inquiry data, then prepare the finished diagram
    * Generate ideas, display ideas, sort ideas into groups, create a group header, and draw the finished diagram
    - Generate ideas, draw the finished diagram, display ideas, sort ideas, and create a group header
    because: The affinity diagram method has the five steps: generate ideas, display ideas, sort ideas into groups, create a header or name for each group, and draw the finished diagram.
  Q Why are ideas sorted into groups in the affinity diagram method?  [36/S2/F2]
    * To find patterns among ideas that may look random by placing similar ideas together
    - To remove duplicate notes before drawing the finished affinity diagram from the board
    - To assign development tasks to programmers after system design is approved and implementation begins
    - To count the ideas recorded by each observer during the execute stage before grouping
    because: Sorting ideas into groups is done to find patterns among seemingly random ideas by moving similar ideas into the same group so meaningful conclusions can be drawn.
  Q What is a group header in an affinity diagram?  [36/S2/F3]
    - A usability requirement written directly from the user's stated goals before design and specifications
    - An original contextual inquiry note selected as the most representative idea for the group
    - A software module name created during the code design stage for later implementation
    * A name assigned after sorting that identifies the pattern binding the ideas in the group
    because: A group header is a name or identifier assigned after the ideas have been sorted; it refers to the pattern that binds the ideas and is not present in the initial ideas.
  Q After the finished affinity diagram is drawn, what does reflection involve?  [36/S2/F5]
    - Coding the system and testing it in the traditional software engineering way
    - Returning to the execute stage to record more observations from the users
    * Deciding what to do with the data and formulating design recommendations based on it
    - Choosing the final layout screens during the design-prototype-evaluate cycle
    because: Reflection after the finished affinity diagram means deciding what to do with the data and formulating a set of design recommendations based on the data.
  Q A design recommendation such as providing an erase-content facility is best described as what?  [36/S2/F7]
    - A diagram header labeling the group of notes about content correction on the board
    - A code design decision specifying the programming structure and tests for erasing notes
    * A requirement stating what must be done for usability, not how to implement it
    - An implementation guideline produced by following a traditional software development lifecycle without inquiry
    because: Such a design recommendation is a requirement, not a prescription for implementation; it states what must be done to make the system usable and does not specify how to implement it.

36/A7  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 23 concepts)
  Q How does the reflect stage of contextual inquiry use an affinity diagram method to move from recorded observations to a design specification and design recommendations?  [36/S1/F5, 36/S1/F6, 36/S2/F5; contextual inquiry, reflect stage, affinity diagram method, design goal, design specification, design recommendation]
    A In the reflect stage, the observer analyzes data collected during the execute stage and identifies the design goals. The affinity diagram method arranges the collected data so that patterns can be found more easily, leading to the design specification of the design goals. After the finished affinity diagram is drawn, reflection means deciding what to do with the data and formulating a set of design recommendations.
  Q Why is a design recommendation derived from contextual inquiry, such as providing an erase-content facility in the class note-taking application, considered an informed requirement rather than a prescription for implementation?  [36/S2/F6, 36/S2/F7; contextual inquiry, design recommendation, informed design choice, uninformed design choice, class note-taking application, requirement, implementation]
    A A design recommendation derived from contextual inquiry is an informed design choice because it is produced by analyzing the collected inquiry data, whereas guidelines created without contextual inquiry are uninformed design choices. The erase-content facility recommendation is a requirement because it states what must be done to make the system usable. It does not specify how the system should implement that facility.
  Q Why must an observer in genuine contextual inquiry act as an apprentice rather than a teacher, and how does this role relate to active and passive modes?  [36/S0/F1, 36/S0/F2; contextual inquiry, master-apprentice model, active mode, passive mode, observation]
    A In genuine contextual inquiry, the observer must act as an apprentice or learner and treat users as masters or teachers, so advice or teaching is prohibited. Contextual inquiry can be performed in active mode, where the observer is physically present, and passive mode, where user activities are recorded and later clarified through interaction. In both modes, the observer is learning how users behave instead of advising or teaching them how to behave.
  Q Why can an affinity diagram for a calendar app refine a group header from work scheduling into overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling without treating the first grouping as simply wrong?  [36/S3/F1, 36/S3/F2; calendar app, affinity diagram, observation, header, work scheduling, overall scheduling, day-wise scheduling, reminder setting]
    A In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the five contextual inquiry observations that do not relate to reminder setting were first grouped under the header work scheduling and then refined into the headers overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling. There is no unique way to group the observations in an affinity diagram, so different groupings are possible. The finished diagram has three groups: reminder setting, overall scheduling, and day-wise scheduling.

    - Only the user groups identified during contextual inquiry
    * All functional and non-functional requirements, including the formal specification of functional requirements

37/A7  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 40 concepts)
  Q Why can usability requirements gathered by contextual inquiry for the Majuli VR Tour be made more suitable for implementation by converting them into functional requirements?  [37/S0/F0, 37/S0/F1, 37/S2/F1; contextual inquiry, usability requirement, non-functional requirement, functional requirement, code design]
    A Contextual inquiry is a usability requirement gathering method, and its outcome can be used as design guidelines, recommendations, or principles, and also as functional requirements. Usability requirements are non-functional requirements, but when they are converted into functional requirements and added to the existing set, they are directly incorporated into the system through code and support code design. A functional requirement specifies a feature as a function with a well-defined input and output, and this functional specification makes conversion to code easier.
  Q How did the Majuli VR Tour use the identified user groups to make a large multimodal virtual tour less likely to cause cybersickness?  [37/S3/F2, 37/S3/F5, 37/S3/F6, 37/S3/F7; Majuli virtual reality tour, user group, large geographical area, multimodal data, cybersickness, data subset restriction]
    A The three potential user groups were students or learners, tourists, and pilgrims. A key design challenge was to provide a comprehensive view of a large geographical area with large multimodal data while avoiding cybersickness. The tour addressed this by allowing each user group to access only a subset of the collected data, based on what that group typically does, which reduced the expanse of information and the need to explore everything in detail. This reduced the possibility of cybersickness and increased interest for each group.
  Q Why is location awareness important in a virtual reality tour of a large geographical area, and how can that insight become part of the system design?  [37/S0/F1, 37/S3/F8, 37/S3/F9; location awareness, location information, virtual reality tour, large geographical area, functional requirement, system design]
    A Accurate location information is crucial in a virtual reality tour, especially for large geographies, because it prevents disorientation and gives users more confidence and purpose by telling them where they are in the geographical space. In the Majuli VR Tour, location awareness was identified during contextual inquiry as an issue for users exploring a large space. A possible resolution was to add a location awareness feature and later convert it into functional requirements during system design, which are easier to turn into code because they specify well-defined inputs and outputs.
  Q How does a software requirements specification help organize functional requirements so that each requirement remains clear for later coding?  [37/S2/F0, 37/S2/F2, 37/S2/F3; software requirements specification, functional requirement, requirement hierarchy, requirement identifier, top-level requirement, sub-requirement, input, output]
    A A software requirements specification is the textual document that specifies all requirements of a system, both functional and non-functional, and it includes the formal specification of the functional requirements. In an SRS, requirements are generally organized in a hierarchy with identifiers such as R1 for a top-level requirement and R1.1 for a sub-requirement. Each requirement identifier represents a function with a clearly defined input, a clearly defined output, and an optional description of what it does, which supports conversion to code.

    - The design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and early evaluation
    - Code design and requirement gathering
    - The design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and implementation
    because: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design.

    - It is the same as interface design in any other non-interactive software development.
    - It is a different kind of code design for immersive systems.
    because: In the interactive system development lifecycle, code design is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development.

38/A4  quiz  38/S3  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q What does Shneiderman's first golden rule of system and interface design require?  [38/S3/F0]
    - Provide informative feedback
    - Design for universal usability
    - Design dialogues to yield closure
    * Strive for consistency
    because: The first golden rule is to strive for consistency in system and interface design.
  Q In Shneiderman's consistency rule, what does internal consistency mean?  [38/S3/F1, 38/S3/F2]
    - Matching virtual-world elements and interactions to the user's real-world experience
    * Using the same elements and interactions for the same task across different parts and usage instances
    - Providing informative feedback whenever the user performs an action
    - Using separate objects and interactions for each part of a design
    because: Internal consistency uses the same elements and interactions for the same task across different parts of a design and different usage instances.
  Q What is external or environmental consistency in system design?  [38/S3/F3]
    - Hotkey options should be preferred because they rely on recognition rather than recall
    * Virtual-world elements and interactions should closely match the user's real-world experience and knowledge
    - A system should provide facilities for all user categories
    - The same elements and interactions should be used for the same task across different parts
    because: External or environmental consistency means virtual-world elements and interactions closely match real-world experience and knowledge so that real-world knowledge transfers to the virtual world.
  Q What does Shneiderman's second golden rule, universal usability, require?  [38/S3/F4]
    * A system should provide facilities for and support different user categories rather than only specific ones
    - A system should use the same elements and interactions for the same task across different parts
    - A system should match virtual-world elements to the user's real-world experience
    - A system should provide informative feedback after every user action
    because: Universal usability means a system should provide facilities for all user categories and support different user categories rather than only specific ones.
  Q Why can menu-based options be preferable to hotkey options for some users?  [38/S3/F5]
    * Menu options rely on recognition rather than recall
    - Recall is a less skilled task than recognition
    - Menu options are faster for users who do not want slower hotkey options
    - Hotkeys rely on recognition while menus rely on recall
    because: Menu options can help users who may not remember hotkey combinations because they rely on recognition rather than recall, while recall is a skilled task. Hotkeys can be faster for users who prefer them over slower menu-based options.

    - Keeping a reversal option available so users can return from an erroneous situation

    because: Closure is achieved by organizing task execution into beginning, middle, and end parts and providing feedback at the end of each group, so the user feels the task is started, executed, and completed.

38/A8  quiz  38/S6  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q What does the keeping-users-in-control usability rule require?  [38/S6/F0]

    * Lay users should feel in control, perceive that their interaction changes system state, and receive feedback.
    - Lay users should be limited to a single hand-gesture input modality for every task.
    - Lay users should depend only on permanent long-term memory for day-to-day information.
    because: Keeping users in control means lay users feel in control, see that their interaction changes the system state, and receive feedback on actions and results; without this they feel at a loss and usability is reduced.
  Q In the broad sense of human memory, what is short-term memory?  [38/S6/F1]
    - An AR headset that tracks eye movements as input data.
    * A non-permanent, note-like store used to bring long-term memory content into day-to-day activities.
    - A permanent store that replaces long-term memory for day-to-day activities.
    - A set of five to nine input modalities used to operate an interface.
    because: Human memory broadly includes short-term and long-term memory, and short-term memory is a note-like non-permanent store used to bring information from long-term memory to aid day-to-day activities.
  Q Why should an interface avoid forcing users to remember too many chunks?  [38/S6/F2, 38/S6/F3]
    - Because the chunk limit applies to long-term memory, not short-term memory.
    * Because too many chunks overutilize short-term memory and are harmful.
    - Because chunks become harmful only when they are reduced to single letters.
    - Because too many chunks underutilize short-term memory and improve recall.
    because: Short-term memory is limited to five to nine chunks at a time, and holding more than that overutilizes it and is harmful.
  Q Why can the generic usability rules be analyzed for extended reality systems?  [38/S6/F5]

    - They were designed specifically for Microsoft HoloLens AR headsets.
    * They are not specific to a particular product or system.
    because: The generic usability rules are not tied to one product or system, so they can be analyzed for applicability to a broad class of interactive systems, including extended reality systems.

38/A10  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (8 facts, 32 concepts)
  Shneiderman's rules | *Prototype | Apple's guidelines | Norman's principles  (Shneiderman's rules, Norman's principles, and Apple's guidelines are design guidelines; a prototype is a way of expressing design ideas, not a design guideline.)  [38/S1/F3, 38/S1/F4, 38/S1/F6]
  Consistency | *Presence | Feedback | Closure  (Consistency, closure, and feedback are Shneiderman golden-rule design concepts; presence is a user psychological quality enhanced by interaction techniques, not one of those rules.)  [38/S2/F2, 38/S3/F0, 38/S4/F3, 38/S7/F1]
  *Selection | Navigation | System control | Object interaction  (Object interaction, navigation, and system-control interaction are the broad categories of immersive-environment interaction; selection is a type of object interaction, not a separate broad category.)  [38/S7/F2]

38/A11  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 41 concepts)
  Q How do the two design stages in the interactive system development lifecycle differ in purpose, and why is the design stage placed in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle?  [38/S0/F0, 38/S0/F1, 38/S1/F0; interactive system development lifecycle, design stage, code design, design-prototype-evaluate cycle, design-prototype-evaluation cycle, non-interactive software development, immersive experience, user requirement]
    A The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design. Code design is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development. The design stage is in the design-prototype-evaluation cycle, which is involved in designing an immersive experience in order to incorporate user requirements.
  Q Why is having a design language important for interface and interaction design, and how can a prototype serve that role?  [38/S1/F1, 38/S1/F5, 38/S1/F6; interface and interaction design, design process, design language, prototype, interface design, code design]
    A Interface and interaction design involves how to start the design process and how to express a design so it can be brainstormed and refined, which means having a design language. A design language is a specification of design, and the language used to specify interface design is generally different from the language used to specify code design. A prototype can be considered a language for expressing interface and interaction design ideas.
  Q Why can Shneiderman's eight golden rules guide an extended reality system, while some virtual reality-specific guidelines are not automatically transferable to augmented reality?  [38/S2/F0, 38/S2/F1, 38/S2/F2; Shneiderman's eight golden rules, generic design rule, extended reality system, interactive system, graphical user interface, specific design guideline, virtual reality, augmented reality, cybersickness, immersion, immersive system]
    A Shneiderman's eight golden rules are generic design rules that are applicable to any interactive system, including extended reality systems, although they are mostly rather than fully applicable to extended reality systems. They were originally developed primarily for graphical user interfaces, but they can be partly or fully applicable to other types of interfaces. Specific design guidelines for avoiding or minimizing cybersickness are typically applicable to virtual reality or immersive systems and may not be specifically applicable to augmented reality systems because augmented reality immersion differs from virtual reality immersion.
  Q How does interaction design in an augmented reality setting differ from design for immersive virtual reality or mixed reality, and what broad categories cover interaction in immersive environments?  [38/S7/F0, 38/S7/F1, 38/S7/F2; augmented reality, touch, gesture, virtual reality, mixed reality, interaction technique, presence, object interaction, navigation, interaction for system control, selection, manipulation, virtual environment]
    A Interaction in non-immersive settings such as augmented reality is similar to familiar interactions such as touch and gesture. For immersive virtual reality or mixed reality experiences, specialized techniques and setups are used, and suitable interaction techniques should be known and used to design the experience properly and enhance presence. Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means changing system-related settings.

===== lecture 39: System Design

39/A0  quiz  39/S0  "Quick quiz"  (1 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q In immersive experience design, which interaction category is mainly used to set up a system, initialize parameters, and choose options or menus?  [39/S0/F0]
    - Object manipulation
    - Environment modeling
    - Navigation
    * System control
    because: System control is the interaction category used for system setup, parameter initialization, and selecting options or menus.
  Q How is navigation distinguished from object interaction in immersive experience design?  [39/S0/F0]
    - It selects a virtual object and then changes one of its properties.
    - It creates a virtual scene by converting surfaces into triangular meshes.
    * It moves the viewpoint from one virtual location to another, mostly without manipulating objects.
    - It aligns virtual content with a matching real-world region.
    because: Navigation involves moving from one point in the virtual world to another with a corresponding change in viewpoint, and it mostly does not involve object interaction.

39/A1  quiz  39/S1  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 22 concepts)
  Q In virtual object interaction, how do selection and manipulation differ?  [39/S1/F0]
    - Selection sets system options; manipulation specifies virtual objects.
    - Selection changes object properties; manipulation specifies objects from a virtual set.
    * Selection specifies objects; manipulation changes properties of an already selected object.
    - Selection moves the user's viewpoint; manipulation changes object properties.
    because: Object interaction includes selection for specifying one or more objects and manipulation for changing the properties of selected objects.
  Q Which variable can determine which object-selection technique is suitable, alongside target distance and direction?  [39/S1/F1]
    - The physical surface property of the target object
    - The triangular mesh complexity of the target object
    - The matched-zone alignment of the target with the real world
    * The density of objects around the target object
    because: Selection performance is influenced by variables such as target distance, direction, size, density around the target, and the number of targets.
  Q What special consideration applies to selecting a fully occluded virtual object?  [39/S1/F2]
    - It requires no specialized technique because occlusion is irrelevant.
    * The user must first be made aware that the object is present.
    - It is usually the majority case in object selection.
    - It becomes easier than selecting a partially visible object.
    because: Partly occluded targets are challenging, and fully occluded targets require awareness of their presence before they can be selected.
  Q Which option lists two object-selection techniques?  [39/S1/F3]
    - Object manipulation and volume-based selection
    * Pointing-based selection and bimanual selection
    - Hand manipulation and camera navigation
    - Navigation and system control
    because: Object selection techniques include hand selection, pointing-based selection, image plane selection, volume-based selection, and bimanual selection.

39/A2  quiz  39/S2  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q What characterizes the virtual hand hand-selection technique?  [39/S2/F2]
    - A virtual hand remains still when the physical hand moves below a specified minimum velocity
    - A virtual hand is guided by a ray that selects the first object it intersects
    * A visible virtual hand follows the physical hand through a one-to-one mapping of motion and orientation
    - A visible virtual hand changes the virtual arm length to reach distant objects quickly
    because: The virtual hand technique uses a visible hand as an avatar of the physical hand, tied to it by a one-to-one mapping of motion and orientation.
  Q In go-go hand selection, why can selecting a distant small object be imprecise?  [39/S2/F4, 39/S2/F5]
    * As distance increases, small physical hand movements are mapped to larger and faster virtual hand movements
    - The physical and virtual hands maintain a fixed one-to-one mapping at all distances
    - The virtual hand remains still when the physical hand moves below a specified minimum velocity
    - The virtual hand moves more slowly when the target object is farther away
    because: Go-go maps smaller physical movements to larger and faster virtual movements for farther objects, so a small movement can miss or cross a distant small target.
  Q How does the prism technique improve on go-go for distant objects?  [39/S2/F6, 39/S2/F7]
    * It slows or stops the virtual hand when the physical hand moves below specified velocity thresholds
    - It bends a virtual ray toward the closest selectable object before selection
    - It requires the user to position virtual fingers around the object to refine the selection
    - It keeps the virtual hand moving at full speed even when the physical hand is stopped
    because: Prism applies scaled-down motion when the physical hand moves slowly and keeps the virtual hand still below a minimum velocity, giving a control benefit not present in go-go.
  Q What does intent-driven selection use to refine which object is selected?  [39/S2/F9, 39/S2/F10]
    - A one-to-one mapping of physical hand motion to a visible virtual hand
    - A scaled mapping in which small physical movements move the virtual hand faster
    * Hand or finger postures that progressively reduce proximity spheres around the target
    - A ray from the head or eye that selects the first intersected object
    because: Intent-driven selection uses virtual hand movement and finger postures, often with proximity spheres that shrink as the user gets closer, to refine the selection.

39/A3  quiz  39/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q In basic pointing-based object selection, how does the user select a virtual object?  [39/S3/F0]
    - Choosing the object nearest to the controller regardless of the ray
    * Extending a visible ray and triggering the controller to select the first intersected object
    - Moving a virtual hand until it directly touches the object
    - Pointing at an object and holding it until it automatically selects
    because: Pointing-based selection works by extending a visible ray into the virtual world and using a controller trigger to select the first object intersected by that ray.
  Q How can the pointing ray be moved without the user using a hand?  [39/S3/F1]
    - By moving the body in place
    * By moving the head or changing the eye gaze
    - By pressing a selection button on a wristband
    - By moving a hand-held controller
    because: Pointing can be done with head movement from a head-mounted display or with eye-gaze tracking, both without hand use.
  Q Why can selecting a small distant object be difficult in ray casting?  [39/S3/F5]
    * It requires precise pointing, especially when other objects surround it
    - It requires the ray to automatically bend toward the object
    - It requires a depth marker to be placed at the object
    - It requires the user to physically reach the object
    because: In ray casting, the ray must be pointed precisely, and the difficulty increases when a small object is surrounded by other objects.
  Q How does bend cast help a user select an object?  [39/S3/F6]
    * It bends the ray toward the closest selectable object
    - It selects the largest object intersected by the ray
    - It extends the ray only to a fixed distance
    - It uses a depth marker to choose among objects
    because: Bend cast improves basic ray casting by bending the ray toward the closest selectable object, so the user does not need to point as precisely.
  Q What does the depth ray technique add to basic ray casting?  [39/S3/F8]
    - An eye-gaze estimate that replaces the pointing ray
    * A user-controlled depth marker that selects the intersected object closest to the marker
    - A circular arc that visually bends the ray
    - A timer that selects the first highlighted object
    because: Depth ray uses a user-controlled depth marker to disambiguate multiple intersected objects and select the intersected object closest to the marker.

39/A4  quiz  39/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q Which description best matches image-plane selection?  [39/S4/F1, 39/S4/F2]
    - A 3D selection made by shaping a box around the object with both hands
    - A selection made by pointing a ray and choosing the first intersected object
    * A 2D selection made by aligning an object with a hand between the eye and the object
    - A selection made by casting a cone and choosing the objects inside it
    because: Image-plane selection is a 2D selection on a view plane. The user holds a hand or finger between the eye and the object and signals when the object lines up with the hand and eye.
  Q How does volumetric selection extend image-plane selection?  [39/S4/F8]
    - By letting the user select the first object intersected by a virtual ray
    - By letting the user select an object on a 2D view plane
    - By letting the user select an object directly under a single finger
    * By letting the user select a 3D region so objects inside it are selected
    because: Volumetric selection allows selection of a 3D region in virtual space, with objects within that region selected. The region can be a box, sphere, or cone.
  Q What does the cone casting flashlight technique do?  [39/S4/F9]
    - It casts a sphere onto the nearest intersected surface and selects objects within the sphere
    * It casts a cone to a distance and selects the objects within the cone
    - It holds a hand between the eye and the object until they line up
    - It uses both hands to shape and reduce a box around a 3D region
    because: The cone casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection method that extends ray casting by casting a cone and selecting objects inside that cone.
  Q What is two-handed box selection?  [39/S4/F12]
    - A technique in which a sphere is cast onto a surface and objects inside the sphere are selected
    - A technique in which a hand is held between the eye and an object to align it
    - A technique in which a cone is cast to a distance and objects inside the cone are selected
    * A bimanual technique in which both hands position, orient, and shape a box to select a 3D region
    because: Two-handed box selection uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube, and progressively reduces it to select a specified 3D region.
  Q When is a volumetric selection technique less effective for selecting smaller objects?  [39/S4/F13]
    - When the pointing ray intersects only a single object
    * When the virtual environment is complex and contains many objects
    - When the user is selecting on a two-dimensional view plane
    - When the target object is small, well-defined, and isolated
    because: Volumetric selection is most useful for small, well-defined isolated objects in a less complex virtual environment. Selecting smaller objects becomes problematic when the environment is complex with many objects.

39/A5  quiz  39/S5  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 20 concepts)
  Q In XR interaction, object manipulation mainly refers to what?  [39/S5/F0]
    - Tracking the user's sense organs to update a VR system's input
    - Estimating the viewer's pose relative to an anchor in the real world
    - Selecting an object by framing it with the hands in a 2D image plane
    * Changing an object's properties, such as position, orientation, scale, or texture, after it is selected
    because: Object manipulation is the modification of an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, behavior, and others, and it typically follows selection of the object.
  Q Which of the following is an object manipulation technique?  [39/S5/F1]
    - Volumetric selection
    - Sense-organ tracking
    - Image plane selection
    * Bimanual manipulation
    because: Manipulation techniques include hand manipulation, indirect manipulation, bimanual manipulation, and integrated hybrid manipulation.
  Q What is the core idea behind hand manipulation?  [39/S5/F2]
    * Using a virtual hand to manipulate objects
    - Applying operations to an object's local coordinate system
    - Framing an object with the hands in a 2D image plane
    - Using a cone to select objects within a 3D region
    because: Hand manipulation extends the virtual hand idea and uses a virtual hand to manipulate objects.
  Q Which statement is true about hand manipulation?  [39/S5/F3]
    - It is a two-dimensional selection technique performed on a view plane

    * It follows hand selection and can use smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controller-based interaction
    - It is the least intuitive way of manipulating objects
    because: Hand manipulation follows hand selection and is implemented using smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controller-based interaction, and it is the most intuitive way of manipulating objects.

    - It requires casting a cone instead of a ray for selection
    - It requires a stationary transmitter that produces a magnetic field
    because: Hand manipulation requires somewhat more computational power or specialized devices, which may be relatively costly.

39/A12  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 40 concepts)
  Q In immersive interaction design, why might head pointing or eye-gaze pointing be useful for selecting virtual objects when hand tracking is unavailable?  [39/S3/F1, 39/S3/F2; pointing-based selection, virtual ray, hand tracking, head position, eye gaze, head-mounted display, eye tracker, hand pointing, eye-gaze pointing, virtual hand]
    A Pointing-based selection can be done by hand pointing, head pointing with a head-mounted display, or eye-gaze pointing with an eye tracker. A virtual ray can be attached to the virtual hand, head position, or eye gaze, with head position or eye gaze used when hand tracking is unavailable.
  Q How do the go-go and prism techniques change virtual hand selection for distant objects, and why might prism still be preferable to go-go?  [39/S2/F3, 39/S2/F4, 39/S2/F7, 39/S2/F8; virtual hand technique, go-go technique, prism technique, virtual arm length, hand velocity, one-to-one mapping]
    A A direct virtual hand can require a long duration of physical hand movement to reach distant objects, so the go-go technique changes the virtual arm length and maps smaller physical hand movements to faster virtual hand movement. Prism applies scaled-down motion when the physical hand moves below a specified speed and leaves the virtual hand still when the physical hand is slower than a specified minimum speed. Prism can therefore be a better solution for distant objects because the virtual hand slows or stops when the physical hand slows or stops, although it does not use a one-to-one mapping, which may be counterintuitive.
  Q Why can selecting small or tightly grouped objects be difficult in both ray casting and volumetric selection, even though they use different selection geometries?  [39/S3/F5, 39/S4/F10, 39/S4/F13; ray casting, volumetric selection, cone casting flashlight technique, virtual ray, object selection technique, virtual environment]
    A Ray casting requires precise pointing of a virtual ray, so selecting small distant objects is difficult, especially when the small object is surrounded by other objects. The cone casting flashlight technique is volumetric and selects the objects within a cone, so selecting smaller or tightly grouped objects can be difficult. Volumetric selection is most useful for small or well-defined isolated objects in a less complex virtual environment and becomes problematic when the environment is complex with many objects.
  Q Why might a single three-dimensional widget not be enough to fully manipulate a virtual object, and how does that follow from the idea of degrees of freedom?  [28/S2/F1, 28/S2/F2, 39/S6/F2; three-dimensional widget, degree of freedom, six degrees of freedom, three-dimensional, virtual object, manipulation]
    A Degrees of freedom describe the different ways an object can move in space, and in three-dimensional space an object can have six degrees of freedom: three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes and three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch. A three-dimensional widget is typically responsible only for a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom. Therefore, specified sets of degrees of freedom are manipulated using individual widgets rather than one widget for all properties.
