40/A8  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (16 facts, 61 concepts)
  Q How do locomotion and wayfinding work together in navigation through a virtual world, and why is wayfinding support important for user experience?  [40/S0/F1, 40/S1/F0, 40/S5/F1, 40/S5/F2, 40/S5/F6; virtual world, navigation, travel, locomotion, wayfinding, mental model, user experience]
    A Navigation in a virtual world includes travel and wayfinding, and locomotion is the motor component that moves the user from one point to another. Wayfinding refers to location awareness and to building a mental model or cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment. Locomotion or travel support alone is not sufficient, because without suitable wayfinding support the user cannot use travel techniques efficiently or effectively in a complex virtual environment.
  Q Why can full gait techniques create a mismatch between physical and virtual movement, and how do partial gait and gait negation techniques handle the user's physical movement?  [40/S2/F3, 40/S2/F4, 40/S2/F5, 40/S2/F6; walking-based locomotion, full gait technique, partial gait technique, gait negation technique, virtual navigation]
    A In full gait techniques, completely free walking is not practical, so walking is restricted in the physical space and translated to any amount of movement in virtual space, creating a mismatch. In partial gait techniques, the user walks in place and specialized devices or active walking interfaces map the in-place walking pattern to different types of virtual movement. In gait negation techniques, a specialized setup cancels lateral movement and keeps the user's physical position fixed before the movement is mapped to virtual navigation.
  Q How does target selection-based locomotion differ from route planning-based locomotion, and why can route planning give a more gradual sense of movement?  [40/S4/F0, 40/S4/F1, 40/S4/F2, 40/S4/F4; selection-based locomotion, target selection-based locomotion, route planning-based locomotion, teleportation, virtual viewpoint]
    A Target selection-based locomotion lets the user select a destination, and the virtual viewpoint changes so the user feels moved to the target, as in teleportation, map dragging, or the jumper technique. Route planning-based locomotion lets the user select a route to the target rather than only the endpoint. Different viewpoint changes while moving through the selected route make the user feel movement along a path, providing more granular control and slightly more natural movement than target-based teleportation.
  Q How is interaction for system control different from navigation and object interaction in an immersive environment?  [40/S6/F0, 40/S6/F1, 38/S7/F2; interaction for system control, navigation, object manipulation, system state, system mode, command]
    A Object interaction in immersive environments means selecting and manipulating objects that are part of the virtual environment, while navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment. Interaction for system control issues commands that change system state or mode, such as launching an application, changing system settings, or opening a file. It can use physical controllers, graphical menus, voice commands, gesture commands, tools, or multimodal interaction techniques.

  check put_in_order:40: empty

41/A13  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 43 concepts)
  Q How does identifying pilgrims, students, and tourists as user categories shape what a user sees in the Majuli VR tour before and during the experience?  [41/S1/F0, 41/S1/F1, 41/S2/F2, 41/S7/F1; user categories, user experience design, contextual inquiry, user group, icon, tablet interface, video player, user type, video]
    A In user experience design, the first stage is to identify the users so the experience can be designed accordingly. The tour identifies pilgrims, students, and tourists, whose preferences were collected through contextual inquiry, and before the tour the user chooses one of these groups using icons. During the tour, the tablet interface lists videos available for the current spot, and the corresponding material is added in a way that depends on the user type, so relevant information is tailored to that user.
  Q How do the virtual vehicle travel technique and the dual maps address the two components of navigation in the Majuli VR tour?  [40/S5/F0, 40/S1/F1, 41/S6/F6, 41/S5/F5, 41/S5/F6; navigation, locomotion technique, wayfinding, virtual vehicle travel technique, selection-based locomotion technique, route, destination, virtual world, dual maps, global map, minimap, orientation awareness]
    A Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding. The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which a route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route, allowing the user to travel in the virtual world and perceive that travel has occurred. The dual maps, made of a global map and a local minimap, support wayfinding and orientation awareness by showing the world in miniature and reducing clutter.
  Q Why is view interpolation important when a place in the Majuli VR tour is built from separate 360-degree images, and how does that choice support user comfort?  [41/S6/F0, 41/S6/F1, 41/S8/F2; 360-degree image, view interpolation, smooth transition, spatial orientation, anxiety, sensory conflict, cybersickness]
    A Each place is designed using a series of 360-degree images, so moving from one point to another is moving from one image to another. View interpolation ensures a smooth visual transition between two 360-degree images by blurring their boundaries, preventing the sudden movement or jerks that an unhandled image transition would cause. Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions help maintain spatial orientation, reduce anxiety and sensory conflict, and in the long term help avoid severe cybersickness effects.

===== lecture 42: System Implementation

42/A0  quiz  42/S0  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 20 concepts)
  Q In an interactive system development lifecycle, what does empirical evaluation assess?  [42/S0/F0]
    - The usability of a single prototype
    * The usability of the whole system
    - The performance of the code after testing
    - The appearance of the interface design
    because: Empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.
  Q At what point in the interactive system development lifecycle is empirical usability evaluation performed?  [42/S0/F2]
    - After every quick evaluation of a prototype
    - During the initial feasibility study
    * After the code is bug-free or runs smoothly
    - Before requirement gathering is complete
    because: The lifecycle places the empirical or usability evaluation stage finally, after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.
  Q Why is the design, prototyping, and quick evaluation cycle repeated?  [42/S0/F3]
    * To refine the design until it stabilizes
    - To rewrite the requirements after each evaluation
    - To replace final usability evaluation with quick checks
    - To finish the full coded system as early as possible
    because: In this cycle, the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes.
  Q Which stage of interactive system development is described as standard software development work with nothing special for VR or AR?  [42/S0/F4]
    - Quick evaluation of a design prototype
    - Final usability evaluation of the whole system
    - Repeated interface design until users are satisfied
    * Coding and implementation after code design
    because: Code design, coding and implementation, code testing, and code or system evaluation are standard software development stages, with nothing special or distinct for VR or AR.
  Q Why should cycles in the interactive system development lifecycle generally be kept infrequent?  [42/S0/F6]
    - To reduce the need for usability evaluation
    * To avoid cost and time overrun
    - To keep the code from being tested too early
    - To let the design stabilize after one pass
    because: Frequent cycles lead to cost and time overrun, so cycles should generally be kept infrequent.

  Order the main stages of the interactive system development lifecycle: Feasibility study > Requirement gathering, analysis, and specification > Design-prototype-quick evaluation cycle > Code design, coding, and implementation > Code testing > Empirical usability evaluation  [42/S0/F2]

42/A2  quiz  42/S1  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 10 concepts)

    * Interface and interaction design
    - Hardware setup and content authoring planning
    - Requirements gathering and system specification

  Q Why is a quick usability evaluation needed in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle?  [42/S1/F2]
    * To keep many iteration cycles within a reasonable timeframe and ensure implemented design ideas become usable
    - To avoid creating any prototype before evaluating the final design
    - To replace the final empirical usability evaluation of the completed system
    - To measure the user's sense of presence after the system is finished
    because: Quick usability evaluation is needed so many cycles can be completed without large time or cost overrun and so design ideas lead to a usable system.
  Q What does the design-prototype-evaluate cycle involve before a design stabilizes?  [42/S1/F0]
    - Checking design guidelines, authoring assets, optimizing resources, and release
    - Building a prototype, writing final code, testing bugs, and measuring presence
    - Requirements gathering, full coding, code testing, and deployment
    * Designing, quick prototyping, evaluation, finding problems, refining, and repeating
    because: The cycle repeats design, quick prototyping, evaluation, problem-finding, and refinement, possibly through many cycles, before the design stabilizes.
  Q What is needed to evaluate a design idea quickly in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle?  [42/S1/F3]
    - A code design document and a resource optimization plan
    - A full implementation and a long-term empirical usability study
    - A set of design guidelines and a presence rating
    * A quick prototype demonstrating the idea and a quick evaluation method
    because: Quick evaluation requires both a prototype that can be built quickly and a quick method for testing that prototype.

42/A3  put_in_order  42/S1  "Order the stages of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle"  (2 facts, 7 concepts)
  Order the stages of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle: Design the interface and interactions > Build a quick prototype > Evaluate the prototype > Find usability problems > Refine the design  [42/S1/F0, 42/S1/F1]

42/A4  quiz  42/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 8 concepts)
  Q What are prototyping techniques mainly used for?  [42/S2/F0]
    - Producing a final product without later refinement or testing
    - Building a complete full implementation before any evaluation
    - Replacing design guidelines with a final verdict on usability
    * Quickly building and evaluating design ideas to collect usability feedback
    because: Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation, and they are typically used to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas.
  Q Why can a prototype be preferred over a full implementation when testing whether a design will work?  [42/S2/F2]
    - It already proves the design is usable without any evaluation
    - It is a full implementation with similar resource, manpower, and cost demands
    - It implements all functionalities in depth before collecting user feedback
    * It is a lightweight implementation with much lower resource, manpower, and cost demands
    because: A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, used to test whether a design idea will work in practice.
  Q Why are design guidelines alone not enough to judge whether a design will work?  [42/S2/F1]
    * They are only a starting point and do not show whether the design is usable or unusable
    - They provide a quick evaluation of the design after implementation
    - They list the final functional requirements that guarantee a usable design
    - They define the user groups that must be tested in the system
    because: Design guidelines are only a starting point for a design and do not indicate whether the design is good, bad, usable, or unusable.
  Q What is a risk of developing a full software implementation before testing the design idea?  [42/S2/F3]
    - The full system is guaranteed to be usable once every function is built
    * Money and time spent on programmers and resources can be wasted if the idea is not good
    - The project avoids cost components such as resource procurement and manpower engagement
    - The design is accepted as good without needing empirical evaluation
    because: A full implementation involves highly skilled manpower and many cost components, so if the idea is later found not good, the money and time invested are wasted.
  Q What can happen to a prototype after it has been used to test design ideas?  [42/S2/F4]
    - It must always be replaced by a separately built full implementation
    - It must remain a horizontal prototype for feedback on appearance
    * It can be discarded, or it can be incrementally refined and tested until it becomes the final product
    - It cannot be changed after its first evaluation has been completed
    because: A prototype can be discarded after it has served its purpose of testing design ideas, or it can be incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it evolves into the fully implemented final product.

42/A5  quiz  42/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q Which description best matches a horizontal prototype?  [42/S3/F1]
    - An in-depth implementation of selected features from first to last screen
    - A series of sketches showing the sequence of actions in a task
    - A complete implementation of every feature in the system
    * A surface-level depiction of the entire interface's look, feel, and appearance
    because: A horizontal prototype shows how the interface appears to the user at a surface level, without functionality or interaction.
  Q What is a horizontal prototype most suitable for?  [42/S3/F2]
    - Capturing the sequence of user actions in a task
    - Testing whether every feature works in the full system
    - Analyzing interactions implemented in selected features
    * Eliciting feedback about whether the interface's appearance is understandable and intuitive
    because: Horizontal prototypes are used to discuss and collect user feedback on the look, feel, and appearance of an interface.
  Q Which description best matches a vertical prototype?  [42/S3/F3]
    * An in-depth implementation of selected commonly used features, from first screen to last
    - A surface-level depiction of the whole interface without interaction
    - A single sketch showing only the layout of one screen
    - A complete implementation of every feature in the system
    because: A vertical prototype implements a few selected features in depth, from the first screen to the last screen after the final action.
  Q Why are vertical prototypes suitable for analyzing interactions and features?  [42/S3/F3, 42/S3/F4]
    - Because they avoid implementing any functionality
    - Because they represent every feature in the full system
    * Because they implement interactions for a few selected features
    - Because they show the entire interface only at a surface level
    because: Vertical prototypes are suitable for analyzing interactions and features because they implement those interactions, rather than merely showing appearance.
  Q Which statement about the terms in a vertical prototype description is correct?  [42/S3/F5]
    - The term 'implemented' means building the full final system, and 'screen' means only a paper sketch
    - The term 'implemented' always means writing code, and 'screen' means only a physical display
    - The term 'implemented' means only VR rendering, and 'screen' means only a virtual scene
    * The term 'implemented' may not mean writing code, and 'screen' may be a 2D screen or an immersive scene
    because: In a vertical prototype, implemented and screen are generic: implementation does not require code, and a screen can be a 2D screen or a virtual or immersive scene.

42/A10  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (21 facts, 53 concepts)
  Q How does the design-prototype-evaluate cycle fit into the development of an extended reality system, and why must its evaluation be quick?  [42/S0/F1, 42/S0/F2, 42/S0/F3, 42/S1/F1, 42/S1/F2, 42/S1/F3, 32/S6/F0; interactive system development lifecycle, extended reality system, design-prototype-evaluate cycle, interface design, interaction design, usability evaluation, quick evaluation, turnaround time, cost overrun, prototype]
    A The interactive system development lifecycle is equally applicable to extended reality systems, and building interactive software is broadly similar to regular software, with differences in requirement gathering, the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, and empirical study stages. The lifecycle includes a design, prototyping, and quick evaluation cycle that is repeated until the design stabilizes, where design means interface and interaction design rather than code design. Quick usability evaluation is required because the cycle may need many repetitions; if evaluation is slow, turnaround time increases and leads to cost overrun, while a quick prototype and quick evaluation method keep the cycles within a reasonable timeframe.
  Q Why can a prototype be a better way to test a design idea than immediately doing a full implementation, especially when design guidelines are available?  [42/S2/F1, 42/S2/F2, 42/S2/F3, 42/S2/F4; design guideline, prototype, full implementation, usability, testing, programmer, final product]
    A Design guidelines are only a starting point for a design and do not indicate whether the design is usable, so the design needs to be implemented and tested. A prototype is a lightweight implementation with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, so it can test whether a design idea will work before programmers and expensive resources are committed. A full implementation uses highly skilled programmers and many cost components, so if the idea is later found not good, the money and time invested are wasted. After serving its purpose, the prototype can be discarded, or it can be incrementally refined and tested until it evolves into the final product.
  Q How do horizontal and vertical prototypes differ, and why can a storyboard support the kind of prototype that a single interface sketch cannot?  [42/S3/F1, 42/S3/F2, 42/S3/F3, 42/S3/F4, 42/S4/F4, 42/S4/F5, 42/S4/F6; horizontal prototype, vertical prototype, interface, user feedback, interaction, feature, functionality, interface sketch, storyboard, keyframe, user action, task, screen]
    A A horizontal prototype depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing look, feel, and appearance without functionality or interaction, so it is suitable for obtaining user feedback about appearance. A vertical prototype primarily represents selected interactions or features by implementing them in depth from the first screen to the last screen, so it is suitable for analyzing interaction. A single interface sketch is primarily a horizontal prototype because it does not show the sequence of user actions and corresponding interface changes. A series of interface sketches forms a storyboard, whose keyframes can capture the sequence of user actions from the beginning to the end of a task and thus give a vertical prototype.
  Q Why can the Wizard of Oz approach be useful for testing an interaction idea, and what did the IBM listening typewriter experiment use it to do?  [42/S2/F2, 42/S6/F0, 42/S6/F1, 42/S6/F3; prototype, interaction, wizard of oz approach, wizard, international business machines, listening typewriter experiment, speech recognition system, microphone, computer]
    A A prototype is used to test whether a design idea will work in practice before full implementation is committed. In the Wizard of Oz approach, a human subject believes they are interacting with an autonomous computer, but an unseen wizard operates the computer and returns the requested response. In the 1984 IBM listening typewriter experiment, the user spoke into a microphone, the hidden wizard heard the speech, typed corresponding characters, and transmitted them to the user's screen, making the user believe speech had been automatically converted. IBM used this to test the acceptability of a speech recognition system before committing resources to build one, because the automatic technology was not yet available.

===== lecture 43: System Implementation

43/A0  quiz  43/S0  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 8 concepts)
  Q Which description matches a throwaway prototype?  [43/S0/F0, 43/S0/F1]
    - It is refined from a simpler whole-system version into the final product
    * It is used for quick evaluation and then discarded
    - It is built by integrating separately tested modules
    - It is represented by a storyboard of interface sketches
    because: Prototypes can be throwaway, incremental, or evolutionary, and throwaway prototypes are specifically used for quick evaluation and then discarded.
  Q Low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches are mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes because:  [43/S0/F2]
    - they support interactive multimedia content for augmented reality evaluation
    - they can be retained and refined into the final product
    * they are low-cost and discarding them does not incur significant cost
    - they allow separate modules to be prototyped and tested before integration
    because: Throwaway prototypes should be easy and fast to create, and low-fidelity mockups and sketches are suitable because they are inexpensive and cheap to discard.
  Q Which description matches incremental prototyping?  [43/S0/F3]
    - It is refined from a simpler whole-system version into the final product
    - It is used for quick evaluation and then discarded
    * It is built by separately prototyping and testing modules and then integrating them
    - It is made as low-cost paper sketches that are easy to discard
    because: Incremental prototypes are created when the system is divided into modules, each module is separately prototyped and tested, and the modules are then integrated into the overall system.
  Q Which description matches evolutionary prototyping?  [43/S0/F4]
    - It is used for quick evaluation and then discarded
    - It is made from cardboard mockups and paper sketches that are easy to discard
    * It starts with a simpler version of the whole system and is refined into the final product
    - It is built by separately prototyping and testing modules before integration
    because: Evolutionary prototypes are created by prototyping and testing the whole system from the beginning, starting with a simpler version and refining it until it becomes the final product.

43/A1  quiz  43/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q What is the main distinction between quick prototype evaluation and a robust evaluation technique?  [43/S1/F0]
    - Quick evaluation is performed only after the final product is available.
    * Quick evaluation is a fast, low-cost way to evaluate a prototype early in design.
    - Quick evaluation requires a full evaluation setup with extensive resources.
    - A robust evaluation is fast and low-cost, while quick evaluation is slow and resource-intensive.
    because: Quick evaluation, also called expert evaluation, is meant to evaluate a prototype quickly and cheaply at an early stage of design, unlike a more robust evaluation setup.
  Q What are the prerequisites for performing quick or expert evaluation?  [43/S1/F1]
    - At least a full implementation and a robust evaluation setup.
    - At least a final product and a single evaluator.
    - At least a high-fidelity prototype and no evaluator team.
    * At least a low-fidelity prototype and a team of evaluators.
    because: Quick or expert evaluation needs at least a low-fidelity prototype, with better-quality prototypes preferred, and a team of evaluators.
  Q Why can quick or expert evaluation rely mainly on design-team members or domain experts instead of end users?  [43/S1/F3]
    * They are assumed to have user-like experience, and engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper.
    - Engaging end users is usually less complicated, quicker, and cheaper.
    - Designers are assumed to be less user-like than end users.
    - Their feedback is used to verify the full implementation rather than the interface.
    because: Design-team members or domain experts are used because they are assumed to have user-like experience and can be engaged more simply, quickly, and cheaply than a full end-user evaluation.
  Q Although usability testing normally involves users, who mainly conducts quick or expert evaluation?  [43/S1/F2]
    * The design team or skilled designers with knowledge of the problem domain.
    - Only software developers, because they are testing code design.
    - Only external evaluators from a robust evaluation setup.
    - Only end users, because usability testing always requires users.
    because: Quick evaluation is a usability test, but its team is primarily the design team or skilled designers with problem-domain knowledge, with a few end users optional.
  Q How is the final list of usability issues produced in expert evaluation?  [43/S1/F5]
    - End users review the independent reports and publish the final list.
    - Evaluators discuss in one group and agree on issues before inspecting the prototype.
    - A single evaluator writes the final list without combining independent reports.
    * Each evaluator independently reports issues, and the design team or team lead combines the reports.
    because: In expert evaluation, evaluators work independently, each producing a report of perceived usability issues, which the design team or team lead then combines into a final list.

43/A2  quiz  43/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q What is the minimum prototype needed for a cognitive walkthrough?  [43/S2/F1]
    - A high-fidelity vertical prototype
    * A low-fidelity vertical prototype
    - A low-fidelity horizontal prototype
    - A complete full implementation
    because: A cognitive walkthrough requires at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, while a high-fidelity prototype is more welcome but not required.
  Q In a cognitive walkthrough, what do evaluators do with the described task?  [43/S2/F3]

    - They evaluate the whole system using a heuristic checklist
    - They ask end users to answer the usability questions directly
    * They convert it into interface-level tasks and perform them in the prototype

    - A resource-optimization recommendation
    * A detailed report explaining where difficulty occurred and why
    - A simple yes or no answer
    - A single tick on a heuristic checklist
    because: For each usability question, evaluators must explain where they felt difficulty in the interface or interaction and why, rather than giving a simple yes or no.

    - A high-fidelity prototype made with Adobe Flash
    - A set of usability heuristics for checklist inspection

    - They are replaced by a checklist of system heuristics
    - They are published as final product requirements

43/A4  quiz  43/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 27 concepts)
  Q What distinguishes heuristic evaluation from a task-specific evaluation?  [43/S3/F0]
    - Evaluators inspect only the parts needed for one task.
    - Evaluators assess a prototype by performing a task scenario.
    * Evaluators check a whole prototype against heuristics without a task scenario.
    - Evaluators measure task performance to evaluate the whole system.
    because: Heuristic evaluation assesses a presented prototype by ticking checklist items, without a task scenario or task performance, to evaluate the whole system rather than one task.
  Q Why do broader usability checklists usually contain fewer heuristics than detailed system-specific checklists?  [43/S3/F1]
    * They are broader in nature and not specific to any particular interface.
    - They are detailed checklists tied to one particular interface.
    - They are broader in nature and specific to a single interface.
    - They are task-oriented checklists tied to one scenario.
    because: Broader usability checklists contain fewer heuristics because they cover broader principles rather than details of a particular interface.
  Q What does the 'recognition rather than recall' heuristic require in an interface?  [43/S3/F3]
    - The user should prevent errors before they occur through design.
    * The user should recognize from visible elements what to do rather than recall it.
    - The user should have freedom to undo or cancel actions.
    - The user should recall commands without relying on visible elements.
    because: Recognition rather than recall means the user should be able to recognize from interface elements what to do, because recollection is more difficult than recognition.
  Q How does the prototype requirement for heuristic evaluation differ from that for a cognitive walkthrough?  [43/S3/F4]
    - Both methods require a vertical prototype to identify usability problems.
    - Heuristic evaluation needs a vertical prototype; cognitive walkthrough can use a horizontal prototype.
    - Heuristic evaluation requires a final product; cognitive walkthrough can use a low-fidelity storyboard.
    * Heuristic evaluation can use low-fidelity, mainly horizontal prototypes; cognitive walkthrough needs a vertical prototype.
    because: Heuristic evaluation can identify problems from simple low-fidelity prototypes, primarily horizontal ones, whereas a cognitive walkthrough requires a vertical prototype.
  Q What does each evaluator do during heuristic evaluation?  [43/S3/F6]
    - They select only a few heuristics to check before the evaluation.
    - They perform task scenarios and report task completion rates.
    - They give a simple yes or no answer without explaining violations.
    * They check each heuristic, report violations with reasons, and the reports are combined.
    because: Each evaluator evaluates the prototype against each heuristic, reports whether it is followed or violated with reasons if violated, and the reports are combined to identify major issues.

43/A5  put_in_order  43/S3  "Order the steps of a heuristic evaluation"  (3 facts, 8 concepts)
  Order the steps of a heuristic evaluation: Prepare a prototype, heuristic checklist, and evaluation team > Evaluators assess the prototype against each heuristic > Evaluators report heuristics violated with reasons > Violated heuristics and major issues are compiled  [43/S3/F0, 43/S3/F5, 43/S3/F6]

  *High-fidelity prototype | Paper prototype | Paper sketch | Cardboard mockup  (Cardboard mockups, paper sketches and paper prototypes are low-fidelity prototype forms; a high-fidelity prototype is a higher-fidelity prototype, not a low-fidelity form.)  [43/S0/F2, 43/S2/F2, 43/S2/F1]

43/A7  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 38 concepts)
  Q Why are low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes, and what condition must such prototypes satisfy to remain useful?  [43/S0/F1, 43/S0/F2; prototype, throwaway prototype, low-fidelity cardboard mockup, paper sketch]
    A Throwaway prototypes are prototypes that are used for quick evaluation and then discarded. Low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches are mainly suitable for them because they are less costly and discarding them does not incur significant cost. They are also a good match because throwaway prototypes should be easy and fast to create, otherwise working with them becomes expensive.
  Q How do incremental prototypes and evolutionary prototypes differ in the way they follow from the structure of a system design?  [43/S0/F3, 43/S0/F4; incremental prototype, evolutionary prototype, system design, module]
    A Incremental prototypes are created when the system design divides the system into units or modules, each module is separately prototyped and tested, and the modules are then integrated into the overall system. Evolutionary prototypes are created by prototyping and testing the whole system from the beginning, starting with a simpler version, refining it, adding more functionalities, and altering it based on testing results. The evolutionary approach does this rather than prototyping separate modules and combining them.
  Q How do cognitive walkthrough and heuristic evaluation differ in the prototype, scenario, and evaluation procedure they require?  [43/S2/F0, 43/S2/F1, 43/S3/F0, 43/S3/F4; cognitive walkthrough, expert evaluation, usability inspection, usability problem, prototype, low-fidelity vertical prototype, scenario, interface-level task, heuristic evaluation, checklist, heuristic, task scenario, task performance, horizontal prototype, vertical prototype]
    A Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation and usability inspection method that identifies usability problems by inspecting a prototype, and it requires at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype plus a scenario whose task is converted into interface-level tasks. Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to evaluate the whole system rather than one task. Because heuristic evaluation can use low-fidelity prototypes, primarily horizontal prototypes, with vertical prototypes optional, it is less dependent on task-driven interaction than cognitive walkthrough.
  Q How can expert evaluation support repeated refinement of a prototype, and why can its evaluation team rely on design team members or domain experts rather than a full end-user team?  [42/S1/F0, 43/S1/F0, 43/S1/F1, 43/S1/F2, 43/S1/F3; prototype, expert evaluation, low-fidelity prototype, evaluation team, design team, skilled designer, problem domain, domain expert, user]
    A When a design is prototyped, evaluated, problems are found, and the design is refined repeatedly, expert evaluation can provide quick and cheap evaluation of a low-fidelity prototype at an early stage of design. The required evaluation team can be the design team itself, skilled designers with knowledge and skill in the problem domain, or domain experts, and it may optionally include a few end users. It can rely on these people rather than a full end-user evaluation team because they are assumed to have user-like experience, their feedback likely reflects users, and engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper.

===== lecture 44: System Implementation

44/A0  quiz  44/S0  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q In user evaluation, what makes the feedback a self-report?  [44/S0/F0, 44/S0/F1, 44/S0/F3]
    - The system automatically records performance scores
    - An evaluation team provides ratings without user involvement
    * Users themselves rate questions or statements
    - Experts observe users and complete the rating scales
    because: User evaluation asks users directly and collects their feedback with rating scales, so the reports come from the users themselves.

    - A team of evaluators

    * Direct involvement of users

    * After each task and at the end of the session
    - Only at the end of the session
    - Only before the session begins
    because: Collecting feedback after every task and at the end of the session is desirable if feasible.

44/A9  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 41 concepts)
  Q How does user evaluation differ from expert evaluation in the role of the evaluator, and why may the questionnaires used after individual tasks be different from those used at the end of an evaluation session?  [44/S0/F0, 44/S0/F5; user evaluation, expert evaluation, questionnaire, post-task data collection, post-session data collection]
    A User evaluation obtains feedback by asking users directly and requires user involvement, whereas in expert evaluation techniques user involvement is optional. In user evaluation, feedback can be collected after every task and at the end of the session, and both points are desirable if feasible. Because questionnaires must be created for the point at which data are collected, the after-task questionnaires need not be the same as the post-session questionnaires.
  Q How do the After Scenario Questionnaire and the System Usability Scale differ in timing and in the kind of usability information they provide?  [44/S1/F0, 44/S1/F2, 44/S2/F0, 44/S2/F5; after scenario questionnaire, system usability scale, post-task data collection, post-session data collection, effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction, usability problem, brainstorming]
    A The After Scenario Questionnaire is a post-task questionnaire whose three statements relate to effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction. The System Usability Scale is a post-session questionnaire administered after users have completed all tasks. The System Usability Scale gives a quick general indication of whether usability problems exist, but it does not explain the reasons, so designers must identify specific problems through further brainstorming or by examining individual statement scores.
  Q Why would an extended reality evaluation use the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire alongside a generic usability questionnaire such as the System Usability Scale?  [44/S3/F0, 44/S3/F1, 10/S0/F0; system usability scale, simulator sickness questionnaire, cybersickness, extended reality, virtual reality, interactive system]
    A The System Usability Scale is a generic questionnaire applicable to any interactive system and is not specifically meant for extended reality. The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire is the most extensively used questionnaire specifically designed for cybersickness in extended reality. Cybersickness is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.
  Q Why did the Majuli VR Tour's Google Cardboard version use compressed images and fewer videos than the Oculus Quest version, and how did the developers first reduce the application size?  [44/S4/F3, 44/S4/F4, 44/S4/F5, 44/S4/F6; Majuli VR Tour, Google Cardboard, Oculus Quest, application size, cloud services, video, 360-degree image, two-dimensional image, video playback, cultural video, drone video, 360-degree video]
    A The initial Majuli VR Tour application was 9.85 GB because its content was heavy to cover the entire geographic spread. Storing videos in cloud services and loading them from the cloud when clicked reduced the application size to 5.1 GB. Because 5.1 GB was still not suitable for mobile deployment, the Google Cardboard version compressed high-resolution 360-degree and two-dimensional images and removed most video playback, reducing the size to 0.7 GB; it used all 597 compressed images, no cultural or drone videos, and one 360-degree video for the initial experience.

===== lecture 45: System Implementation

45/A0  quiz  45/S0  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 5 concepts)
  Q What does empirical evaluation do in interactive system development?  [45/S0/F0]
    * It evaluates the usability of a developed system with end users.
    - It gathers the functional requirements before design.
    - It specifies the work context for the system.
    - It tests code until the system is executable.
    because: Empirical evaluation is the stage in which the usability of a developed system is evaluated with end users.
  Q Which stage does empirical evaluation follow in interactive system development?  [45/S0/F1]
    - The requirement-gathering stage.
    * The code testing stage.
    - The system-design stage.
    - The optimization stage.
    because: In interactive system development, empirical evaluation follows the code testing stage.
  Q Why does code testing not prove that an interactive system is usable?  [45/S0/F1]
    * It produces an executable system but does not establish usability.
    - It compares interface speed by measuring characters per minute.
    - It only evaluates a limited prototype rather than the end system.
    - It depends mainly on users' subjective quality judgments.
    because: Code testing produces an executable system, but it does not establish that the system is usable.

45/A1  quiz  45/S1  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 8 concepts)
  Q Why can quick prototype evaluations not provide a conclusive usability assessment?  [45/S1/F0]
    - They evaluate the fully implemented system, so their results are too late to judge the overall usability of the end system.
    - They collect behavioral data in a controlled experiment, so their results are too formal to judge the overall usability of the end system.
    * They are limited-scale evaluations, so their results are too limited to judge the overall usability of the end system.
    - They use a large number of evaluators, so their results are too broad to judge the overall usability of the end system.
    because: Quick prototype evaluations are limited-scale early evaluations that use a limited number of evaluators and evaluate prototypes, so they can identify major issues but cannot give a conclusive result about overall end-system usability.
  Q What is required for a conclusive usability assessment of an overall system?  [45/S1/F1]
    - Evaluating a limited prototype, preferably with a smaller number of users, through a quick early check.
    - Collecting subjective quality opinions from a small group of users.
    - Comparing the system with a familiar application by asking users which one is better.
    * Evaluating the fully implemented system, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.
    because: A conclusive usability assessment requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with more users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.
  Q What type of research is a controlled experiment used for usability evaluation?  [45/S1/F2]
    - A code testing stage
    - A requirement-gathering stage
    * Empirical research
    - A quick prototype evaluation
    because: A controlled experiment used for usability evaluation is generally referred to as empirical research, an empirical study, or a user study, and in usability evaluation it can also be called a usability study.
  Q What is a quick prototype evaluation?  [45/S1/F0]
    - A code testing stage that produces an executable system but does not establish usability.
    * A limited-scale early evaluation that uses a limited number of evaluators on prototypes.
    - A controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data from the fully implemented system.
    - A large-scale final evaluation that uses many evaluators on the fully implemented system.
    because: Quick prototype evaluations are limited-scale early evaluations that use a limited number of evaluators and evaluate prototypes.

45/A2  quiz  45/S2  "Quick quiz"  (1 facts, 7 concepts)
  Q Which sequence lists the four stages of an empirical or usability study?  [45/S2/F0]
    * Formulate research questions, determine variables, design and execute the experiment, and analyze the data.
    - Gather requirements, design the system, implement the code, and test the executable.
    - Choose a user group, run the virtual tour, collect subjective opinions, and compare with MS Word.
    - Evaluate a prototype, test the code, optimize resources, and deploy the system.
    because: An empirical study moves from research questions to variable determination, then to experiment design and execution, and finally to objective data analysis.
  Q Why are variables determined after the research questions in an empirical study?  [45/S2/F0]
    - Because subjective user feedback cannot be collected without them.
    * Because a controlled experiment cannot be designed or executed without them.
    - Because an executable system cannot be produced without them.
    - Because a quick prototype evaluation cannot identify major usability issues without them.
    because: Determining variables follows the research questions; without those variables, a controlled experiment cannot be designed or executed.

45/A3  put_in_order  45/S2  "Order the stages of an empirical usability study"  (1 facts, 7 concepts)
  Order the stages of an empirical usability study: Frame research questions > Determine variables > Design and execute an experiment to collect data > Analyze data to reach a reliable conclusion  [45/S2/F0]

45/A4  quiz  45/S3  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 9 concepts)

    - Writing functional requirements before the system is designed

    - Determining the experimental variables
    - Analyzing the empirical data
    * Formulating a research question

  Q Why is the research question "Is the new text entry GUI good?" considered problematic?  [45/S3/F2]
    - Because it produces an objective speed measurement in characters per minute
    * Because user judgments may be divided, so no clear conclusion can be drawn
    - Because it compares the new interface directly with Microsoft Word
    - Because it can be settled by evaluating a quick prototype
    because: Asking several users to judge whether the GUI is good can produce split judgments, making an answer and conclusion unlikely.

45/A5  quiz  45/S4  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q Why does asking whether a proposed text input interface is better than Microsoft Word not provide a definitive quality conclusion?  [45/S4/F0]
    - Because it asks users to complete a timed text-entry task.
    - Because it can be decided by comparing characters per minute.
    - Because 'better' has the same meaning for every user.
    * Because 'better' can mean more or fewer features depending on the user.
    because: A 'better' question does not give a definitive quality conclusion because different users may mean more or fewer features by 'better'.
  Q Why is a question about entering text faster than Microsoft Word less prone to subjective interpretation than a vague quality question?  [45/S4/F1]
    - Because it lets each user choose any text and typing goal.
    - Because it asks users to rate the overall quality of the interface.
    - Because it removes the need to collect user feedback.
    * Because it asks users to complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on speed.
    because: The speed question is less subjective because it focuses on a completed text input task and compares interfaces on speed.
  Q Why can subjective feedback still fail to support a definitive conclusion for a clear question about which text-entry interface is faster?  [45/S4/F2]
    - Because text-entry speed is impossible to measure.
    - Because every user would naturally agree on the faster interface.
    - Because the two interfaces cannot be tested with a task.
    * Because users' responses can split.
    because: Even for a clear faster-interface question, subjective feedback may not support a definitive conclusion because user responses can split.
  Q How does an experiment collect objective data to determine which text-entry interface is faster?  [45/S4/F3]
    - By counting the number of features provided by each interface.
    * By having all users input the same text and comparing their logged characters per minute.
    - By asking each user which interface feels faster after use.
    - By letting users choose different texts and report their satisfaction.
    because: The experiment collects objective data by using the same input text for all users and comparing their logged speed values in characters per minute.

45/A6  quiz  45/S5  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q Which characteristic makes a research question testable?  [45/S5/F0, 45/S5/F1, 45/S5/F3]
    * It supports objective data collection.
    - It asks whether an interface is good.
    - It depends on overall user preference.
    - It relies on subjective user interpretation.
    because: A testable research question allows a study to collect objective data and draw conclusions independently of users' subjective interpretation.
  Q Why is a research question framed around whether an interface is good generally problematic?  [45/S5/F2, 45/S5/F3]
    - It asks for objective text entry speed.
    - It compares two interfaces on one measurable variable.
    - It is too specific to test.
    * It uses an ambiguous generalized concept.
    because: Questions framed from generalized concepts such as whether something is good are ambiguous and can lead to untestable questions.
  Q Why may a testable question about whether one interface is faster than another not fully answer whether it is better?  [45/S5/F4]
    * Speed and overall quality are different concepts.
    - A faster interface must be better for all users.
    - Speed cannot be measured objectively in a study.
    - Faster and better mean the same thing in usability.
    because: A testable question about speed may answer one aspect, but faster and better are different concepts, so it may not answer the broader better question.
  Q How can a study address a broader untestable usability question while remaining scientifically testable?  [45/S5/F5]
    - By choosing one testable question and treating it as the whole answer.
    - By replacing testable questions with subjective ratings.
    - By asking a single generalized question about overall goodness.
    * By combining conclusions from multiple testable questions about different aspects.
    because: An empirical study can frame multiple testable questions covering different aspects and combine their conclusions to reach a conclusion about a broader untestable generalized question.

45/A7  quiz  45/S6  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 7 concepts)
  Q What is an independent variable in an empirical usability experiment?  [45/S6/F0]
    - A set of values assigned to a factor in an experiment
    - A variable whose value depends on the levels of a factor
    * A variable whose values are assigned and controlled
    - A condition created when a factor is combined with its values
    because: An independent variable, also called a factor, is defined as a variable whose values are assigned and controlled.
  Q What are the levels of an independent variable?  [45/S6/F1]
    - The dependent variables that depend on the factor levels
    - The test conditions produced when factors are combined with values
    * The values assigned to the independent variable or factor
    - The independent variables assigned and controlled in the experiment
    because: The values assigned to an independent variable or factor are called the levels of that independent variable or factor.
  Q In a text-entry interface experiment, what do the levels of the interface factor define?  [45/S6/F2]
    - Two dependent variables, interface and text entry speed
    * Two test conditions, one for the course's design and one for MS Word
    - Two user characteristics used to choose experiment participants
    - Two research questions about text entry speed and overall usability
    because: Factors combined with their levels give the test conditions for an experiment; in the text-entry example, the interface factor's two levels create two test conditions.
  Q Why is text entry rate a dependent variable in the text-entry interface experiment?  [45/S6/F3]
    * Because its value depends on the interface levels
    - Because its values are assigned and controlled to create test conditions
    - Because it is a user characteristic measured in the study
    - Because it is combined with its levels to produce experiment conditions
    because: A dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on an independent variable or factor, specifically on its levels; text entry rate depends on the interface levels.

    - Evaluation of a system using only design documents
    - Observation of simulated users in a virtual environment

    - After requirements have been gathered but before design

45/A10  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 34 concepts)
  Q Why does empirical evaluation come after code testing in interactive system development, and why does code testing not complete the usability assessment?  [45/S0/F0, 45/S0/F1, 24/S2/F0; empirical evaluation, code testing, interactive system development, usability]
    A Empirical evaluation is a stage in interactive system development that evaluates the usability of a developed system with end users. Code testing produces an executable system, but it does not establish whether the system is usable. Usability is how good a system is from the user's point of view, so user-based evaluation is needed after code testing.
  Q Why are quick prototype evaluations insufficient for a final usability assessment, and what form does a conclusive assessment of an implemented system take?  [45/S1/F0, 45/S1/F1; quick prototype evaluation, prototype, usability assessment, fully implemented system, controlled experiment, user behavioral data]
    A Quick prototype evaluations use a limited number of evaluators on prototypes, so they can identify some major usability issues but cannot give a conclusive result about overall usability. A conclusive usability assessment requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with more users. It is conducted through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.
  Q Why is a question such as whether an interface is good weak for empirical research, and how can a study still reach a conclusion about that broader question?  [45/S3/F2, 45/S5/F2, 45/S5/F3, 45/S5/F5; research question, generalized concept, testable research question, untestable question]
    A Asking whether an interface is good can produce divided subjective judgments, so no answer or conclusion can be drawn. Generalized concepts such as goodness are ambiguous and can lead to untestable questions. To balance testability and generalization, an empirical study frames multiple testable questions covering different aspects, reaches reliable conclusions for them, and combines those conclusions to answer the broader untestable question.
  Q In a usability experiment comparing an XR text input interface with Microsoft Word on text entry speed, how are the independent variable, its levels, and the dependent variable related?  [45/S6/F0, 45/S6/F1, 45/S6/F2, 45/S6/F3, 45/S4/F3; independent variable, level, test condition, dependent variable, text entry rate, text entry speed, characters per minute]
    A The interface is the independent variable, also called a factor, and the values assigned to it are its levels. In the text-entry example, the interface levels, such as the course's design and Microsoft Word, create test conditions in which text entry speed is observed. The text entry rate is the dependent variable because it depends on those interface levels, and logging speed as characters per minute provides an objective comparison.

  Q In experiment design, why should the selected participants be representative of all potential users?  [46/S0/F0]
    * To make the conclusions about that user group valid and reliable
    - To reduce the practice effect in a within-subject design
    - To make a between-subjects design easier to manage
    - To ensure the task set covers common interface tasks
    because: Participants are a subset of all potential users, so if the subset is not representative, the conclusions drawn from it are not valid or reliable.
  Q When is it acceptable to use a homogeneous group of experiment participants?  [46/S0/F1]
    * When the system is intended for that homogeneous user group
    - When the system is intended for heterogeneous users
    - When the task sequence is randomized to reduce practice effects
    - When the task set is limited to commonly used tasks
    because: A homogeneous user subset is acceptable when the system is for that homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions about a heterogeneous user group.
  Q In experiment design, what is a user profile?  [46/S0/F2]
    - The objective data collected while participants perform tasks in the interface
    * A set of well-defined characteristics used to define the user before selecting participants
    - The allocation of test conditions to participants in a within-subject design
    - A small subset of tasks that participants perform during the experiment
    because: A user profile is a set of well-defined user characteristics; the user is first defined by that profile, and participants are selected only on its basis.
  Q Why should age and computer-use frequency be considered when selecting participants for a typing task?  [46/S0/F3]
    - Because they indicate whether a random text is representative for the typing task
    - Because they determine whether a between-subjects design is needed
    * Because they can lead to different typing behavior and typing speeds
    - Because they determine how many participants are needed for reliable conclusions
    because: Older people may have different typing behavior from teenagers, and regular computer users are likely to have different typing speeds from infrequent users.

    - Mostly user profile characteristics.
    - Mostly subjective user preference data.
    * Mostly objective task performance data.

    - Because each participant must learn the whole system before starting.

46/A2  quiz  46/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q In a between-subjects experimental design, how are the tasks for the test conditions assigned?  [46/S2/F0]
    - Every participant performs the tasks corresponding to all test conditions.
    * They are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.
    - Tasks are assigned according to participants' user characteristics.
    - Each participant receives the same numbered task sequence.
    because: In a between-subjects design, the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.
  Q Why may a between-subjects design be selected even when a within-subject design is easier to manage?  [46/S2/F1]
    - Because it lets every participant perform all test conditions.
    - Because it requires the same task sequence for all participants.
    * Because the availability of participants and resources may force it.
    - Because it makes the practice effect statistically zero.
    because: Choosing between within-subject and between-subjects designs depends on circumstances, and participant or resource availability may force a between-subject design.
  Q In a within-subject design, what is the practice effect?  [46/S2/F2]
    * An improvement in task performance from repeated practice.
    - A decrease in task performance from repeated practice.
    - A variation in performance caused by differences in user characteristics.
    - An improvement in task performance caused by the interface under test.
    because: The practice effect is an improvement in task performance from repeated practice, and it can confound analysis by making gains appear due to practice rather than the interface.
  Q In a within-subject design, how can the practice effect be reduced?  [46/S2/F3]
    - By assigning tasks according to participants' user characteristics.
    * By randomizing or systematically varying the task sequence.
    - By assigning the same task sequence to every participant.
    - By selecting only the tasks most commonly used in practice.
    because: Random or systematic variation of the task sequence is used to nullify the practice effect in a within-subject design.
  Q What does a Latin square design do in task assignment?  [46/S2/F4]
    * It systematically varies the task sequence by shifting it one position for each successive participant.
    - It gives the same task sequence to every participant.
    - It divides the tasks for all conditions among subsets of participants.
    - It randomly changes the task sequence independently for each participant.
    because: A Latin square design systematically varies the task sequence allocated to each participant, for example by shifting a numbered sequence one position for each successive participant.

  Q In empirical interface studies, what is the relationship between the data collected and the conclusions of interest?  [46/S3/F1]

    * The data come from a sample of users, while the conclusions concern the larger population
    - The data come from one participant, while the conclusions concern the larger population
    - The data come from the sample of users, while the conclusions concern the sample of users
    because: Empirical interface studies obtain data from a sample of users, while the conclusions of interest are about the larger population.
  Q What does a statistically significant difference between observed data values indicate?  [46/S3/F3]
    - It indicates that the participants are the actual population rather than a sample
    - It indicates that the two groups have exactly the same absolute mean value
    * It indicates that the difference is not due to chance but to the tested conditions
    - It indicates that the difference is due to chance rather than the tested conditions
    because: A statistical significance test shows whether an observed difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions; a significant difference is not due to chance.
  Q When comparing two text-entry interfaces, what does the analysis focus on?  [46/S3/F4]

    * The higher mean may be due to chance, so a statistically significant difference is required
    - The higher mean may be due to the tested conditions, so no significance test is required
    - The higher mean may be due to a randomized task sequence, so a longer experiment is required
    - The higher mean may be due to chance, so an absolute mean comparison is required
    because: A higher mean alone may be due to chance; a statistically significant difference between the means is needed to conclude that one design is better in speed or efficiency.

    * The design of the experiment and the nature of the input data
    - The number of participants and the availability of resources

  Q In a statistical significance test, what is the p-value?  [46/S4/F2]
    - The probability that the tested conditions are true
    - The absolute difference between the group means
    * The probability of obtaining the data by chance
    - The probability that the observed result is practically important
    because: The p-value is the probability of obtaining the data by chance, and a lower p-value means the result is less likely to have been obtained by chance.
  Q For an experimental design with one factor having two levels, which parametric test is used for a within-subject design?  [46/S4/F5]

    * Friedman test
    - Kruskal-Wallis test

    - Mann-Whitney U test

46/A7  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 37 concepts)
  Q Why must both the participants and the tasks in an empirical interface study be representative of real users and real use?  [46/S0/F0, 46/S1/F2, 46/S1/F3; sample, user group, task, representative task set, interface, usability]
    A Participants are a sample of the whole user group, so if the sample is not representative, the conclusions drawn from the experiment are not valid or reliable. The experiment can use only a small subset of all tasks, so it should choose from the representative task set of tasks that users commonly use; otherwise the observed data may not support a reliable conclusion about the overall usability of the interface.
  Q When comparing two text-entry interfaces, why is a statistically significant difference between mean text-entry speeds required rather than simply noticing that one mean is higher?  [46/S3/F2, 46/S3/F3, 46/S3/F5; mean text-entry speed, statistical significance test, observed data difference, statistically significant difference, text-entry interface, efficiency]
    A A straightforward conclusion from experimental data can be misleading because an observed data difference may be due to chance, and changing the participants or conditions may produce different data and a different conclusion. A statistical significance test indicates whether the observed data difference is reliable by showing whether it is due to chance or to the tested conditions. Therefore, a higher mean text-entry speed alone is not enough; a statistically significant difference is required to conclude that one text-entry interface is better in speed or efficiency.
  Q What is one practical reason to prefer a within-subject design, and what method can be used to reduce its main confounding effect?  [46/S2/F0, 46/S2/F1, 46/S2/F2, 46/S2/F3, 46/S2/F4; within-subject design, between-subjects design, practice effect, confounding variable, task sequence, Latin square design, interface]
    A In a within-subject design every participant performs the tasks for all test conditions, while a between-subjects design divides the tasks for all test conditions among different participants, so within-subject designs are easier to manage. Repeated practice can improve task performance, creating a practice effect that is a confounding variable and may be mistaken for an effect of the interface. To reduce this effect, the task sequence can be randomized or systematically varied, for example by using a Latin square design, and these variations are supposed to nullify the practice effect.
  Q How does data analysis in stage 4 of the system implementation process support a conclusive usability assessment of a fully implemented system?  [46/S3/F0, 45/S1/F1, 45/S4/F3, 24/S2/F0; data analysis, system implementation process, usability, controlled experiment, empirical data, text entry speed, objective data]
    A Data analysis is stage 4 of the system implementation process, where empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before conclusions are drawn about a design, such as text entry speed. A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data. For a text entry speed question, the experiment can collect objective data by having all users input the same text and logging speed as characters per minute. This allows data analysis to turn objective behavioral data from the implemented system into evidence for a usability judgment.

47/A9  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 40 concepts)
  Q Why did the Majuli virtual reality tour evaluation ask participants to complete the simulator sickness questionnaire before and after exploration, while the questionnaire for environmental presence was completed only after exploration?  [47/S0/F1, 47/S2/F0, 47/S2/F1, 47/S2/F5, 47/S3/F1, 47/S3/F3; usability, presence, cybersickness, simulator sickness questionnaire, questionnaire for environmental presence, exposure, Majuli virtual reality tour]
    A The evaluation aimed to measure usability aspects such as presence and comfort and to identify potential improvements by analyzing cybersickness symptoms. Presence is a psychological state measured by standard questionnaires, and the questionnaire for environmental presence was used as the presence measure after exploration. Because cybersickness depends on exposure, the simulator sickness questionnaire was completed before exploration and after the session so pre- and post-exposure scores could be compared to assess the tour's effect.
  Q How do the presence results and the Welch t-test finding on prior exposure explain the risk of prior virtual reality experience biasing the Majuli virtual reality tour evaluation?  [47/S1/F2, 47/S3/F0, 47/S4/F4, 47/S4/F5, 47/S6/F0; virtual reality experience, pre-experiment training session, prior-experience bias, presence, Welch t-test, statistically significant difference, prior exposure, digital avatar, Majuli virtual reality tour]
    A Twenty-one of the 27 participants had prior virtual reality experience, which may bias the evaluation output, and a pre-experiment training session can reduce or nullify such prior-experience bias. The presence measure gave mostly good results, and a Welch t-test revealed a statistically significant difference between users with and without prior exposure to digital or virtual tours, supporting that prior exposure helps users gain a better experience. Previous visitors gave more favorable presence ratings despite higher expectations, suggesting they felt comfortable with digital exploration, that the system reasonably well mimicked the physical island environment in its design elements, interaction, and implementation, and that the digital avatar was close to reality.
  Q What do the simulator sickness questionnaire box plots and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test together suggest about which parts of cybersickness the Majuli virtual tour affected?     A The box plots showed little difference for nausea and disorientation, indicating that the Majuli virtual tour did not generally induce cybersickness, although total severity and oculomotor severity showed some difference. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test found a statistically significant difference between pre- and post-exposure outcomes for the oculomotor item and the total sickness item. This indicates that the tour design had some effect on total sickness, with the oculomotor component possibly being affected.

  Q How do the sources of requirements in the requirement gathering stage of interactive system development compare with the way requirements are formed in an agile sprint?  [48/S0/F0, 48/S1/F4, 48/S1/F5; requirement gathering, requirement, functional requirement, non-functional requirement, usability requirement, end user, client, sprint backlog, feedback, sprint]

Quick feedback from stakeholders and customers is collected regularly and shared with the team before the next sprint.
  Q Why can deployment in an interactive system development lifecycle take a very long time?  [48/S0/F7, 48/S0/F8, 48/S0/F9, 48/S0/F10; deployment, documentation, interactive system development lifecycle, feasibility study report, software requirements specification, design document, code testing document, usability study report]
    A The interactive system development lifecycle can be rigid in requiring all activities and requirements in a stage to be completed before the next stage starts and before deployment. Deployment is reached only after requirement gathering, coding, code testing, and usability testing, and each stage also needs time for documentation. Before deployment, it requires a feasibility study report, a software requirements specification, design documents, a code testing document, and a usability study report.
  Q Why is code testing not enough to establish that an interactive system is usable, and how does empirical study fit with earlier prototype evaluation?  [48/S0/F4, 32/S4/F2, 43/S2/F0, 43/S3/F0; code testing, usability testing, empirical study, design-prototype-evaluate cycle, quick evaluation, prototype, cognitive walkthrough, heuristic evaluation]
    A Code testing shows that a system is executable, but it does not show whether the system is usable, so an empirical study is needed to estimate usability. In the iterative software development life cycle, early evaluation in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, code testing, and empirical study are the evaluation points. Early quick evaluation can use cognitive walkthrough or heuristic evaluation to inspect a prototype and identify usability problems.
  Q How does agile development keep delivering value without first developing the entire interactive system?  [48/S1/F0, 48/S1/F1, 48/S1/F4, 48/S1/F5; agile development, sprint, delivery, development, testing, training, documentation, feedback, sprint backlog, daily meeting, demonstration, production]
    A Agile development starts small and does not collect all requirements or develop and test the entire system from the beginning. It keeps delivering by adding features over successive deliveries. In a sprint, requirements come from the product sprint backlog and customer and stakeholder feedback, then development occurs, followed by testing including training and documentation and delivery to production, while daily meetings or brainstorming, demonstrations, and quick feedback keep the team able to change quickly.

    - Designing the experience to reduce resource requirements
    - Designing the experience to reduce hardware display latency

    * They make systems less affordable and harder to create for mass markets

    - Reducing resource requirements by accepting a lower immersive experience

    - The distance between two places in the VR tour.

    - The user's preferred VR walking speed.

49/A5  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 26 concepts)
  Q Why can a virtual reality optimization choice that lowers cybersickness still weaken the immersive experience, and why does that matter for user experience?  [49/S0/F1, 49/S1/F3, 49/S1/F4, 8/S2/F0; virtual reality, cybersickness, cybersickness mitigation strategies, presence, immersive experience, user experience]
    A In virtual reality, experience optimization is often about designing the experience to minimize cybersickness. Cybersickness mitigation strategies can make the environment feel more artificial, so they may reduce presence, which is the psychological side of perceiving immersive qualities. Because presence is indirectly related to user experience, the challenge is to reduce sickness without compromising presence.
  Q Why can a system-controlled virtual reality tour feel easier for a user while also making presence harder to achieve, and how can a realistic walking experience address that problem?  [49/S2/F2, 49/S2/F3, 49/S2/F4, 49/S3/F1; system-controlled virtual reality tour, virtual reality tour, presence, realistic walking experience]
    A A system-controlled virtual reality tour is a tour where the system controls the user's movement, often along a predetermined path. It can feel effortless and reduce cognitive demands because the user does not decide how or where to move, but this lack of user involvement makes it less realistic and can defeat presence. A realistic walking experience helps the user feel present rather than controlled by the system and reduces awareness of unrealistic elements.
  Q Why should a system-controlled virtual reality tour that simulates walking match the user's real-world walking speed rather than a constant virtual walking speed, and why is instantaneous matching more realistic?  [49/S3/F2, 49/S3/F3, 49/S3/F4, 49/S3/F5; system-controlled virtual reality tour, system-controlled tour, user input, walking speed, optic flow, real-world walking speed, virtual reality walking speed, instantaneous walking speed, walking speed model, constant optic flow]
    A System-controlled tours typically do not allow continuous user input, so it is difficult to align user input with walking speed or to judge whether the speed provided by the system is natural. Optic flow is the speed at which the visual scene changes, and user movement in a virtual reality tour appears as a constantly changing scene. If the tour assumes walking, its optic flow should match the user's actual or typical real-world walking speed rather than virtual reality walking speed; constant optic flow is not very realistic because people rarely walk at constant speed, so a more realistic tour matches instantaneous walking speed using a walking speed model.
  Q Why does technological optimization in virtual reality connect resource requirements with affordable mass-market products, and how must it be balanced with immersive experience?  [49/S0/F0, 49/S0/F2, 49/S0/F3; virtual reality, extended reality, technological optimization, resource requirement, immersive experience, optimization]
    A Virtual reality optimization can be considered from the perspective of technological optimization, which in virtual reality concerns resource requirements and immersive experience. Extended reality and virtual reality systems are generally resource-hungry, and if their resource requirements are too high, products will not be affordable for the masses. Effective resource optimization therefore means minimizing resource requirements while maximizing the immersive experience without compromising it, which requires balancing the trade-off between resource requirements and immersive experience.
