50/A7  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (23 facts, 59 concepts)
  Q How does the corridor experiment with paintings support the development of a realistic walking behavior model for system-controlled virtual reality navigation?  [50/S0/F0, 50/S0/F1, 50/S1/F0, 50/S1/F3, 50/S1/F4, 50/S1/F5, 50/S2/F0; realistic walking behavior model, corridor experiment, point of interest, system-controlled virtual reality navigation, speed estimation model, empirical research]
    A The corridor experiment is the empirical-research step used to collect real-life data of a user moving from one point to another to propose a speed estimation model. Placed paintings simulated points of interest, and the instruction to stop and click a photograph made participants stop after predefined distances. Analyzing the recorded foot-strike timestamps and distances produces step-frequency data for creating and validating the model. The resulting realistic walking behavior model can then be used for system-controlled virtual reality navigation.
  Q Why is a Fourier series an appropriate mathematical way to model the slow-in-slow-out step-frequency pattern observed in natural walking?  [50/S2/F1, 50/S3/F0, 50/S3/F1, 50/S3/F2, 50/S3/F8; slow-in-slow-out pattern, fourier series, square pulse wave, continuous periodic function, instantaneous step frequency, empirical data]
    A The observed step-frequency pattern starts low, rises, plateaus, and decreases to zero, which resembles a square pulse wave. A Fourier series can approximate continuous periodic functions by adding harmonically related sinusoids, and a practical approximation can be obtained from the first few terms. Thus the slow-in-slow-out pattern is modeled by a Fourier-series expansion whose sinusoid weights are calculated from empirical data to compute instantaneous step frequency.
  Q How does visual gain change the scene-change speed in a virtual tour relative to a user's actual movement speed?  [50/S3/F3, 50/S3/F4, 50/S3/F5, 50/S3/F6, 49/S3/F3; visual gain, virtual tour, actual movement speed, perceived movement speed, optic flow]
    A Optic flow is the speed at which the visual scene changes, and in virtual walking a user generally perceives optic flow more slowly than actual movement speed. Because of this, a virtual tour should not change the scene at the actual walking velocity; instead the perceived scene-change speed should differ from the actual movement speed. The perceived speed is computed as v_visual = g x v_actual, with g typically set to 2.10, so the user perceives natural walking behavior.
  Q What role do randomized order and paired sample t-tests play in validating the natural walking speed model?  [50/S4/F1, 50/S4/F4, 50/S4/F5, 50/S4/F6, 46/S2/F2, 46/S4/F1; randomized order, paired sample t-test, natural walking speed model, practice effect, statistical significance, perceived realism, user preference]
    A The empirical study was carried out to confirm whether the natural walking speed model enhances perceived realism compared with constant speed. Participants experienced constant speed and instantaneous speed in a randomized order, with breaks, to avoid the practice effect and bias in a within-subject comparison. Box plots showed higher realism and user preference for instantaneous speed, and paired sample t-tests with a p-value of 0.05 showed that these differences were statistically significant.

    because: The original graph is completed by leaving existing edges unchanged and adding a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path in G for non-direct pairs.
  Q What are the edge weights of the complete graph G'' that is given to the solver?  [51/S6/F2]
    * The travel time between each pair of vertices.
    - The Euclidean distance between each pair of vertices.
    - The shortest path length between each pair of vertices, without converting it to travel time.
    - The original edge weights of G, unchanged for all pairs.
    because: After completion, the Euclidean-distance weights are replaced by travel times, so G'' is time-weighted rather than distance-weighted.
  Q How is the complete time-weighted graph G'' solved?  [51/S6/F3]
    - By searching for a Hamiltonian path directly in the original graph G.
    * With a standard travelling salesman problem solver, which returns the optimal time and path for G''.
    - By selecting the longest path that stays below the cybersickness time threshold.
    - With a new algorithm designed to minimize cybersickness directly in the original graph G.
    because: G'' can be solved with a standard TSP solver without needing a new algorithm, producing the optimal time and optimal path for the modified graph.
  Q How is the TSP solver's path made valid in the original graph G?  [51/S6/F4]
    - Each edge whose endpoints were directly connected in G is replaced by a hypothetical edge.
    * Each edge whose endpoints were not directly connected in G is replaced by the shortest path between those endpoints in G.
    - Every hypothetical edge is deleted and the remaining edges are returned as the final path.
    - Each hypothetical edge is replaced only by the Euclidean distance between its endpoints.
    because: The solver's path may use hypothetical edges, so the post-processing step expands each such edge into the corresponding shortest path in the original graph.
  Q What limitation can remain in a very large terrain or virtual environment?  [51/S6/F5]
    - The optimal minimum travel time is guaranteed to stay below the cybersickness time threshold.
    * The optimal minimum travel time may still exceed the cybersickness time threshold.
    - The complete graph G'' becomes disconnected because the environment is large.
    - The standard TSP solver cannot return a path for the complete graph G''.
    because: Even after finding the minimum-time path, the travel time can be too long in a large environment, so the cybersickness-limit goal may be defeated.

51/A8  quiz  51/S7  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 22 concepts)
  Q What motivates the use of a time limit in the alternative path optimization approach?  [51/S7/F0, 51/S7/F6]
    * A minimum-time route covering all points of interest may exceed the cybersickness time threshold
    - A minimum-time route covering all points of interest may require a new TSP algorithm
    - A minimum-time route covering all points of interest may be shorter than the cybersickness time threshold
    - A minimum-time route covering all points of interest may cover too few points of interest
    because: The all-points minimum-time approach can still produce a travel time beyond the threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur, so a time limit can be used to maximize covered points within that limit.
  Q How is the virtual world graph initially represented in the minimum-time approach?  [51/S7/F1]
    - Its nodes are points of interest, and every pair of points is directly connected
    - Its nodes are points of interest, and directly connected edges are weighted by natural walking time
    - Its nodes are matched zones, and directly connected edges are weighted by Euclidean distance
    * Its nodes are points of interest, and directly connected edges are weighted by Euclidean distance
    because: In the minimum-time approach, the graph's nodes are points of interest, directly connected edges use Euclidean distance as weights, and the graph need not be complete.
  Q Why are travel times computed for pairs of vertices in the minimum-time approach?  [51/S7/F3, 51/S7/F4]

    * To form a complete, time-weighted graph that can be given to a TSP solver

    * Any hypothetical edges in the path must be removed

51/A10  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (17 facts, 46 concepts)
  Q Why can a realistic natural walking model be used in a cybersickness-aware VR tour optimizer even though the model itself is not an optimization technique?  [51/S0/F0, 51/S0/F1, 51/S0/F2, 51/S0/F3; natural walking model, optic flow, perceived instantaneous walking speed, presence, cybersickness, exposure duration, virtual reality tour]
    A The natural walking model creates a realistic sense of movement by displaying optic flow that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed, and its direct role is to enhance presence rather than optimize the experience. It can still be used in cybersickness-aware optimization because cybersickness is correlated with VR exposure duration, and shorter exposure can reduce or minimize symptom onset. Therefore, the optimizer can keep the tour realistic while the path-planning task limits the exposure duration that contributes to cybersickness.
  Q Why does a VR travel-time optimization algorithm convert an incomplete virtual-world graph into a complete time-weighted graph before using a standard TSP solver?  [51/S3/F0, 51/S3/F1, 51/S3/F2, 51/S5/F2, 51/S6/F1, 51/S6/F2, 51/S6/F3, 51/S6/F4, 51/S7/F3; virtual world, weighted graph, point of interest, travelling salesman problem, complete graph, hypothetical edge, complete time-weighted graph, travelling salesman problem solver, natural walking speed model]
    A The virtual world is represented as a weighted graph whose vertices are points of interest and whose directly connected edges are weighted by Euclidean distance, but the graph need not be complete because not every point of interest has a direct path to another. Standard TSP is posed on a complete graph, so the algorithm adds hypothetical edges with shortest-path lengths and then produces a complete time-weighted graph by replacing edge weights with travel times computed by the natural walking speed model. A standard TSP solver can then find the optimal time and path, and any hypothetical edge in that path is replaced by the corresponding shortest path in the original graph.
  Q Why might a minimum-time path that covers all points of interest still be insufficient for reducing cybersickness, and how does a time-limited path approach address that limitation?  [51/S0/F3, 51/S2/F1, 51/S6/F5, 51/S7/F0, 51/S7/F6; minimum-time approach, alternative path optimization approach, cybersickness time threshold, time limit, point of interest, cybersickness, exposure duration]
    A The minimum-time approach searches for a route that covers all points of interest in the least possible time, but if the virtual environment is large, that optimal time can still exceed the cybersickness time threshold. The alternative approach therefore uses a fixed time limit and searches for a route that covers the maximum possible number of points of interest within that limit. This is useful because cybersickness increases with exposure duration, so bounding the total tour time bounds the exposure that can cause symptoms.

52/A7  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (21 facts, 52 concepts)
  Q Why can a virtual tour that visits every point of interest in the shortest possible time still be unsuitable for a user, and how does the time-constrained optimization goal address this issue?  [52/S0/F0, 52/S0/F1, 52/S0/F2; virtual tour, point of interest, virtual world graph, cybersickness, traversal time, time threshold, virtual reality exposure time, optimal path, time-constrained virtual tour optimization approach]
    A A virtual tour optimized to cover all vertices of a virtual world graph in minimum time may still induce cybersickness if its traversal time exceeds the threshold above which cybersickness occurs. The time threshold is the maximum duration of a virtual reality tour, so movement time, experience time, or virtual reality exposure time should be kept within it because crossing it may cause cybersickness. The time-constrained optimization goal therefore seeks an optimal path that completes within the threshold while covering the maximum number of points of interest.
  Q How do importance and waiting time work together when selecting a virtual reality path that must finish within the time threshold?  [52/S1/F1, 52/S1/F2, 52/S1/F3, 52/S2/F1, 52/S2/F2, 52/S2/F3; node, point of interest, importance, importance function, total importance, waiting time, waiting time function, total waiting time, path, time threshold, virtual reality path optimization model, total completion time]
    A An importance function maps each node to a positive real number, and a larger number indicates higher importance, so importance helps determine which points of interest to cover. The total importance of a path is the sum of the importance values of the nodes in that path. Waiting time is the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with an object at a node, and total waiting time is the sum of those individual waiting times over the path. The virtual reality path optimization model maximizes the path's total importance subject to the constraint that its total completion time, T(P) plus W(P), is less than or equal to the time threshold.
  Q Why does a time-limited virtual tour fit the vehicle routing problem with profit better than a formulation that requires every point of interest to be visited?  [52/S1/F0, 52/S1/F4, 52/S3/F0, 52/S3/F1; tour, node, point of interest, vehicle routing problem with profit, vehicle routing problem, route, profit, importance, optimal path, time threshold, vehicle routing problem with profit solver]
    A When planning a tour to be completed within a given time threshold, visiting every node representing a point of interest is neither mandatory nor always possible. The vehicle routing problem with profit is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit within a time constraint, with profit interpreted as the importance of the nodes. Existing vehicle routing problem with profit solvers can therefore find the optimal path that maximizes total importance within the given time threshold.
  Q How does the optimal-path algorithm convert a virtual environment's original graph into the input needed by a path-planning solver, and how is the solver's result turned into a path in the original environment?  [52/S4/F0, 52/S4/F2, 52/S4/F3, 52/S4/F4, 52/S4/F5, 51/S4/F0, 51/S3/F2, 51/S6/F1; virtual environment, original graph, fully connected graph, complete graph, node, shortest path, edge weight, euclidean distance, natural walking model, travel time, final graph, virtual reality path planning solver, optimal path, modified optimal path]
    A The input is the original graph G, a fully connected graph but not necessarily a complete graph, with importance and waiting time specified for each node. The algorithm first creates the complete graph G dash by replacing every pair of vertices that is not directly connected with the shortest path between those vertices, while directly connected edges keep their Euclidean-distance weights. It then replaces the edge weights with travel times computed using the natural walking model, producing the final graph G double dash whose edges are weighted by travel duration. The final graph, together with each node's importance and waiting time, is given to a virtual reality path planning solver, and the returned optimal path is modified by replacing each hypothetical edge with the shortest path between those vertices in the original graph.

53/A3  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (7 facts, 20 concepts)

  Node | Edge | Point of interest | *Path  (Nodes, edges, and points of interest are elements of the Satra graph, while a path is a route found through the graph rather than an element of the graph itself.)  [53/S1/F0, 53/S1/F3, 53/S1/F6]

53/A4  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (11 facts, 33 concepts)
  Q Why can a virtual reality navigation path that minimizes total time to visit every point of interest in Auniati Satra still be unsuitable for a user, and what does the time-constrained path choose instead?  [53/S0/F0, 53/S0/F1, 53/S0/F5; optimal path approach, optimal path under a time constraint approach, cybersickness, point of interest, time threshold, Auniati Satra]
    A In a very large virtual world, the minimum time to explore all points of interest may still be very large compared with expected user exposure duration, so it may lead to cybersickness. Exploring the whole Auniati Satra by walking can take up to a day, and a full-day VR exposure is not recommended because it would induce cybersickness. The optimal path under a time constraint approach sets an upper time limit, the time threshold, and within that duration it selects a path that covers the maximum number of the most important points of interest, including interacting, inspecting, and navigating between them.
  Q What kinds of information must be captured when converting the Auniati Satra site into a graph for navigation optimization, and why can field study influence which locations become nodes?  [53/S1/F0, 53/S1/F1, 53/S1/F2, 53/S1/F3; graph, node, edge, point of interest, euclidean distance, field study, contextual inquiry, Auniati Satra]
    A The graph represents points of interest as nodes, with at least 25 nodes for the Satra campus, and edges between pairs of nodes are weighted by Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest. Converting the site into a graph is iterative and requires detailed field study and revision. The field study is a contextual inquiry in which people’s travel and stopping behavior are observed and recorded, and residents and Satra committee members are interviewed about typical places and recommended places. A point of interest does not have to be a physical object; for example, a lake is not treated as a point of interest, but the corners of the lake are.
  Q How do a traveling salesman problem solver and a vehicle routing problem with profit solver support different virtual tour goals for Auniati Satra, and what additional information does the vehicle routing problem with profit approach require from the graph nodes?  [53/S1/F4, 53/S1/F5, 53/S1/F6, 52/S3/F0; traveling salesman problem, traveling salesman problem solver, vehicle routing problem with profit, vehicle routing problem with profit solver, time threshold, point of interest, relative importance, maximum wait time]
    A A TSP solver can find a minimum-time path that covers all 25 nodes, while a VRPP solver can find a path within a chosen time threshold that covers the maximum number of the most important points of interest. VRPP treats the importance of nodes as profit and allows not all nodes to be visited within the time constraint. For this second approach, each point of interest needs a relative importance from discussions and an estimated maximum wait time from observed visitor behavior. The maximum wait time is the time a user needs to stop at the point, inspect it, interact with it if possible, and resume navigation.

  Q Why is graphics rendering usually assigned to a dedicated component rather than to the CPU?  [54/S2/F3, 54/S2/F4]

    - To store the generated image in a dedicated area of the computer's memory hierarchy
    * To avoid consuming all CPU time with rendering and keep the system efficient
    - To convert the digital image into analog voltages that activate the display's pixels
    because: If the CPU performed all rendering, its time would be used for rendering and little would remain for other tasks; a dedicated rendering component improves efficiency.
  Q What is the primary responsibility of the display controller in a generic graphics system?  [54/S2/F2, 54/S2/F5]

    - Converting the stored digital image into analog voltages for the screen

    - It creates the two-dimensional image representation of the scene
    - It sends display commands and receives interaction data from the CPU
    * It converts the digital image into analog voltages that control pixel excitation
    because: The video controller uses the data in video memory to convert the digital image into analog voltages needed to activate the screen's pixels.

54/A4  quiz  54/S3  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q Graphic devices are broadly classified into vector scan and raster scan devices based on what?  [54/S3/F0]
    - The amount of video memory available
    - The type of geometric primitives stored
    - The resolution of the display screen
    * The method used for excitation of pixels
    because: Graphic devices are broadly of two types, vector scan and raster scan, determined by the method used for excitation of pixels.
  Q A vector scan device renders an image by  [54/S3/F1]
    * Exciting only selected pixels that represent lines and curves
    - Storing an intensity value for every pixel in a frame buffer
    - Converting the image into analog voltages for the screen
    - Activating all pixels in sequence across the screen
    because: A vector scan device views an image as continuous geometric primitives such as lines and curves and renders it by exciting only selected pixels that represent those primitives.
  Q Why is vector scan display technology less common in mass-produced consumer products?  [54/S3/F2]
    - It needs high precision to activate all pixels in sequence, which makes it costly
    - It needs high precision to convert digital image data into analog voltages, which makes it costly
    - It needs high precision to store one intensity value for each pixel, which makes it costly
    * It needs high precision to target and excite specific pixels, which makes it costly
    because: Vector scan devices require high precision to target and excite specific pixels, making them costly and typically unaffordable for mass production or mass consumption.
  Q In a raster scan device, what does scanning refer to?  [54/S3/F3]
    - The storage of intensity values for all pixels in the frame buffer
    - The excitation of selected pixels that represent lines and curves
    - The conversion of stored digital image data into analog voltages
    * The sequential activation of all pixels, typically left to right and top to bottom
    because: A raster scan device activates all pixels in sequence, typically left to right and top to bottom, and this sequential activation is called scanning or raster scanning.
  Q Why do raster scan displays dominate commercial displays?  [54/S3/F4, 54/S3/F5]
    * Raster scan rendering requires less precision and is much cheaper than vector scan rendering
    - Raster scan rendering requires high precision to target and excite specific pixels
    - Vector scan rendering requires less precision and is much cheaper than raster scan rendering
    - Raster scan rendering is typically affordable only in specialized settings where limited quantities are required
    because: Raster scan rendering requires less precision and is much cheaper than vector scan rendering, so commercial products such as smartphones, televisions, and devices with a computer and display typically comprise raster scan displays.

54/A5  quiz  54/S4  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 19 concepts)

    - Display commands from the host CPU
    - Geometric primitives representing lines and curves
    - The refresh rate of the screen
    * Intensity values as bit strings
    because: The frame buffer stores the intensity values for all pixels, with one memory location per pixel holding the intensity as a bit string of 0s and 1s.
  Q What is the size of a frame buffer in a raster scan device?  [54/S4/F1]
    - The number of primary colors in a pixel
    - The amount of light emitted by a pixel
    - The refresh rate of the display
    * The screen resolution
    because: The size of a frame buffer is the size of the screen and is equal to the screen resolution of a raster scan device.
  Q Why is periodic screen refreshing needed on a raster scan display?  [54/S4/F2, 54/S4/F4]
    * To re-excite pixels whose emitted light decays, preventing fading and distortion
    - To store a new bit string for each pixel in video memory
    - To excite pixels in right-to-left order
    - To change the frame buffer size
    because: The light emitted from excited pixel elements decays over time, so periodic re-excitation keeps the image from fading or appearing distorted.
  Q Why is a higher refresh rate especially preferable for a VR experience?  [54/S4/F6]
    - Because VR displays have more primary colors per pixel
    - Because VR rendering uses vector scan devices
    - Because VR screens use a smaller frame buffer
    * Because the VR screen is much closer to the eyes than in typical computer use
    because: A higher refresh rate is preferable for VR because the VR screen is much closer to the eyes than a screen used at a reasonable distance in typical computer usage.
  Q How is a color perceived from a color display pixel?  [54/S4/F7, 54/S4/F8]
    * By mixing red, green, and blue light in the eye
    - By choosing the strongest emitted primary color
    - By storing the perceived color in the frame buffer
    - By re-exciting the pixel during screen refreshing
    because: A color display pixel contains elements that emit red, green, and blue light at different intensities, and the observed color is the combination of those lights mixed in the eye.

54/A9  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (19 facts, 53 concepts)
  Q Why does virtual reality resource optimization usually concentrate on client-end hardware instead of trying to optimize every kind of resource?  [54/S0/F0, 54/S0/F1, 54/S0/F3, 54/S0/F4, 54/S1/F0; virtual reality resource optimization, resource, resource requirement, client-end hardware, rendering, computer graphics, virtual reality experience]
    A Extended reality and virtual reality require a lot of resources, and the goal of virtual reality resource optimization is to minimize resource requirements while maximizing the virtual reality experience. Because resource types include hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure, optimizing them separately can involve money, availability, policy, and geopolitical issues. Therefore virtual reality resource optimization generally assumes some resources are given and focuses on client-end hardware, which is needed to support rendering and computer graphics, with scene complexity requiring high-end hardware support.
  Q Why is rendering usually moved from the central processing unit to a display controller with a graphics processing unit in a virtual reality client system?  [54/S1/F0, 54/S1/F4, 54/S2/F3, 54/S2/F4; central processing unit, graphics processing unit, display controller, image generation, rendering, computer graphics, client-end hardware]
    A The fundamental problem of computer graphics is to represent objects, synthesize them into a scene, and render that scene on a display. If the central processing unit performed all rendering-related computations, its time would be consumed by image generation, leaving little time for other tasks. Therefore, in a virtual reality client system, rendering is usually passed to a dedicated display controller or graphics card with a graphics processing unit, because client-end hardware must support the complexity of rendering and computer graphics.
  Q Why does a raster scan display need periodic screen refreshing, and why is a higher refresh rate especially important for a virtual reality screen?  [54/S3/F3, 54/S4/F2, 54/S4/F3, 54/S4/F4, 54/S4/F5, 54/S4/F6; raster scan device, pixel grid, pixel, screen refreshing, refresh rate, virtual reality screen]
    A A raster scan device activates all pixels in sequence, so the image is represented by the whole pixel grid. The light emitted by excited pixels decays over time, and because pixels are excited sequentially they can fade out of sync, making the image non-uniform or distorted. Screen refreshing periodically re-excites the pixels to avoid fading and distortion, while the refresh rate measures how many times per second the scene is refreshed. A higher refresh rate is preferable for virtual reality because the virtual reality screen is much closer to the eyes than a typical screen.
  Q How do the input, processing, and output hardware in virtual reality connect to the display chain that creates the final image?  [24/S4/F4, 13/S3/F0, 54/S2/F4, 54/S2/F5, 54/S2/F6, 54/S2/F8; virtual reality, input device, output device, processing device, display controller, video memory, video controller, pixel]
    A In an XR system, input devices track the user's actions and positions, and the XR engine uses hardware resources to generate output data that output devices use to stimulate the user's senses. Virtual reality hardware includes displays, sensors, and computers, and rendering tasks are passed from the central processing unit to a display controller or graphics card. The display controller generates a digital image and sends it to video memory, sometimes called VRAM. The video controller uses that stored data to convert the digital image into analog voltages required to activate pixels.

    * Balancing realistic object detail with efficient pipeline processing
    - Balancing realistic object detail with lighting color accuracy
    - Balancing simplistic geometric approximations with efficient pipeline processing
    because: The objective is to represent objects of varied shapes and sizes with intricate details realistically while keeping later graphics pipeline operations efficient in space and time.
  Q Why can a more complex 3D object representation hurt rendering performance?  [55/S2/F1]
    - It makes the calculation of pixel intensities independent of the representation
    * It makes the calculation of pixel intensities more complex
    - It makes the calculation of pixel intensities occur before object representation
    - It makes the calculation of pixel intensities use a fixed number of operations
    because: Pixel-intensity computation depends on object representation, and more complex representations require more complex calculations, which can cause lags or need expensive hardware.
  Q Why is a single 3D object representation technique not sufficient by itself?  [55/S2/F2]

    - Because every technique is sufficient for every problem
    - Because the technique must be chosen only for the lighting stage
    - Because the technique must be chosen only for the display hardware

  Q Which options are the broad categories of 3D object representation?  [55/S2/F3]
    - Point sample rendering, mesh representation, and octree method
    - Octree method, binary space partitioning method, and constructive solid geometry method
    * Point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation
    - Mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation
    because: The broad categories are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation.

55/A4  quiz  55/S3  "Quick quiz"  (8 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q Which set names the broad object-representation categories?  [55/S3/F0]
    - Point sample rendering, boundary representation, and implicit representation
    * Point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning-based representation
    - Point sample rendering, mesh representation, and spline representation
    - Mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation
    because: The broad representation categories are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning-based representation.
  Q How does point-sample rendering create a synthetic image?  [55/S3/F1, 55/S3/F2, 55/S3/F3]
    * It processes captured real-world points, each carrying attributes, and maps them to pixels.
    - It partitions the scene into spatial regions, then renders only the visible regions.
    - It defines synthetic objects with polygonal surfaces, then renders the connected mesh.
    - It computes pixel intensities from implicit surface equations instead of captured points.
    because: In point-sample rendering, real-world scene information is captured as points with attributes and then processed or mapped to pixels to generate an image, relying on real-world information rather than synthetically defining objects.
  Q What distinguishes boundary representation from other object representations?  [55/S3/F4]
    - Objects are represented directly by the pixel intensities stored in a frame buffer.
    - Objects are represented by dividing the scene into hierarchical spatial regions.
    * Objects are represented by the surfaces that define their boundary, which may be polygonal or curved.
    - Objects are represented as isolated raw data points that carry scene attributes.
    because: Boundary representation represents objects by the surfaces that define the object's boundary, and those surfaces can be polygonal or curved.
  Q What is the role of mesh representation in a rendered computer-graphics scene?  [55/S3/F5, 55/S3/F8]
    - It is the only form used to store raw points captured by range scanners.
    * It is the basic object form, made of connected polygons, to which other representations are converted before rendering.
    - It is a partition of space used to skip invisible objects before pixel calculation.
    - It is a higher-level curve representation that stores spline pieces for curved surfaces.
    because: Mesh representation assumes polygonal surfaces connected into a mesh, and it is the most basic form for objects in a rendered scene; other representations are converted to mesh before rendering.
  Q What trade-off is involved when using a greater number of polygons in a mesh?  [55/S3/F7]
    - Lower storage requirements with fewer surface details.
    * Better surface approximation with a more complex vertex list that is harder to construct.
    - Simpler reconstruction with fewer boundary surfaces.
    - Faster pixel mapping with less realistic object detail.
    because: In mesh representation, more polygons give a better approximation of the surfaces but make the vertex list more complex and harder to construct.

55/A5  quiz  55/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q What type of object representation is spline representation?  [55/S4/F0, 55/S4/F6]
    - A point sample rendering technique
    * A higher-level parametric boundary representation
    - A basic mesh boundary representation
    - A space partitioning tree method
    because: Spline representation falls under parametric representation and is a higher-level boundary representation. Mesh is the most basic boundary representation, while higher-level forms can be implicit or parametric.
  Q Why would a scene designer choose spline representation for curved surfaces?  [55/S4/F1]
    - To capture real-world points using range scanners
    * To create quality rendered scenes for complex artificial surfaces
    - To partition object space into disjoint regions
    - To represent objects by connected polygonal triangles
    because: Spline representation is typically used by developers or designers to construct quality rendered scenes and to represent complex artificial surfaces that cannot be represented by simple polygons or simple polynomial equations.
  Q How is a complete curve represented in a spline?  [55/S4/F3]
    - As connected triangles forming a mesh
    * As several lower-degree polynomial pieces, each called a blending or basis function
    - As a list of raw points from sensors
    - As one higher-degree polynomial covering the entire curve
    because: In spline representation, a complete curve is made of several lower-degree polynomial pieces rather than one higher-degree polynomial, and each piece is a blending function or basis function.
  Q What is the main computational advantage of using lower-degree pieces in a spline?  [55/S4/F2, 55/S4/F3]
    - It captures real-world points directly from sensors
    - It partitions the object's volume into non-overlapping regions
    * Point computation on each curve segment is simpler and less time-consuming
    - It reduces the number of polygons in a mesh
    because: Computing points on a higher-degree polynomial becomes more time-consuming, while spline pieces use simpler lower-degree polynomials to compute points on their curve segments.
  Q What must be true about the polynomial pieces in a spline curve?  [55/S4/F5]
    - They must divide the scene into disjoint spatial regions
    - They must be stored as a complete vertex and edge list
    * They must join smoothly and satisfy required geometric and other properties
    - They must each be a single high-degree polynomial
    because: The polynomial pieces that make up a complete spline curve must join smoothly, and each piece must satisfy certain geometric and other properties.

55/A9  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 47 concepts)
  Q How do the coordinate systems in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline connect object definitions to the final pixel-level description?  [55/S1/F2, 55/S1/F3, 55/S1/F7, 55/S1/F8, 55/S1/F9; three-dimensional graphics pipeline, local coordinate system, modeling transformation, world coordinate system, viewing pipeline, three-dimensional view coordinate system, two-dimensional view coordinate system, device coordinate system, scan conversion, screen coordinate system, pixel]
    A The pipeline first defines objects in their local coordinate systems, then modeling transformation places them into the common world coordinate system to construct the scene. The viewing pipeline maps the scene from the world coordinate system through the three-dimensional and two-dimensional view coordinate systems to the device coordinate system. Finally, scan conversion changes the continuous device-coordinate description into the discrete screen coordinate system, where each pixel has integer coordinates. Together, these transformations use the local, world, three-dimensional view, two-dimensional view, device, and screen coordinate systems to turn object definitions into pixel-level scene descriptions.
  Q How does scan conversion prepare the scene for the frame buffer and pixels of a raster scan display?  [55/S1/F0, 55/S1/F8, 54/S4/F0; scan conversion, device coordinate system, screen coordinate system, three-dimensional graphics pipeline, frame buffer, pixel, video controller, display mechanism]
    A Scan conversion transforms the continuous device coordinate system description, whose points can have real-number coordinates, into the discrete pixel-grid or screen coordinate system, where each pixel coordinate is an integer. The three-dimensional graphics pipeline then computes and stores intensity values for these pixels in the frame buffer, which drives the display mechanism through the video controller. In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory that stores one intensity value for each pixel as a bit string of 0s and 1s.
  Q Why is no single three-dimensional object representation technique sufficient for all rendered scenes, and why is mesh representation especially important at the end of the pipeline?  [55/S2/F2, 55/S2/F3, 55/S3/F8; three-dimensional object representation technique, point sample rendering, boundary representation, space partitioning based representation, mesh representation, pipeline, computer graphics, rendering]
    A A single representation technique is not sufficient because different techniques are available and the appropriate one must be chosen for a particular problem. The broad categories are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation. Mesh representation is the most basic form of representation in computer graphics, and all other representations are converted to mesh representation at the end of the pipeline before objects are rendered.
  Q Why can spline representation make complex curves more practical to compute than representing them with a single high-degree polynomial?  [55/S4/F2, 55/S4/F3, 55/S4/F4, 55/S4/F5; polynomial representation, spline representation, polynomial, polynomial piece, basis function, curve segment, third-order polynomial, spline curve, curve]
    A In polynomial representation, a more complex curve is represented by a higher-degree polynomial, and computing points on a higher-degree polynomial becomes more time-consuming. In spline representation, the complete curve is made of several lower-degree polynomial pieces, each called a blending function or basis function, so simpler polynomials can compute points on each curve segment. The pieces must join smoothly, and third-order polynomials are the most common form used to construct spline curves.

56/A12  quiz  56/S10  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 19 concepts)
  Q In intensity mapping, how do lighting-model intensities differ from device-supported intensities?  [56/S10/F0]

    * The model can produce any value from 0 to 1, while a display supports only a finite set of values.
    - The model produces only integer bit patterns, while a display can represent any real value from 0 to 1.
    - The display supports more intensity values than the lighting model can compute.
    because: A lighting model computes pixel intensities over an infinite 0-to-1 range, whereas a display has only a finite set of supportable intensity values.
  Q Why are successive device-supported intensity levels related by a multiplicative factor r?  [56/S10/F3]
    * Because humans perceive relative changes between intensity values rather than absolute changes in intensity.
    - Because the lighting model computes only absolute intensity values.
    - Because a display stores absolute bit patterns for each pixel.
    - Because a photometer can measure only absolute intensity values.
    because: The multiplicative factor reflects the psychophysiological property that perception is based on relative changes between intensities, not absolute intensity changes.
  Q What information is used to determine the device-supported intensity values?  [56/S10/F1]
    - The number of pixels, the minimum reflection coefficient Ka, and the maximum reflection coefficient Ks.
    - The source intensity vector Is, the colored reflection coefficient vectors, and the ambient intensity.
    - The distance d, the radial coefficients a0, a1, and a2, and the angular limit theta.
    * The number of levels n, the measured minimum intensity I0, and the known maximum intensity value 1.
    because: Device-supported values are determined from the number of levels, the photometer-measured minimum intensity I0, and the known maximum intensity value 1.
  Q How is a lighting-model pixel intensity stored for display?  [56/S10/F4]
    - It is mapped to the next higher table intensity, and that bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.
    * It is mapped to the nearest table intensity, and the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.
    - It is mapped to the next lower table intensity, and that bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.
    - It is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location as the unmodified model intensity.
    because: A table stores the device-supported intensities and their bit patterns; the model intensity is mapped to the nearest table intensity and its bit pattern is written to the frame buffer.
  Q How is the multiplicative factor r for the device-supported intensity levels found?  [56/S10/F1, 56/S10/F2]
    - By taking the average of the minimum intensity I0 and the maximum intensity value.
    * By using the relation In = r^n I0 with the known maximum intensity value.
    - By measuring each intermediate intensity value with a photometer.
    - By using the reflection coefficients of the simple lighting model.
    because: Successive levels are I1 = r I0, I2 = r^2 I0, and so on up to In = r^n I0, so r is obtained from that relation using the maximum intensity.

56/A13  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (6 facts, 51 concepts)
  *Projection | Scaling | Rotation | Translation  (Translation, rotation and scaling are basic modeling transformations; projection is a transformation in the viewing pipeline, not a basic modeling transformation.)  [56/S2/F2, 56/S1/F0]
  Specular reflection intensity | *Source light intensity | Ambient light intensity | Diffuse reflection intensity  (Ambient light intensity, diffuse reflection intensity and specular reflection intensity are the three intensities summed in the simple lighting model; source light intensity is a factor used to compute reflection components, not one of those summed intensities.)  [56/S6/F2, 56/S7/F4]
  Specular reflection coefficient | Diffuse reflection coefficient | *Angular attenuation exponent | Ambient reflection coefficient  (Ambient, diffuse and specular reflection coefficients are the three reflection coefficients of the simple lighting model; the angular attenuation exponent is a spotlight parameter, not a reflection coefficient.)  [56/S7/F1, 56/S8/F3]

56/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 54 concepts)
  Q How does modeling transformation connect object representation with lighting in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline?  [55/S1/F2, 55/S1/F3, 56/S2/F0, 56/S1/F0; object representation, modeling transformation, local coordinate system, world coordinate system, lighting, three-dimensional graphics pipeline]
    A Object representation defines the objects that form the rendered image in each object's own local coordinate system. Modeling transformation then maps those local descriptions into a common world coordinate system so multiple objects can be assembled into a scene. Because lighting takes place in the world coordinate reference frame, it can use the assembled scene after modeling transformation.
  Q Why is the right-to-left order of transformation matrices important when forming a composite transformation matrix?  [56/S4/F0, 56/S4/F3, 56/S4/F6; composite transformation matrix, transformation matrix, basic transformation, matrix multiplication, order of application, world coordinate scene]
    A A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic transformations. It is formed by arranging the individual transformation matrices from right to left according to the order of application: the first transformation applied is placed rightmost, and subsequent transformations are placed to its left. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so an incorrect sequence may produce an incorrect transformed result.
  Q How are lighting models related to shading models, and why can shading be useful in a graphics rendering pipeline?  [56/S5/F0, 56/S5/F1, 56/S5/F2; color computation, lighting model, shading model, depth, quality of experience, computer graphics pipeline]
    A In the computer graphics pipeline, color computation uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects in the scene. If a color is not assigned, depth cannot be perceived and the quality of experience is reduced. Shading models are approximations of the color-assignment methods used by lighting models and involve less computation, so they can reduce computation without compromising the quality of experience.
  Q Why does intensity mapping need device-supported intensity levels when a lighting model has already produced pixel intensities?  [56/S10/F0, 56/S10/F1, 56/S10/F2, 56/S10/F3, 56/S10/F4; lighting model, pixel intensity, intensity mapping, 8-bit display, device-supported intensity value, multiplicative factor, psychophysiological property, table, bit pattern, frame buffer]
    A A lighting model can compute a pixel intensity as any continuous value between 0 and 1, but a display such as an 8-bit display supports only a finite set of intensity values, such as 256 values per pixel. Device-supported intensity values are determined from the number of levels, the minimum device-supported intensity value, and the known maximum value, using a multiplicative factor based on the psychophysiological property that humans perceive relative changes rather than absolute changes. A table stores these device-supported intensity values and their bit patterns, so the continuous pixel intensity is mapped to the nearest table intensity and the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer.

57/A3  quiz  57/S2  "Quick quiz"  (10 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q Which statement correctly describes perspective projection?  [57/S2/F4, 57/S2/F5, 57/S2/F6]
    - Its projectors are parallel to each other.
    * Its projectors converge at a center of projection.
    - Its view volume is a rectangular parallelepiped.
    - Its center of projection is at infinity.
    because: Perspective projection uses projectors that are not parallel and converge at a center of projection. In parallel projection, projectors are parallel, the center is at infinity, and the view volume is a rectangular parallelepiped.
  Q What is the role of clipping in projection?  [57/S2/F2, 57/S2/F3]
    * It discards scene objects outside the view volume before projection.
    - It changes scene objects from world coordinates to view coordinates.
    - It converts an arbitrary view volume into a canonical unit cube.
    - It projects scene objects inside the view volume onto the view plane.
    because: Clipping is the process of discarding objects that are part of the scene but outside the view volume, and it takes place before projection.
  Q Which shape describes the view volume for parallel projection?  [57/S2/F1, 57/S2/F6, 57/S2/F8]
    - A rectangular view plane
    - A normalized unit cube
    - A perspective frustum
    * A rectangular parallelepiped
    because: For parallel projection, the view volume is a rectangular parallelepiped. A frustum is the perspective view volume, a normalized unit cube is a canonical view volume, and a view plane is a rectangular area.
  Q How is a canonical view volume obtained for perspective projection?  [57/S2/F8, 57/S2/F9, 57/S2/F10]
    * By scaling and shearing the frustum into a unit cube.
    - By transforming the world coordinate system into the 3D view coordinate system.
    - By scaling a rectangular parallelepiped into a unit cube.
    - By computing intersections between object and view volume boundaries.
    because: For perspective projection, the frustum is converted to a normalized unit cube using scaling and shearing. Parallel projection only scales a rectangular parallelepiped, while intersection computation describes clipping.
  Q In what order are matrices multiplied to project a point from world coordinates to the view plane?  [57/S2/F13]
    - World-to-view, projection, canonical view volume
    - Projection, canonical view volume, world-to-view
    * World-to-view, canonical view volume, projection
    - Canonical view volume, world-to-view, projection
    because: The point is first transformed from world coordinates to the 3D view coordinate system, then the view volume is transformed to a canonical view volume, and finally the point is projected. The matrices are multiplied in that order.

57/A9  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 42 concepts)
  Q Why does virtual reality place a larger resource burden on the viewing pipeline than augmented reality, and which two operations in the viewing pipeline reduce that burden?  [57/S0/F0, 57/S4/F0, 57/S4/F1; virtual reality, augmented reality, viewing pipeline, clipping, hidden surface removal]
    A Realistic scene generation is more important in virtual reality than in augmented reality and requires more resources in virtual reality. Clipping discards objects or portions outside the view volume before projection, so projection is applied to fewer vertices. Hidden surface removal removes occluded objects, surfaces, or surface points before rendering, reducing computational complexity and supporting a realistic image.
  Q As the fourth stage of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline, how do the viewing transformation and projection transformation work together to produce the image shown on a head-mounted display?  [55/S1/F1, 57/S0/F2, 57/S1/F1, 57/S2/F0; three-dimensional graphics pipeline, viewing pipeline, viewing transformation, projection transformation, three-dimensional view coordinate system, view plane, head-mounted display, three-dimensional scene, two-dimensional display]
    A The viewing pipeline is the fourth stage of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline, and it produces an image on a head-mounted display by selecting a portion of a three-dimensional scene and projecting that portion onto a two-dimensional display or view plane. The three-dimensional viewing transformation transforms the scene from world coordinates to a three-dimensional view coordinate system to simulate looking at the scene with a camera viewing mechanism. The projection transformation then maps objects in the three-dimensional view coordinate system to the two-dimensional view plane.
  Q Why is a perspective view volume converted into a canonical view volume before clipping, and how does that conversion differ from the parallel projection case?  [57/S2/F6, 57/S2/F7, 57/S2/F8, 57/S2/F9, 57/S2/F10; perspective projection, parallel projection, frustum, canonical view volume, unit cube, clipping, naive clipping method, scaling, shearing]
    A For perspective projection the view volume is a frustum, and naive clipping that computes intersections with arbitrarily shaped volumes is computationally intensive. Converting the frustum to a canonical normalized unit cube simplifies pipeline computations. For parallel projection the view volume can be scaled into the unit cube, whereas the perspective frustum requires scaling and shearing and thus more computation.

    - Because a simple lighting model cannot represent realistic VR content
    - Because user input changes the content of a dynamic virtual world
    * Because pixels are rendered near, but not exactly at, points on the original shape

    - The rendered line can exactly match the original line

    - They make motion appear in a static virtual world

    - Because it removes the other rendering stages from the overall computation

    - To remove user interaction so the virtual world remains static
    - To make every pixel exactly match the original shape
    - To avoid anti-aliasing because it adds operations
    because: VR rendering becomes computationally complex because of realistic content, dynamic user input, high interaction, motion, and lighting limitations; the challenge is to handle this without perceived lag or distortion.

    - Undefined sets of tasks that programmers must define and implement for every project.

  Q Which underlying system or platform details are examples of details that using graphics library APIs removes the need to know?  [58/S4/F3]

    - Only memory details, not processor details or operating-system details.
    - Only processor details, not memory details or operating-system details.
    * Processor details, memory details, and operating-system details.
    because: Graphics-library APIs eliminate the need to know every underlying system detail, including processor, memory, and operating-system details, in order to build a graphics application.

58/A8  quiz  58/S6  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 27 concepts)
  Q Why are GPUs especially suited to real-time computer graphics and virtual reality?  [58/S6/F0]
    - Graphics operations are mostly sequential, so a single fast core is sufficient.
    - GPUs have no dedicated memory, so all intermediate data must be kept in CPU memory.
    - GPUs generally are not designed for large-scale parallel activities.
    * Their architecture is designed to exploit the inherent parallelism of highly parallel graphics operations.
    because: Graphics operations are highly parallel, and GPUs are used to exploit that parallelism, while CPUs generally are not designed for large-scale parallel activities.
  Q What happens during the GPU modeling transformation stage?  [58/S6/F3]
    - The CPU completes the vertex transformations and sends finished world-space triangles to the GPU.
    * The same transformation matrix is multiplied with each vertex vector simultaneously, producing transformed triangles from local coordinates to world coordinates.
    - The GPU rasterizes the scene first and then applies the modeling transformation to the resulting pixels.
    - A different lighting matrix is multiplied with each pixel vector sequentially, converting world coordinates into screen coordinates.
    because: Modeling transformation applies transformations such as rotation by multiplying the same transformation matrix with all vertex vectors at once, converting local coordinates into world coordinates.
  Q What computation does the GPU perform simultaneously for multiple vertices to compute vertex color in the simple lighting model?  [58/S6/F6]
    - Depth-buffer comparisons
    - Composite projection matrix multiplications
    * Vector dot products
    - Texture-image lookups
    because: Vertex color is computed by performing vector dot products, as in the simple lighting model, simultaneously for multiple vertices.
  Q What property makes rasterization able to determine pixel colors in parallel?  [58/S6/F8]
    - The color of one pixel depends on the colors of all other pixels in the triangle.
    - A pixel can be processed only after every other pixel in the triangle has been completed.
    * Each pixel can be treated independently from all other pixels.
    - The pixels of a triangle must be processed in a fixed sequential order.
    because: Rasterization exploits the fact that each pixel can be treated independently, so the colors of all pixels can be determined simultaneously.
  Q Which two activities occur in the GPU pixel processing stage?  [58/S6/F9]
    - Rasterization and hidden surface removal
    - Projection transformation and rasterization
    - Vertex assembly and vertex lighting
    * Surface texturing and hidden surface removal
    because: In the GPU pixel processing stage, the two activities are surface texturing and hidden surface removal.

58/A9  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (6 facts, 42 concepts)
  Projection transformation | *Modeling transformation | Viewing transformation | Viewport transformation  (Viewing, projection and viewport transformations are combined in the GPU projection stage; modeling transformation is an earlier graphics-pipeline stage.)  [58/S6/F7, 58/S0/F1]
  Circle | Ellipse | Polygon | *Line  (Circle, ellipse and polygon are the other geometric shapes whose efficient rendering algorithms are more complex than line rendering; a line is the simpler case.)  [58/S2/F7, 58/S2/F9]

[58/S5/F0, 58/S6/F0]

58/A10  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (24 facts, 96 concepts)
  Q Why can a mathematically defined line become distorted after scan conversion, and why is anti-aliasing still computationally expensive?  [58/S1/F0, 58/S1/F1, 58/S1/F2, 58/S3/F0, 58/S3/F1, 58/S3/F2, 58/S3/F3; device coordinate system, display device, pixel grid, scan conversion, line, aliasing, anti-aliasing, quality of experience, pixel intensity, rendering stage]
    A The device coordinate system that defines the viewport is continuous, so coordinate values can be real numbers, but a display device uses a pixel grid whose points have integer coordinates. Scan conversion maps continuous viewport coordinates to the nearest integer-coordinate pixels, so a rendered line approximates rather than exactly matches the original shape. This approximation can produce aliasing, a distortion that can be visible with a change in resolution and can reduce quality of experience. Anti-aliasing removes or reduces that distortion, but it adds further computation to the overall calculation of pixel intensities along with the other rendering stages.
  Q How does the GPU process a scene from vertices to pixels, and which parts of the graphics pipeline can be performed in parallel?  [58/S6/F3, 58/S6/F4, 58/S6/F5, 58/S6/F6, 58/S6/F7, 58/S6/F8; graphics processing unit, scene, triangle, triangular mesh, vertex, modeling transformation, vertex color, dot product, projection stage, rasterization, pixel, parallelism]
    A Most graphics systems assume a scene is made of triangles, and the GPU assembles vertices sent through graphics-library APIs into triangles. It applies modeling transformation by multiplying the same transformation matrix with each vertex vector simultaneously and computes vertex color by performing dot products for multiple vertices at once. The projection stage combines viewing, projection, and viewport transformations into a composite matrix, producing triangles in continuous screen coordinates. Rasterization then determines the pixels overlapped by device-space triangles, treating each pixel independently so pixel colors can be determined simultaneously.
  Q Why can a VR developer rely on SDK and engine layers instead of writing direct low-level graphics code, and where do native rendering libraries fit in the layered architecture?  [58/S4/F0, 58/S4/F1, 58/S4/F2, 58/S4/F3, 58/S5/F0, 58/S5/F1; layered virtual reality software architecture, virtual reality application layer, software development kit, virtual reality engine, native rendering library, application programming interface, operating system layer, hardware layer, graphics processing unit, processor, memory, operating system, graphics application]
    A In the layered VR software architecture, the VR application layer calls the SDK layer, the SDK calls the VR engine, and the engine calls the APIs of native rendering libraries such as OpenGL, Vulkan, and Direct3D. Those native libraries sit on top of the operating system layer, which sits on top of the hardware layer that includes the GPU. Because APIs are predefined functions that perform lower-level tasks, they eliminate the need to know every processor, memory, or operating-system detail while building a graphics application. This lets the developer use the SDK to access the engine and avoid directly accessing the native rendering libraries.
  Q How do depth-buffer hidden surface removal and surface texturing in the GPU pixel processing stage relate to hidden surface removal in the view pipeline?  [55/S1/F6, 57/S4/F1, 58/S6/F9, 58/S6/F10, 58/S6/F11; view pipeline, hidden surface removal, pixel processing stage, depth buffer, depth, surface texturing, texture, pixel, three-dimensional scene, two-dimensional plane]
    A The view pipeline includes hidden surface removal, which removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are occluded from a particular viewer position before the scene is rendered. In the GPU pixel processing stage, hidden surface removal uses a depth buffer that stores the viewer's distance, or depth, for points in the three-dimensional scene before projection onto a two-dimensional plane. The same pixel processing stage also performs surface texturing, replacing computed pixel colors with texture colors from stored texture images. Thus the pixel stage depends on stored depth and texture data for each pixel.

59/A6  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 52 concepts)
  Q Why would the Majuli virtual tour application need different resource optimizations for an Oculus Quest 2 headset and for a smartphone placed in a cardboard virtual reality headset?  [59/S0/F5, 59/S0/F6, 59/S0/F7, 59/S1/F1, 59/S1/F2, 59/S1/F3, 59/S2/F1, 59/S2/F2, 59/S2/F4; Majuli virtual tour application, Oculus Quest 2, smartphone, cardboard virtual reality headset, resource optimization, cloud-based video loading optimization, image compression, video playback, gigabyte]
    A The Majuli virtual tour application is almost 10 gigabytes in size because its collected multimodal content is vast, and its interactive videos and animations make rendering much more demanding than rendering a static image. Regular systems cannot support the application, and the Oculus Quest 2 has less computing power and relatively less storage than a high-end graphics workstation, so the Quest 2 application was optimized by storing videos in the cloud and loading them on demand, reducing it to 5.1 gigabytes. The smartphone/cardboard deployment had to compress images and remove video playback because the full system's size and computation exceed what average smartphones typically support. That strategy reduced the overall size of the Majuli virtual reality system to about 0.7 gigabytes.
  Q How can cloud-based video loading reduce the storage needed on the Oculus Quest 2 while still depending on network conditions for the Majuli virtual tour?  [59/S1/F2, 59/S1/F3, 59/S1/F4, 10/S2/F3; cloud-based video loading optimization, Oculus Quest 2, video, cloud, storage, bandwidth, network coverage, latency, real time, gigabyte, network connectivity]
    A In the Oculus Quest 2 application, videos were not stored locally because videos take up more storage, and a video is loaded from the cloud when the user selects its thumbnail, reducing the deployed application to 5.1 gigabytes. This cloud-based video loading optimization requires high bandwidth, network coverage, and minimal latency to load high-quality videos in real time. Latency is the time delay between a user's movement and the corresponding change in the virtual world, so if network connectivity issues are not resolved, the cloud-based optimization would not be of much help.
  Q How does the three-dimensional graphics pipeline explain why a platform that cannot render the required immersive content cannot host the whole Majuli virtual reality system?  [55/S1/F0, 59/S0/F6, 59/S2/F6; three-dimensional graphics pipeline, rendering, Majuli virtual tour application, Majuli virtual reality system, computational requirement, static image, real-time interactive rendering, platform, device]
    A The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller. Rendering the Majuli virtual tour application's rich multimodal content involves a computational requirement many times higher than rendering a static image and requires fast storage and retrieval support for real-time interactive rendering. When such rendering cannot be performed on the device, deploying the whole Majuli virtual reality system on that platform is not possible.

  Sphere | *Prefab | Capsule | Cube  (Cube, sphere, and capsule are primitive object types; a prefab is a stored template of a game object, not a primitive object type.)  [60/S4/F6, 60/S4/F7]
  Scene construction | *Audio file | Lighting effects | Object definition  (Object definition, scene construction, and lighting effects are stages of the computer graphics pipeline; an audio file is an importable Unity asset, not a pipeline stage.)  [60/S1/F2, 60/S4/F1]

60/A6  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 32 concepts)
  Q How does Unity help a developer build an immersive extended reality experience without implementing every stage of the computer graphics pipeline from scratch?  [60/S1/F0, 60/S1/F2, 60/S2/F2, 58/S4/F0; Unity, extended reality, immersive experience, computer graphics pipeline, application programming interface]
    A Unity is a programming environment for developers who wish to work with extended reality systems, and it is intended to provide implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, including object definition, scene construction, lighting effects, view transformation, and rendering. Its editor allows developers to build and deploy realistic immersive environments without having to master and implement that pipeline. This is similar to using graphics libraries and their APIs instead of implementing pipeline stages from scratch.
  Q Why does Unity provide both a scene view and a game view when a developer is creating a Unity scene?  [60/S3/F2, 60/S3/F3; scene view, game view, game object, scene, camera]
    A The scene view is the developer's interactive view of the scene while it is being built, and it lets the developer select, manipulate, and modify the game objects that comprise the scene. The game view is the final view used to preview the developed scene, and it renders the scene from the camera set by the developer to represent the final published or deployed application.
  Q How do Unity game objects and prefabs help a developer assemble a scene in the Unity editor?  [60/S3/F2, 60/S4/F4, 60/S4/F7; Unity game object, component, Unity prefab, scene view, Unity scene, instance]
    A A Unity game object is a fundamental container for components, and the scene view lets the developer select, manipulate, and modify the game objects that together comprise the scene. A prefab is a template created by configuring and storing a Unity game object. This lets the developer make instances of that game object in a Unity scene.
  Q How does the Unity preference tab reflect the distinction among virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality under the broader term extended reality?  [60/S3/F0, 1/S1/F0, 1/S2/F1, 1/S2/F3; preference tab, virtual reality, augmented reality, mixed reality, extended reality]
    A The Unity preference tab lets the developer select extended reality settings for virtual reality, mixed reality, and augmented reality. Extended reality is an umbrella term covering augmented reality, virtual reality, and mixed reality. Augmented reality is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content, while mixed reality is the broader space between the real and virtual extremes, and Unity's mixed reality setting lets Unity's own environment and the user's real world environment interact.

61/A9  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (17 facts, 53 concepts)
  Q Why might a developer choose Unity's Universal Render Pipeline rather than High Definition Render Pipeline for an XR experience that must run on varied or resource-constrained platforms?  [61/S0/F4, 61/S0/F5, 61/S0/F6, 61/S0/F7; Universal Render Pipeline, High Definition Render Pipeline, resource requirement, high-end platform]
    A URP is a quick and easy way to customize graphics and create optimized graphics across a wide range of platforms. It has many pipeline stages optimized by the pipeline implementation, so it minimizes resource requirements. HDRP is meant for high-fidelity photorealistic graphics but requires a good amount of resources and is typically for high-end platforms with good GPU support.
  Q Why does the camera component matter for both the rendered view and the audio heard by a user in a Unity XR scene?  [61/S2/F9, 61/S2/F10, 61/S2/F11, 61/S5/F5; camera, camera component, view transformation, three-dimensional graphics pipeline, audio listener]
    A View transformation is an important stage in the 3D graphics pipeline, and Unity supports it through its camera concept after the developer sets up a camera. The camera is created by adding a camera component to a game object. The audio listener, which by default is attached to the camera, determines the positioning with respect to which all scene audio is heard.
  Q How do rigid bodies, colliders, and physics materials combine to make object interactions feel physical in Unity, and what changes when a collider is made a trigger?  [61/S4/F0, 61/S4/F2, 61/S4/F4, 61/S4/F6, 61/S4/F7; Unity physics engine, rigid body, collider, physics material, friction, bounce, trigger, collision, gravity]
    A The Unity physics engine simulates physical laws so objects accelerate and respond to collisions, with rigid bodies making game objects respond to gravity. A collider defines the shape of a game object for collisions, and a physics material configures surface friction and bounce. If the collider is configured as a trigger, it does not behave as a solid object and allows other colliders to pass through.
  Q How does Unity's reliance on native graphics libraries relate to the earlier idea that a developer may rely on platform-specific SDKs rather than handling all lowest-level operations directly?  [61/S3/F0, 61/S3/F1, 61/S3/F5, 19/S2/F5; native graphics library, application programming interface, autographics application programming interface, Unity]
    A In practical VR development, a developer may use a platform-specific SDK to handle lowest-level operations, while still needing to understand that SDK. Unity does not implement the graphics pipeline itself; it uses functions of native rendering libraries such as DirectX, Metal, OpenGL, and Vulkan. With the AutoGraphics API option, a Unity player build includes built-in graphics APIs and selects the appropriate one at runtime, so the developer does not manually choose the platform-specific API.

  Q In the editor, how is a prefab attached to a script for runtime instantiation?  [62/S3/F1]
    * After adding the script to a game object, drag the prefab from the project window into the script component's My Prefab field
    - After adding the script to a game object, drag the prefab from the project window into the hierarchy window
    - After adding the script to a game object, drag the script from the project window into the prefab's My Prefab field
    - After adding the script to a game object, drag the prefab from the project window into the scene view
    because: The prefab is attached for runtime instantiation by dragging it from the project window into the script component's My Prefab field.
  Q How is a do-while loop different from a for loop or while loop?  [62/S3/F3]
    * Its condition is checked after the body, so the body runs at least once
    - Its condition is checked before the body, so the body may not run
    - It is used to work directly with a collection of homogeneous data types
    - It is entry-controlled because its condition is checked after the body
    because: For and while loops are entry-controlled because their condition is checked before the body executes, while a do-while loop is exit-controlled because its body executes at least once and its condition is checked after the body.
  Q What is a foreach loop used for in the scripting environment?  [62/S3/F4]
    * Working directly with an array or collection of homogeneous data types
    - Pausing execution and continuing on the following frame
    - Working directly with a single transform component's position, rotation, and scale
    - Checking a loop condition before any loop body executes
    because: A foreach loop can be used for arrays or collections of homogeneous data types, allowing the programmer to work with the collection directly instead of dealing with individual data types.

62/A11  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (1 facts, 25 concepts)
  FixedUpdate function | *Start function | Update function | LateUpdate function  (Update, FixedUpdate, and LateUpdate are Unity regular update event functions; Start is an initialization event function.)  [62/S2/F3]
  OnMouseOver function | *OnCollisionEnter function | OnMouseDown function | OnGUI function  (OnGUI, OnMouseOver, and OnMouseDown are graphical user interface event functions; OnCollisionEnter is a physics event function.)  [62/S2/F3]
  OnCollisionStay function | *OnTriggerEnter function | OnCollisionEnter function | OnCollisionExit function  (OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit are physics event functions for contact being made or broken; OnTriggerEnter is a physics-related event function called for a collider configured as a trigger.)  [62/S2/F3]

62/A12  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (11 facts, 41 concepts)
  Q Why can a basic virtual or augmented reality system be built in Unity without scripting, while a customized experience requires scripting?  [62/S0/F0, 62/S8/F0; Unity, scripting, integrated development environment, programming, virtual reality, augmented reality]
    A Unity's built-in support gives a good-quality experience, but only what the system provides, so a programmer must write scripts to change it. Building and deploying virtual and augmented reality systems are primarily programming tasks, with the amount depending on required functionality. A basic system with basic functionalities can be built without scripting using menu-based integrated development environment support, whereas a customized experience requires scripting and therefore more programming.
  Q How does a C# script attached to a Unity game object let a developer create realistic interactive behavior during game execution?  [62/S0/F3, 62/S0/F4, 62/S2/F4; C#, script, component, game object, interactive behavior, user input, event function]
    A A C# script can be attached as a component to a game object, and creating the script is essentially creating a new type of component that behaves as the developer wants. Once attached, it starts working when the game is executed, allowing the developer to trigger game events, modify component properties over time, and respond to user input. Unity event functions can then impose realistic behavior, such as interactive behavior in graphical user interface event functions.
  Q Why must a gradual opacity fade of a Unity object be implemented as a coroutine rather than a fade function that is called only once?  [62/S4/F1, 62/S4/F3; Unity, coroutine, opacity fade, frame]
    A A coroutine is a method that spreads tasks across several frames by pausing execution, returning control to Unity, and continuing where it left off on the following frame. A gradual opacity fade is visible only when its opacity value is reduced over a sequence of frames so Unity can render the intermediate values. A fade function called only once is not perceivable, so the fade must be defined as a coroutine and started so the change is spread frame by frame.
  Q How does Vuforia enable marker-based augmented reality in Unity when Unity's built-in support for object recognition is limited?  [62/S6/F3, 62/S7/F0, 62/S7/F9, 3/S2/F2; Unity, Vuforia, augmented reality, object recognition, computer vision, marker-based augmented reality, three-dimensional model, marker]
    A Unity's built-in support for object recognition or computer vision operations is not extensive and not very good, so seamless and efficient performance requires external packages. Vuforia is an augmented reality software development kit that supports advanced computer vision for recognizing images and objects and interacting with spaces in the real world. In marker-based augmented reality, a marker triggers the experience, and when the Vuforia engine recognizes the matching image, it displays a three-dimensional model in place of the marker.

  Q How does computer vision relate to the way augmented reality and mixed reality combine real and virtual content?  [63/S1/F0, 1/S2/F1, 1/S2/F3; computer vision, augmented reality, mixed reality]
